title: FACTBOX-Five facts on Slovak cbank governor Sramko
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 31 (Reuters) - Ivan Sramko, governor of the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS), will take a seat on the policy-making Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) after Slovakia becomes the 16th member of the euro zone on Jan. 1.

Following are five facts about Ivan Sramko:

-- Sramko was born on Sept. 3, 1957 in Bratislava and graduated from the Bratislava-based Economic University in 1980. He is married and has three children.

-- He became NBS governor on Jan. 1, 2005, after having served as the bank's deputy governor since Jan. 11, 2002.

-- Sramko joined the central bank from his post as a board member of Tatra Banka, Slovakia's third largest bank and a unit of Austria's Raiffeisen Bank. He was the CEO of small local bank Istrobanka before.

-- Under Sramko's leadership, the NBS repeatedly intervened to slow the appreciation of the Slovak crown. It also propped up the crown in 2006 when it weakened due to investors fearing the new leftist government would dismantle market-friendly reforms and abandon the 2009 euro adoption target.

-- Sramko oversaw Slovakia's entry to the exchange rate mechanism ERM-2 in 2005 and two revaluations of the crown's parity rate within the pre-euro currency grid. Before the unit was irrevocably fixed to the euro in July 2009, Sramko said the exchange rate had a minor impact on inflation and cautioned about the negative effect of too strong a currency on the economy, which the market viewed as a sign he was against an overly strong conversion rate for the euro switchover.

In the end, Prime Minister Robert Fico had advocated as strong a conversion rate as possible, and the fixing rate of 30.1260 crowns per euro was the unit's strongest level ever. (Reporting by Peter Laca; Editing by Michael Winfrey/Tony Austin)

title: Slovak  cbank April  intervention  hit 700 mln euros
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 29 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) said on Tuesday it had bought 700 million euros in one intervention aimed at curbing the crown's strength on April 4.   

The crown, the fastest rising currency in central Europe last year, hit a record of 32.710 per euro on March 19 after its peg to the euro within the exchange rate mechanism ERM-2 was revalued by 8.5 percent.   

The Slovak unit has lost 3.9 percent to the euro since then, partly due to NBS efforts to stem its rise.   

Apart from interventions, the central also flooded the market with excess crown liquidity to make it less attractive for hot money.   

The crown was quoted at 34.035 per euro <EURSKK> as of 1300 GMT, following the central bank Tuesday's decision to leave key two-week repo rate unchanged at 4.25 percent, after two 25 basis-points cuts in March and April.

title: Slovak crown further down on region, euro rumour
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 25 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown weakened through 34.0 level against the euro to a 10-week low on Friday amid easing on global emerging markets and rumours of an early setting of an euro conversion rate for the currency.   

The crown traded in a volatile session as low as 34.130 to the euro, its weakest level since its peg to the euro in the exchange rate mechanism ERM-2 was revalued by 8.5 percent in mid-March, before rebounding slightly to 34.050 as of 1330 GMT.   

It traded at 33.850 late on Thursday.   

"There is profit taking in the whole region, which is mostly felt on the crown," said Tatra Banka trader Milan Cavojec. "It is partly an the effect of the interventions."   

The Slovak central bank sold an estimated 2.5 billion euros on the market in March and April interventions aimed at halting fast firming of the crown. Analysts have said the interventions allowed foreign players to open bigger positions, which has made the crown more vulnerable to changes of sentiment on emerging markets.   

The crown also traditionally comes under pressure in April and May as local companies pay dividends to their foreign shareholders, traders said.   

In addition, several traders in Bratislava said the crown was also affected by a rumour that its conversion rate to the euro will be fixed in the near future.   

Slovakia plans to adopt the euro in 2009, with the conversion rate expected to be set at around mid 2008, but it has yet to meet inflation and fiscal criteria for euro zone entry.   

"The rumour is a factor moving the crown, however incredible or improbable it sounds," a foreign bank trader in Bratislava said.

title: Slovak  cbank March  interventions  hit 1.93bln euros
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 24 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) said on Tuesday it had bought 1.93 billion euros in two direct interventions aimed at curbing the crown's strength in March.   

The bank said it bought 530 million euros on March 8, and 1.4 billion euros on March 20.   

The crown, the fastest rising currency in central Europe last year, firmed to an all-time high of 32.710 per euro on March 19 after its peg to the euro within the exchange rate mechanism ERM-2 was revalued.   

The Slovak unit has lost 2.8 percent to the euro since then, partly due to NBS efforts to stem its rise. Apart from interventions, the central has also flooded the market with excess crown liquidity to make it less attractive for hot money.   

The crown firmed to 33.575 per euro on Tuesday after the central bank cut the key interest rates by 25 basis points, as expected, but it retreated back to 33.680 per euro <EURSKK=> as of 1445 GMT.

title: Slovak Fin Min Says Euro-Zone CPI Criteria Will Be Met In 2H
text:
BRATISLAVA (Dow Jones)--Slovak Finance Minister Jan Pociatek Tuesday said that the country will meet all criteria necessary for euro-zone accession in the second half of 2007.   

Speaking at a conference in the Slovak capital, Pociatek also said that the requirement to maintain stability of the Slovak koruna's foreign exchange rate isn't in jeopardy. [ 17-04-07 0732GMT ]   

The inflation and exchange rate stability requirements are perceived as the only potential threats to Slovakia's euro-zone entry, scheduled for 2009.   

Slovakia posted an annual 2.1% rise in its European Union-harmonized index of consumer prices, or HICP, in March, compared with a 2% year-on-year rise in February.   

Pociatek said that inflationary pressures will continue to abate, providing consumer price growth stays at the required levels in the second half of 2007.   

In order to qualify for the euro-zone membership the Slovak currency has been pegged to the euro since late 2005 within the European Exchange RateMechanism, or ERM II, which allows the koruna to fluctuate plus or minus 15% around its peg to the euro.   

Fueled by rapid economic growth and foreign direct investment inflows, the koruna has firmed strongly since the country's accession to the European Union in May 2004.   

In March, Slovakia was allowed to revalue the koruna-euro peg by 8.5%. The Slovak central bank has also carried out several interventionsin an attempt to ease pressure on the currency.   

Pociatek said despite the recent revaluation of the koruna's peg, the Slovak currency remains stable.   

"Fulfillment the foreign exchange rate stability criterion is not threatened," he added.

title: Emerging  FX -Cautious pre-US data; risk appetite on the up
text:
(Please note that there will not be an emerging FX report from London on Friday April 6 and Monday April 9 due to the Good Friday and Easter holidays.)   

LONDON, April 5 (Reuters) - Emerging currencies shuffled in tight ranges on Thursday despite a rebound in risk appetite, with many investors cautious ahead of U.S. jobs data that could shed light on the health of the world's biggest economy.   

Markets have calmed down as the release of 15 captive British sailors by Iran soothed fears of a standoff between Tehran and the West. Emerging equities <.MSCIEF> jumped 0.2 percent to a new record high, beating levels hit before a Feb 27 fall in China helped trigger a two-week global selloff.   

Now, the focus has shifted back to the U.S. economy, after recent data did little to sway expectations the Federal Reserve will cut interest rates later in the year but left the potential timing of such a move uncertain.   

"The theme today is that high-yield currencies are stronger...the carry theme is alive and kicking," said Olivier Desbarres, currency strategist at Credit Suisse in London.   

"Risk appetite is back -- all the indicators confirm that."   

But Desbarres said strong growth in the euro area and the rest of the world posed the risk that the market was overpricing the possibility of a rate cut by the Federal Reserve and underpricing posible monetary tightening elsewhere.   

"For now equities and high yield currencies are benefiting, but there is a risk the market is being too complacent about Fed rate cuts and the possibility of monetary tightening globally," he added.   

But for now high yield currencies were faring well.   

The Turkish lira <TRY=> was up nearly 0.4 percent at 1.37 per dollar, matching an 11-month high hit in the previous session. Traders said however there is potential for volatility in the run-up to elections this summer.   

South Africa's <ZAR=> rand eased 0.3 percent versus the dollar as traders took profits off a run to five-week highs. The rand will likely be rangebound ahead of an April 12 central bank meeting which may deliver a 50 basis point interest rate rise.   

THIN VOLUMES   

Currency traders said volumes were thinner than usual, with the risk some investors might take profits on emerging market trades before the long weekend. Many central European markets are closed on Friday. The Slovak crown stayed weak after central bank intervention on Wednesday pushed the currency down one percent. By 1045 GMT it had eased 0.2 percent to 33.42 per euro <EURSKK=>, off the two-week high around 33.100 per euro hit just before the central bank stepped in.   

The Polish zloty firmed 0.10 percent to 3.84 per euro and dealers said a close below that level would open the door for a strong zloty next week. The currency hit a three-month high on Wednesday.   

Investors will be watching closely the U.S. non-farm payrolls data due on Friday. The U.S. economy is expected to have added 120,000 jobs in March, up from 97,000 in February, according to a Reuters poll of analysts.   

Carsten Fritsch, currency strategist at Commerzbank in Frankfurt, said a very soft number would hit recovering risk appetite.   

"If we get some very soft U.S. data causing fears of    


recession...or some geopolitical stuff from Iran or other areas
which could cause high risk aversion...then the currencies would
move and we might see a correction," he said.

title: UPDATE 1- Slovak  cbanker says SKK  intervention  effective
text:
(adds more quotes, background)   

BRATISLAVA, April 5 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank's (NBS) intervention to halt the rise of the crown currency on Wednesday morning was effective, NBS board member Peter Sevcovic told Reuters on Thursday.   

"The intervention was certainly effective because the exchange rate depreciated slightly," he said on the sidelines of an economic conference, adding the bank was prepared to act further if needed.   

Dealers in Bratislava said the NBS started selling crowns on the market early on Wednesday when it traded at around 33.100 per euro, its strongest level since March 20 when the central bank last intervened.   

The bank confirmed it had intervened, saying it had done so because of the crown's increased volatility and "unjustified" moves in recent days.   

But it did not comment on the details of the intervention, which weakened the crown as far as 33.700 per euro <EURSKK=>. The unit traded at 33.465 as of 1007 GMT.   

"The intervention was correct because the firming of the crown over the past weeks, and past few days was too fast when compared to economic developments," Sevcovic said.   

"The central bank will keep monitoring, assessing and reacting (to forex market developments)," he added.   

The NBS has repeatedly said the crown should move around the ERM-2 central rate of 35.4424 per euro, which it sees to be near the equilibrium level justified by economic fundamentals.   

The strong crown has helped the NBS to curb inflation as Slovakia moves closer to its aim of entering the euro zone in 2009.   

The NBS cut the main two-week repo rate by 25 basis points to 4.50 percent at the end of March after the rising crown tightened monetary conditions.

title: UPDATE 2- Slovak  cbanker says SKK  intervention  effective
text:
(Adds more central bank quotes, analyst comment, background)   

BRATISLAVA, April 5 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank's intervention to halt the rise of the crown currency on Wednesday morning was effective, board member Peter Sevcovic told Reuters on Thursday.   

Sevcovic also said the NBS agreed with the OECD that energy prices are among key risks to Slovakia meeting the EU's inflation criterion to adopt the euro as planned in 2009, though the bank was not worried by a recent spike in oil prices.   

"The intervention was certainly effective because the exchange rate depreciated slightly," he said on the sidelines of a presentation of the OECD's report on Slovakia, adding the bank was prepared to act further if needed.   

"Every intervention is effective, because you never know whether the exchange rate would have fallen to 32.0 (per euro) if we had not intervened," he said.   

Dealers said the NBS started selling crowns on the market early on Wednesday when it traded at around 33.100 per euro, its strongest level since March 20 when the NBS last intervened.   

The bank said it had intervened because of the crown's increased volatility and "unjustified" moves in recent days.   

But it did not comment on the details of the intervention, which weakened the crown as far as 33.700 per euro. The unit traded at 33.465 as of 1040 GMT.   

"The intervention was correct because the firming of the crown over the past weeks, and past few days was too fast when compared to economic developments," Sevcovic said.   

"The central bank will keep monitoring, assessing and reacting (to forex market developments)," he added.   

The NBS has repeatedly said the crown should move around the ERM-2 central rate of 35.4424 per euro, which it regards as near the equilibrium level justified by economic fundamentals.   

"The fact that market players seem to be reluctant to push EUR/SKK lower prevents the pair from moving further south today," said 4Cast analyst Piotr Matys.   

"But next week we expect the crown to recover further on the back of domestic data and positive sentiment in the region which means the NBS will be forced to intervene again when the pair falls to around 33.10," he said.   

The strong crown has helped the NBS to curb inflation. It cut the main two-week repo rate by 25 basis points to 4.50 percent at the end of March after the rising crown tightened monetary conditions.   

Sevcovic also said inflation risks stemming from high oil prices have decreased with changes in consumption.   

"It is still one of the most serious risks. But if you look one or two years back, energy had a weighting of 22-25 percent in the consumer basket, but ... it's only 17 percent now," he said.   

"If the average oil price is around $75 a barrel ... we are still meeting everything without problems with inflation at 1.8 percent and this does not worry us," he said.   

The NBS predicts end-year inflation using the EU measure at 1.5 percent, below February's record low of 2.0 percent, assuming an average oil price of $65 a barrel, Sevcovic said. The bank will present new forecasts on April 27.

title: Emerging  FX -Risk appetite cautiously returns
text:
LONDON, April 4 (Reuters) - Investors' appetite for risk appeared to be recovering on Wednesday as emerging equity and bond markets bounced to record highs but currencies turned in a mixed picture with central Europe underperforming.   

Intervention by the central bank knocked the Slovak crown down one percent to a week-low on Wednesday, pressuring central Europe but the Turkish lira hit an 11-month high against the dollar while the South African rand traded at a five-week high.   

Emerging equity markets jumped over one percent <.MSCIEF> to a record high, surpassing levels hit just before a Feb 27 fall in China helped trigger a two-week global selloff. Emerging sovereign bond spreads over U.S. Treasuries hit record tight levels late on Tuesday as cash poured into the high-risk sector.   

"Risk appetite is cautiously back," said Koon Chow, emerging markets strategist at  Barclays Capital in London.   

Chow said high-yield currencies like the Turkish lira, the Phillipine peso and the Brazilian real are benefiting most, with investors still nervous about global backdrop.   

"People are adding long EM currency positions only where they can get compensated for risk by the yield. It's mainly global risks -- a combination of oil prices with the ongoing concerns about U.S. equity markets," he added.   

Dealers said volumes were thinner than usual as the long Easter break approaches and there was some reluctance to push currencies much higher in the meantime.   

Recent U.S. economic data has painted a mixed picture with no clarity on when the Federal Reserve could start cutting interest rates and investors are hoping to gauge the health of the economy from Friday's non-farm payrolls data.   

But some easing of tensions with Iran over the release of 15 captive British sailors and general expectations for a U.S. rate cut have helped re-ignite carry trades, in which investors sell low-yield currencies like yen to buy high-yield assets overseas.   

In some countries such as Poland and Mexico, currencies may also receive support from monetary tightening, Chow said, noting local stories within many emerging markets have also improved.   

SLOVAKIA INTERVENTION

In Slovakia, where the currency continues to experience bullish appreciation momentum, the central bank stepped in to check the crown which rose to a two-week high around 33.100 per euro <EURSKK=> pushing the currency down one percent.   

The bank has repeatedly said it will not tolerate rampant crown appreciation, quashing investors who piled in after the crown parity to the euro was revalued 8.5 percent last month.   

The Slovak crown fall hit neighbouring currencies but the forint is near two-week high against the euro and the zloty close to 10-week highs hit on Tuesday.   

"Local (central Europe) markets were spoiled by the intervention by the Slovak central bank. Apart from that, everything looks tip-top as far as risk sentiment is concerned," said  Unicredit CA-IB economist Piotr Chwiejczak. "We also saw yen weakening over the last couple of days, which shows that risk appetite is increasing," he added.   

Another outperformer was the Israeli shekel which, despite the worries on Iran, inched higher to the strongest level since end-May 2001 against the dollar <ILS=>, thanks to equities which have powered higher after a series of rate cuts.   

"The prime conditions are in place for a strong shekel -- an equity rebound and a weak dollar," said Lucy Bethell, strategist at the  Royal Bank of Scotland.

The rand eased 0.20 percent to 7.17 per dollar, failing to pierce resistance around 7.15 -- a five-week high <ZAR=>. The lira hit an 11-month high of 1.3630 before paring gains <TRY>. Turk bonds and stocks have benefited from data showing March inflation below forecast, with equities up one percent <.XU100>.

title: UPDATE 3- Slovak  c.bank  intervenes  to curb crown
text:
(Adds NBS Governor, analyst comments)   

BRATISLAVA, April 4 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) fought again to curb the crown's strength with a second market intervention in as many weeks on Wednesday, and warned it would continue to correct unwanted currency swings.   

Dealers in Bratislava said the NBS started selling crowns on the market early on Wednesday when it traded at around 33.100 per euro, its strongest level since March 20 when the central bank last intervened.   

The bank confirmed it had intervened, saying it was because of the crown's increased volatility and "unjustified" moves in recent days.   

"We are prepared to act in the same way in the future," NBS board member Karol Mrva told Reuters. "If we see too sharp volatility and unjustified moves we are willing and prepared to intervene."   

The NBS would not comment on the details of the intervention, which weakened the crown as far as 33.700 per euro <EURSKK=>. The unit traded at 33.440 as of 1450 GMT.   

NBS Governor Ivan Sramko told reporters that the crown's strength remained excessive: "We are consistently stating that we will use all tools because we think that the crown's exchange rate is overvalued."   

The crown reached a record high of 32.710 after its peg in the ERM-2 exchange rate mechanism, the precursor to euro adoption, was revalued by 8.5 percent on March 16.   

The NBS has repeatedly said the crown should move around the new ERM-2 central rate of 35.4424 per euro, which it sees to be near the equilibrium level justified by economic fundamentals.   

The strong crown has helped the NBS to curb inflation, aiding Slovakia's aim of entering the euro zone in 2009.   

The NBS cut its main two-week repo rate by 25 basis points to 4.50 percent at the end of March after the rising crown effectively tightened monetary conditions.   

"The intervention increased prospects of a further interest rate cut by 25 basis points this month," said Lucia Steklacova, a senior analyst at ING Bank.   

The crown has been rising on the back of accelerating economic growth, which is expected to surpass last year's 8.3 percent in 2007, and because investors expect to profit from further appreciation before euro adoption.   

Mrva reiterated a warning that the crown's conversion rate to the euro, which is expected to be set at around mid-2008, may differ from market levels at that time.   

The central bank appeared determined not to let the crown rise too far but analysts said it would probably manage only to slow its climb.   

"The crown has potential to firm further due to fundamentals in a longer term ... benefiting from higher economic growth and productivity gains," said Maria Valachyova, senior analyst at Slovenska Sporitelna.   

"We see the final conversion rate at 32.50, which could be an equilibrium level when the currency will be fixed (to the euro) roughly in the mid-2008," she said.   

Some market watchers said NBS interventions, estimated to be worth between 2-3 billion euros in total so far this year, were increasing investors' exposure to the crown, which could make the local currency more vulnerable to global capital flows.   

"The crown might become more sensitive to shake-ups on emerging markets, although Slovak fundamentals are good," said Miroslav Plojhar, chief economist at Citibank Czech Republic. (Additional reporting by Martin Santa)

title: Slovak crown weakens, mkt prepares for rate cut
text:
BRATISLAVA, March 23 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown weakened by 0.6 percent versus the euro on Friday as investors cut local exposure to take profits and prepared positions for an expected interest rate cut, dealers said.  

The crown <EURSKK=> was at 33.575 to the euro as of 1525 GMT, compared with 33.375 seen late on Tuesday.  

The crown had a volatile week, first jumping on revaluation of its parity rate in the ERM-2 exchange rate mechanism, then erasing part of the gains due to central bank interventions to stop the rally.  

The Slovak unit rose by over 3 percent after the ERM-2 parity shift, hitting a record high of 32.710 per euro on Monday.  

The central bank then intervened to weaken its currency, saying the new parity rate of 35.4424 per euro was near the equilibrium level justified by economic fundamentals.  

The market now expects the central bank (NBS) to cut interest rates at the monthly monetary policy meeting on March 27, according to a Reuters poll of analysts.  

"The Slovak crown could come under pressure next week, because of the NBS's meeting and possible rate reduction by as much as 50 basis points," said Komercni Banka analysts.  

Some market watchers, however, said the rate decision would be a close call and that the central bank might keep the main two-week repo rate unchanged at 4.75 percent because of persisting inflation risks from energy prices. ------------------ MARKET SNAPSHOT AT 1525 GMT ----------------- Crown/euro <EURSKK=> at 33.575 vs 33.370 on Thursday Crown/dollar <SKK=> at 25.242 vs 24.955 5-yr govt bond <SK5YT=RR> yield 4.242/4.002 pct vs 4.227/4.007 7-yr govt bond <SK7YT=RR> yield 4.394/4.194 pct vs 4.209/3.988 ---------------------------------------------------------------

title: Slovak crown flat, seen stabilising after jumps
text:
BRATISLAVA, March 22 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown was little changed on Thursday morning after a roller coaster ride earlier this week caused by a shift of its peg to the euro within the ERM-2 currency mechanism.  

Market watchers saw the crown stabilising at around current levels in the near future as the market waited for fresh impetus from a central bank monetary policy meeting on March 27.  

The crown traded at 33.370 to the euro as of 0845 GMT, flat from late on Wednesday.  

"For the next few days, at least until the central bank's meeting next Tuesday, we do not expect attempts to move the crown to the stronger side, but rather calmer wait-and-see trading," Slovenska Sporitelna analysts said in a market note.  

The crown jumped by over 3 percent on Monday, reaching an all-time high of 32.710 per euro, after its parity rate in the ERM-2 exchange rate mechanism was revalued by 8.5 percent.  

The Slovak central bank (NBS) intervened on the foreign exchange market and flooded the money market with crown liquidity on Tuesday to weaken its currency.  

NBS's action has weakened the local unit, but Governor Ivan Sramko repeated on Wednesday the crown remained overvalued and that the bank would use its tools to move it to levels justified by economic fundamentals.

title: Slovak crown ticks up again, market eyes c.bank
text:
BRATISLAVA, March 21 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown firmed slightly on Wednesday morning and dealers said investors might try to push the unit up further to test the central bank's determination to prevent the currency from rising too fast. The crown was at 33.300 per euro as of 0915 GMT, compared with 33.400 late on Tuesday.  

The Slovak central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market and flooded the money market with crown liquidity on Tuesday to weaken the crown after the revaluation of its euro peg in the ERM-2 currency grid pushed it to record highs.  

"There will be probably more firming pressure on the crown," said Slovenska Sporitelna trader Vladimir Gajdos.  

Market watchers said the central bank was likely to continue in its fight against what it sees as an overly sharp crown firming.  

"We expect the central bank to keep intervening if the (euro/crown) exchange rate moves down again," said CSOB bank analyst Marek Gabris.  

The central bank's battle against crown firming followed the currency's jump by over 3 percent against the euro on Monday after the unit's parity rate in the ERM-2 exchange rate mechanism was revalued by 8.5 percent.  

The crown has gained 16 percent over the past year, driven by Slovakia's booming economy. Slovak gross domestic product grew 8.3 percent in 2006 and is expected to accelerate further in 2007, helped by foreign direct investments and the country's aim to adopt the euro in 2009.  

The NBS has repeatedly said the new ERM-2 central rate was close to what it considered an equilibrium rate justified by economic fundamentals, and that the crown should move near that level.

title: Hungary forint weakens on  Slovak intervention  talk
text:
BUDAPEST, March 20 (Reuters) - Hungary's forint <EURHUF=D2> eased on Tuesday morning versus the euro taking a breather after a jump on Monday, triggered by the revaluation of Slovakia's crown and speculation about the future of the forint's band.  

Dealers said the forint eased on Tuesday on market talk that the Slovak central bank has intervened to halt the crown's rise, which weakened the crown by about one percent.  

They said there were option deals with knock out levels at and also above the top of the forint's 30-percent trading band at 240.01 which may attract speculation to push the currency stronger, but at the moment interest was two-sided and the currency lacked the momentum to firm.  

At 0855 GMT the forint traded at 246.35 versus the euro, weaker from 245.50 on Monday and also down from opening levels at 245.95.  

Government bond yields were largely steady after a big fall on Monday.  

"I am not sure the spot has enough momentum to push to the end of the band and for speculators to attack the band," a dealer said.  

"But there are lots of option levels at 238 and 239 ... it is really up to London players whether they want to knock these out," he added.  

Another dealer said the next technical support level for the forint was at 241.  

Dealers also said they believed it was not in the interest of the government to let the forint appreciate further as a strong unit hurts exporters which is especially bad at a time when the economy is slowing anyway due to austerity measures.  

The revaluation of the central parity in the crown's band by 8.5 percent reignited speculation on Monday that Hungary could abandon its exchange rate band.  

The band can only be changed or abolished if both the bank and the government agree on it.  

"A more likely scenario in the short run is that the National Bank ends up accelerating its monetary easing, but here too the market may be in danger of expecting too much: the 9x12 FRA is now pricing in 100 bps of rate cuts this year," Citigroup said in a comment.  

"Much will depend on how clearly the government - which defines the exchange rate regime together with the NBH - communicates its intentions with respect to the fx intervention band," he added.  

Hungarian central bank governor Andras Simor and Hungarian central bankers have either refused commenting on the forint band or said the issue was not on the agenda and the government has also said the issue was not on the agenda.

title: FOCUS: Slovak Koruna Revalution Lifts Other CEE Units
text:
PRAGUE (Dow Jones)-Eastern European currencies bounced higher Monday after Slovakia revalued the koruna by 8.5%, sparking speculation that similar moves in the region could follow.  The Czech koruna, Polish zloty and Hungarian forint led gains elsewhere. The forint rose nearly 2% against major currencies as markets speculated that the Hungary central bank would adjust its own, self-devised trading bands.   The standout exception was Latvia, where the Lat continued to come under pressure amid concerns the economy was overheating. The Baltic country's central bank was forced to intervene Monday morning with Lat purchases in the open market to strut the currency.   Slovak authorities, the European Commission and the European Central Bank late Friday agreed that the Slovak koruna should trade in a new band with the E.U.'s Exchange Rate Mechanism II.   

The Slovak central bank is now obliged to intervene to prevent the koruna from firming above SKK30.1260 against the euro, or weakening below SKK40.7588 to the euro. In the region, Slovakia, Latvia, Estonia are considered to be within three years of joining the euro zone. As an interim step, they belong to the ERM II system of fixed currency trading ranges versus the euro. Hungary has a reference trading of its own devising. Appreciating currencies are all good news for the region hoping to keep exports competitive, say economists. The Slovak revaluation was "good news for Slovakia: the economy is growing at near-Chinese rates, and a revaluation, two years ahead of euro entry, is better now than later," said Maya Bhandari at Lombard Street Research. "It isn't such good news for some of other CEE currencies lifted by the stronger koruna - the HUF now looks seriously dear." Countries that wish to join the euro zone must spend at least two years in the ERM, keeping their currencies within a 15% range above or below a central exchange rate against the euro. The koruna has appreciated more rapidly than the currencies of other countries that joined the European Union in 2004. While the Slovak koruna has appreciated by 10% since late 2005, the Czech koruna has strengthened by 3.8%, and the Polish zloty and Hungarian forint have each appreciated by 2.4%. The Slovak currency's strength has come on continued foreign investment, in particular large car manufacturers accessing a qualified and cheap pool of labor, said Beat Siegenthaler, an economist at TD Securities in London. The Latvian Lat, by contrast, has come under unremitting pressure. Lars Christensen, senior analyst at Danske Bank, says the Latvian government needs to do more to control mounting economic imbalances fueled by rampant domestic credit growth of 56% in 2006. "It's worrisome in the sense that it's an indication of the erosion of the credibility of the peg," says Christensen, but added, "The central bank can only do so much."  

By Leos Rousek, of Dow Jones Newswires; leos.rousek@dowjones.com, +420-221-085-272 [ 19-03-07 1552GMT ]

title: Slovak Koruna Revaluation Points To New ERM Flexibility
text:
PRAGUE (Dow Jones)--Slovakia remains on course to join the euro zone in 2009 after it secured the agreement of the European Union to revalue its currency.  

And Brussels' assent to the 8.5% revaluation of the Slovak koruna should set a precedent for other countries that aim to join the currency area early in the next decade, giving them more flexibility to meet one of the key criteria for adopting the euro.  

Slovakian authorities, the European Commission and the European Central Bank late Friday agreed that the Slovak koruna should trade in a new band with the E.U.'s Exchange Rate Mechanism II. The Slovak central bank is now obliged to intervene to prevent the koruna from firming above SKK30.1260 against the euro, or weakening below SKK40.7588 to the euro.  

Countries that wish to join the euro zone must spend at least two years in the ERM, keeping their currencies within a 15% range above or below a central exchange rate against the euro.  

Slovakia first joined the ERM II in November 2005, when the midpoint of the koruna's trading range was set at SKK38.4550. But with its economy growing at rates closer to those of China than the rest of the E.U., and foreign direct investment flooding into the country's auto and electronics industries, the koruna has appreciated steadily since then.  

In recent weeks, only intervention on the part of the Slovak National Bank has prevented the koruna from becoming too strong against the euro.  

"(The revaluation) is the story of economic convergence," said Juliet Sampson, an economist at HSBC in London. "And the economic convergence is currency supportive."  

Slovakia isn't alone among candidates to join the euro zone in seeing its currency appreciate against the single currency in recent years. But the koruna has appreciated more rapidly than the currencies of other countries that joined the European Union in 2004. While the Slovak koruna has appreciated by 10% since late 2005, the Czech koruna has strengthened by 3.8%, and the Polish zloty and Hungarian forint have each appreciated by 2.4%.  

Slovakia appears likely to enter the euro zone in 2009, some three years before either the Czech Republic, Hungary or Poland join the currency area.  

It is alone among that group in being realistically able to target a reduction in its budget deficit to less than 3% of gross domestic product by 2009, while it has recently brought its annual rate of inflation down below the maximum allowed under the Maastricht Criteria.  

The revaluation of the koruna should help keep the inflation below that maximum level, since a stronger currency means that prices of imported goods should fall, or rise less sharply than would otherwise have been the case.  

It is the first time in the history of the ERM II that a currency has been revalued, and may set a precedent for other countries facing a similar dilemma as they near euro-zone membership. But the fact that Slovakia was seeking a revaluation of its currency, rather than a competitiveness- boosting devaluation, makes it much less surprising that it was granted the additional flexibility.  

"They're bending the Maastricht rules and this may imply that the Commission may be a little more lenient on others too in the future," said Nigel Rendell, an economist at Calyon investment bank.  

The firming of the Slovak koruna has been driven by the country's stellar economic performance, with gross domestic product growing by 8.3% in 2006 and 6% in 2005.  

The Czech economy grew 6.1% on the year in both 2006 and 2005. Hungary's GDP expanded by 3.9% in 2006 and 4.2% in 2005, while the Polish economy grew 5.8% last year and 3.5% in 2005.  

Analysts expect the Slovak koruna to continue firming in the near-term, although not excessively.  

"There is no doubt that this is likely to lead to a strengthening of the (koruna) in the near-term," Lars Christensen, the senior analyst at Danske Bank, wrote in a research note.  

At 1400 GMT, the koruna was trading at SKK32.89 against the euro, having weakened from SKK32.02 earlier in the day but strengthened from SKK33.80 late Friday.  

The revaluation raises new questions about the exact rate at which the koruna is swapped for the euro when the country enters the euro zone in 2009.  

The entry rules give ERM members a choice between using the central parity rate or the market spot rate at the time they join the currency area.  

The Slovak central bank officials have so far indicated that the conversion rate would reflect the market rate.  

"They are (Slovakia) under no obligation to join at the market rate," Sampson said.

title: Slovakia Revalues Its ERM II Euro Peg To 35.4424
text:
Corrected March 19, 2007 04:15 ET (08:15 GMT) [ 19-03-07 0801GMT ]  

DOW JONES NEWSWIRES  

Slovakia has revalued its currency by 8.5% against the euro as the country heads for the euro-zone accession.  

The new parity rate - the level at which the koruna is pegged against the euro in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, or ERM II - is set at SKK35.4424, with fluctuations in the koruna restricted to no more than 15% above or below this rate.  

The previous parity rate, set in late 2005, was SKK38.4550 to the euro.  

As reported late last week, when the parity change was first unveiled by the European Commission, the koruna's new peg against the euro will help the Slovak government to keep its economy stable as it aims to adopt the euro in 2009. [ 19-03-07 0819GMT ]  

At 0830 GMT, the koruna was trading at SKK32.02 against the euro, from SKK32.99 earlier Monday and SKK33.8 late Friday.  

The Slovak central bank has also set the new minimum and maximum levels at which it is obliged to intervene to stem the koruna from further firming or weakening at SKK30.1260 and SKK40.7588 to the euro.  

The Slovak koruna has appreciated significantly, fueled by solid foreign direct investment inflows.  

The country's stellar economic growth of 8.3% on the year in 2006 and 6% a year earlier has also bolstered the currency.  

The Slovak Central Bank has intervened several times since mid-2006 to slow the strengthening of the currency.  

Some markets participants expected the bank to consider revaluing the koruna-euro parity peg to create more breathing room for itself.

While the Slovak koruna has appreciated by 10% since late 2005, the Czech koruna has strengthened by 3.8%, and the Polish zloty and Hungarian forint have each appreciated by 2.4%. The Slovak currency's strength has come on continued foreign investment, in particular large car manufacturers accessing a qualified and cheap pool of labor, said Beat Siegenthaler, an economist at TD Securities in London. The Latvian Lat, by contrast, has come under unremitting pressure. Lars Christensen, senior analyst at Danske Bank, says the Latvian government needs to do more to control mounting economic imbalances fueled by rampant domestic credit growth of 56% in 2006. "It's worrisome in the sense that it's an indication of the erosion of the credibility of the peg," says Christensen, but added, "The central bank can only do so much."

title: UPDATE 3- Slovak  crown hits new record, c.bank  intervenes
text:
(Writes through with central bank intervention)   

BRATISLAVA, March 8 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened on the market on Thursday to halt firming of the crown after news of foreign direct investment inflows and accelerating economic growth drove the unit to new record highs.   

The Slovak unit firmed as far as 33.800 per euro, up 1 percent from Wednesday, but several waves of central bank (NBS) interventions knocked it back to 34.080 as of 1550 GMT, dealers said.   

NBS officials were not available for comment on the intervention. Analysts said the NBS looked unhappy with the fast rise of the crown, which was the reason it had cited in the past when it tried to regulate the unit's movements.   

"An intervention was expected, the only question was at what level it would come," said Maria Valachyova, a senior analyst at Slovenska Sporitelna.   

"In the central bank's view, the crown is stronger than what would be justified by fundamentals," Valachyova said.   

The Slovak currency has firmed more than 4 percent against the euro in the past six weeks, from this year's lows of 35.440. The previous all-time high was 34.050 per euro, which the unit hit at the end of December.   

Slovakia posted record gross domestic product growth of 8.3 percent in 2006, driven mainly by investments in its export-oriented car industry. Latest data for industrial output showed a 17.5 percent year-on-year increase in January.   

Investors have been lured to crowns by Slovakia's plan to adopt the euro in 2009, ahead of the neighbouring Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary which are struggling to cut fiscal deficits.   

The Slovak crown received a fresh boost on Thursday as South Korea's  Samsung Electronics confirmed it had picked Slovakia for a new liquid crystal display assembly plant.   

Economic growth is expected to accelerate further this year and beat the 2006 rate as new car assembly plants of  PSA PeugeotPeugeot Citroen and  Kia Motors, completed last year, boost production.   

ERM-2 PARITY TALK   

The crown was the best performing currency in central Europe in 2006, rising by almost 10 percent against the euro. The last intervention on the market by the central bank to knock the crown down from its previous record highs came in December.   

However, it used repo tenders early in 2007 to leave the banks with billions of crown of excess liquidity in order to make the local currency less attractive for hot money.   

"With strong economic fundamentals, it will be difficult for the central bank to undermine bullish sentiment towards the crown," said 4Cast analyst Piotr Matys.   

"The bank is now likely to use its strategy of rejecting part of the bids at 2-week repo auction next week," he said.   

The unit's firming has helped to keep a lid on consumer prices, aiding Slovakia's attempts to meet its euro adoption plan.   

The crown is now 11.8 percent above the central parity rate of its plus/minus 15 percent fluctuation band set in the exchange rate mechanism ERM-2, within which an euro-applicant country must prove currency stability.   

The crown's latest rise has renewed market talk about a possible shift in the parity rate as analysts said economic growth and rising productivity would justify a stronger level.   

"The NBS may try to slow down crown firming for some more time, but fundamentals speak in favour of a parity shift," said CSOB bank analyst Marek Gabris.

title: Slovak crown stronger, seen testing firmer levels
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 21 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown hovered in sight of seven-week highs against the euro in early trade on Wednesday with dealers expecting it to test even stronger levels in the coming days amid positive regional sentiment.   

The crown traded at 34.285 to the euro <EURSKK=> as of 0840 GMT, from 34.330 late on Tuesday and 0.2 percent down from a seven-week high of 34.210 per euro hit in the previous session.   

The crown rose to hit its strongest levels since December 28 on Tuesday, driven by a central bank decision to accept all bids in its liquidity draining repo tender, but failed to build on gains as investors took quick profits.   

"The crown is stable," one Bratislava-based dealer said. "The crown might test lower (firmer) levels, as yesterday's repo tender might be seen as a signal that the central bank will let the unit move to 34.0 per euro."   

The NBS rejected bids in the repo tender to leave the market flooded with excess funds at the beginning of the year to stem the crown, which hit a record of 34.05 per euro in December, a level where directly intervened on the market.

title: Slovak  crown flat after  intervention , upside seen
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 29 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown was quiet on Friday after central bank interventions knocked it off its record highs versus the euro in the previous session, but dealers expected more upward pressure early in 2007.  

The crown traded in a narrow range of 34.440-610 per euro on Friday, dealers said, slightly stronger from 34.640 late on Thursday.  

The Slovak unit, the fastest rising currency in central Europe this year, firmed to an all-time high of 34.050 per euro on Thursday. The central bank then stepped into the market with direct sales of crowns to stop the currency's climbing further.  

The intervention halted the rise, but analysts did not expect it to reverse investors' view on the currency.  

"For the time being, we think the appreciation trend will continue," ING Bank said in a note to clients.  

"Should the central bank add much more crowns back to the market, say to the tune of 2-3 billion euros, we would re-think the trend for the next couple of months."  

This week's gains pushed the crown to 11.5 percent above the crown's central parity and close to the 15 percent upper limit of the ERM-2 currency mechanism, which Slovakia joined a year ago as part of its plan to adopt the single currency in 2009.  

The market now waits to see whether the central bank takes further steps to influence the exchange rate when more investors return to the market after year-end holidays.

title: UPDATE 3-Slovak cbank sells crowns to halt its fast rise
text:
(Adds crown close, new analyst quote on crown outlook)  

BRATISLAVA, Dec 28 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened on Thursday to halt the crown's record-breaking rise, selling the local unit in the currency market for the first time this year.  

The bank said it acted to stop what it saw as an exaggerated move in a thin market.  

"The central bank intervened on the market; the reason was too quick strengthening of the crown on a market with low liquidity," NBS spokesman Igor Barat said. He gave no further details.  

Traders said the central bank stepped in after the crown hit another all-time high at 34.050 per euro and began selling the local currency at around 34.200 to the euro. It sold the crown in several waves pushing it to 34.640 at the close of local trading hours as of 1530 GMT.  

The crown has risen by more than 10 percent this year, outperforming the rest of central Europe, helped by improved emerging market sentiment and Slovakia's buoyant economic growth which reached almost 10 percent in the third quarter.  

"Slovakia is a strong growth story, there is improvement in the balance of payments in prospect and a lot of the concerns over the new government and possible worsening of fiscal policy have not materialised," said Gillian Edgeworth, central Europe economist with Deutsche Bank in London.  

Analysts said they saw more crown firming at least in the first weeks of 2007, unless a major change in investors' mood turned the flow of capital away from emerging markets as such.  

"Domestic fundamentals are clearly positive," said Tatra Banka analyst Robert Prega. "The NBS will be in a difficult position if external factors don't work against the crown's firming trend, as the firming pressure is likely to continue."  

CLOSE TO LIMIT  

This week's gains pushed the crown to 11.5 percent above the crown's central parity and close to the 15 percent upper limit of the ERM-2 currency mechanism, which Slovakia joined a year ago as part of its plan to adopt the single currency in 2009.  

The move sparked market speculation Bratislava may need to revalue the ERM-2 central parity to avoid breaking through the grid's upper limit.  

Earlier this month, NBS head Ivan Sramko played down such a scenario, saying it remained a theoretical option in case there was a risk of a lasting break through the ERM trading band.  

The crown's strength has helped the central bank to curb inflation, seen as the biggest challenge for the euro adoption plan. But Sramko has suggested some of the recent gains could be reversed because they no longer reflected economic fundamentals and were amplified by low year-end liquidity.  

Dealers estimated the central bank may have bought 200-250 million euros in Thursday's intervention, much less than the some 3 billion euros that the central bank sold in the market to stop the fall of the crown after June elections.  

Market sentiment turned after new Prime Minister Robert Fico convinced investors his leftist cabinet remained commited to his centre-right predecessors' euro adoption timetable.  

Analysts said the strong crown had tightened monetary conditions enough to suggest the NBS may be done with raising interest rates, but it was premature to consider an easing.  

The bank has raised its main rate by 175 basis points in four steps to 4.75 percent in 2006.  

"The move (intervention) might support expectations of a rate cut," said Slovenska Sporitelna analyst Michal Musak.  

"But we would be cautious about this, as one of the prime aims of the central bank is to meet the inflation criterion, so we think rate cuts should only come once it is sure of meeting it." (Additional reporting by Patrick Graham in Warsaw)

Ivan Sramko, governor of the Slovak central bank, Friday said that a joint action with the European Central Bank is possible to stem the rapid appreciation of the Slovak koruna.  

"I feel we can reach a solution within the ERMII (exchange rate mechanism framework)...and if necessary by a common action with the ECB," Sramko told reporters, without elaborating, after a central bankers' conference in Warsaw.

BRATISLAVA, Aug 25 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) sold 1.750 billion euros in interventions on the foreign exchange market in July aimed at defending the crown against weakening pressures, the NBS said on Friday.  

The crown fell after a June 17 election as negative sentiment on emerging markets combined with investors worries the new leftist Slovak government will loosen fiscal policy and cause a delay in euro adoption from the target year of 2009.  

The bank also intervened directly on the market in June to the tune of 1.335 billion euros. The total amount of interventions in June and July was in line with analysts estimates of around 3 billion euros.  

The Slovak crown has since stabilised and pared most of the losses from the post-election turbulence, helped by government assurances that adopting the euro in 2009 will be a top priority.  

In addition, the central bank raised interest rates by 50 basis points in July to fight off inflation risks, which also made investment into crown more attractive.  

The crown currently trades at 37.730 to the euro, around 2.5 percent stronger from levels of around 38.700 where the central bank intervened in July.  

The crown has been locked in the ERM-2 exchange rate mechanism, a waiting room for euro adoption, since November 2005 and the country must fulfil a currency stability criterion to be allowed to enter the euro zone.  

The central bank also needs a firming currency to help it slash inflation by early 2008 as Slovakia sticks to its euro adoption timetable.

title: UPDATE 1- Slovak  cbank reserves drop on crown  interventions
text:
(adds background, analyst)  

BRATISLAVA, July 21 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank's foreign currency reserves dropped sharply in the week to July 19, data released on Friday showed, raising questions over the bank's ability to ward off a speculative attack on the crown.  

The central bank (NBS) said in a statement its reserves dropped to $13.060 billion in the week to July 19, from $15.466 billion a week earlier.  

The NBS said the reserves data included changes from several rounds of interventions on the foreign exchange market after investors fled Slovak assets fearing a new leftist government -- elected in mid-June -- will loosen policy.  

The bank did not reveal the exact amount of the interventions and their effect on reserves, though the amounts were roughly in line with market expectations.  

"We will unveil the intervention volumes for June on Tuesday (July 25)," central bank spokesman Igor Barat told Reuters adding July's intervention volumes will be published by the end of August.  

Analysts have said the Slovak central bank's costly battle to defend the currency looks doomed to fail unless the new government convinces investors it is equally serious about swift euro zone membership.  

Newly-appointed Prime Minister Robert Fico, long ambiguous about the euro, recently met with central bank governor Ivan Sramko and sought to calm those fears by declaring his commitment to the euro target and promising to co-ordinate policies with the central bank.  

But markets refused to take those assurances at face value, worried that some of his proposals did not square with budget targets laid out in the country's euro roadmap and that the central bank did not have the reserves to fight speculators for an extended period.  

"With the market already uncertain about the sufficiency of NBS reserves to continue the defence against EUR/SKK upside, the deterioration (of reserves) will intensify rising talk over the possibilty of a speculative attack on the currency," said Craig Otter, an analyst at 4castweb.  

Analysts say a small, open economy such as Slovakia needs a strong currency to slash inflation to the bank's 2.0 percent target from 4.5 percent, and a Reuters poll of analysts on Friday showed most expect the bank to start to use interest rate increases to help in the battle.  

Some economists have said the current market turbulence, against the backdrop of a generally less favourable emerging markets investment climate, showed Slovakia's entry into the ERM-2 grid last November may have been premature.

title: Slovak PM Fico Reiterates Govt Plan To Adopt Euro In '09
text:
PRAGUE (Dow Jones)--Slovakia's new prime minister Robert Fico on Saturday said that his government is determined to enter the European Monetary Union in 2009, reiterating his statement from earlier this week.  

"It is in our utmost interest to adopt the euro as of Jan. 1, 2009," Fico said at a conference after meeting his Czech counterpart Jiri Paroubek.  

"The new Slovak government will do all what is necessary so that we meet all criteria required for the euro adoption in 2009," Fico added.  

Fico's left-of-center SMER-Social Democratic Party, or SMER, won the June 17 poll by attracting disgruntled voters who failed to reap fruits from the former Communist country's transition to a market economy. Fico has promised to undo some of the belt-tightening measures, such as health care payments and welfare cuts, introduced by the former right-of-center government.  

This has prompted concerns among investors that Fico's government will fail to make Slovakia fiscally fit to switch to the euro. [ 15-07-06 0958GMT ]  

The country's central bank has intervened three times since mid-June to support the Slovak koruna to stop the currency sell-offs prompted by investors' fears that adoption of the euro will be delayed because of rising fiscal spending and spiraling inflation.  

Earlier this week, seeking to placate market jitters, Fico also said that his government will coordinate its economic policies with the Slovak central bank and will honor the euro-adoption criteria, including a budget deficit below 3% of gross domestic product, as spelled out in the 1992 Maastricht Treaty on the European Monetary Union.  

While winning most votes in the June polls, SMER didn't get an outright majority in the 150-seat Slovak parliament.  

Fico has stunned most local market participants by forming his coalition government with two fringe parties: the Slovak Nationalists, or SNS, and populist People's Party Movement for Democratic Slovakia, or LS-HZDS.  

Fico's decision to team up with SNS and LS-HZDS has raised criticism of some politicians in the European Union's parliament.  

After meeting Fico Saturday on his first state visit abroad after taking over the Slovak government, the Czech Prime Minister sought to calm down such concerns, saying that the new Slovak government should be judged by its deeds and not impressions.

Prime Minister Robert Fico and Finance Minister Jan Pociatek are scheduled to meet central bank Governor Ivan Sramko at 3 p.m. (1300 GMT) to debate Slovakia's euro adoption plans.

The central bank (NBS) bought crowns in several waves on the market after the unit fell by 0.6 percent to around 38.700 per euro, a far deeper drop than the neighbouring Polish zloty and the Hungarian forint, which were hit by weak regional sentiment.  

The Slovak currency has been jumpy since a June 17 election in which the leftist Smer party beat the centre-right government, praised by the markets for economic reforms, and created a ruling coalition with two fringe factions.  

Apart from a bearish mood on emerging markets, which started in the spring with rising yields on major markets, investors also worry that the new Slovak government will loosen fiscal policy and miss the target of adopting the euro in 2009. "There is a lot of uncertainty on the political scene, and there are a lot of question marks about economic policies at this point," said CSOB Bank analyst Marek Gabris.  

"The market does not like uncertainty."  

The intervention pushed the unit to 38.400 at 1334 GMT, but market watchers said further weakness was possible. "The intervention came because of a too sharp weakening of the crown, the volatility of the crown was too sharp," central bank spokesman Igor Barat said. He declined to elaborate.  

The NBS spent over a billion euros, according to dealer estimates, when it intervened to halt the crown decline in June.  

CONFLICTING SIGNALS  

The government led by leftist Smer chief Robert Fico has sent conflicting signals about its plans, increasing market jitters over the feasibility of Slovakia's euro adoption plans.  

Finance Minister Jan Pociatek said the goal of cutting the fiscal deficit and adopting the euro in 2009 will take priority over measures aimed at strengthening the welfare system.  

But Fico has already snubbed Pociatek's idea to scrap the plan of raising taxes for banks, which kept market watchers guessing whether the finance minister will be able to push through other fiscal ideas.  

The government office said Fico and Pociatek will meet with central bank governor Ivan Sramko on Thursday to debate entry to the euro zone.  

Apart from undesired crown volatility, which could affect the currency stability criterion for euro adoption assessment, the weak crown also conflicts with the central bank's plans to curb upward pressures on consumer prices.  

"It is obvious that the central bank does not agree with the current level of the crown, which also negatively influences inflation," said Lucia Steklacova, a senior analyst at ING Bank.  

Market watchers said they expected the central bank to continue defending the crown as long as Slovakia does not alter the euro adoption schedule.

The crown has been under pressure since a June 17 election amid investor concerns a new leftist government will loosen fiscal discipline and endanger the goal of adopting the euro in 2009.  

Last week a coalition comprising the leftist Smer party, along with two fringe parties was appointed after Smer won the most votes, but not a majority, in a June 17 election.  

Finance Minister Jan Pociatek told Reuters last week the goal of cutting the fiscal deficit and staying on track for adopting the euro in 2009 will take priority over measures aimed at strengthening the welfare system.  

But Smer leader Robert Fico immediately snubbed Pociatek's idea to scrap a plan of raising taxes for banks, which has raised fears in the market that the finance minister will not be able to push through other fiscal plans.

THE POLISH ZLOTY:  

Traders said the U.S. Federal Reserve Board's interest rate hike of 25bp as expected and its surprisingly dovish statement may relieve investors in emerging market assets, because the prospect of still more U.S. rates could have siphoned off funds from emerging markets.  

The zloty weakened against the euro Thursday as the market awaited the U.S. rate decision, due after the close of trade in the Central and Eastern Europe region. Investors worried a rate hike would be accompanied by a hawkish statement. "We live in the world of rising rates, thus there's capital outflow from emerging markets," a trader said. The zloty clawed back some of its losses late Thursday after the Slovak government intervened to support the koruna. The National Bank of Slovakia intervened after the koruna weakened amid political uncertainties. Late Thursday, the zloty traded at PLN4.0775 to the euro, from PLN4.0640 late Wednesday and PLN4.0955 earlier Thursday. Against the dollar, the zloty was at PLN3.2500, from PLN3.2392 late Wednesday and PLN3.2690 during trade Thursday.  

THE HUNGARIAN FORINT: CIB Bank analysts see little chance of a significant correction by the forint against the euro, given Hungary's "far from spotless" fiscal track record. "And the market still lacks confidence in the government's reform package," said. Traders said a Hungarian central bank interest rate hike of between 50 and 75 basis points is needed to stem forint weakness and the inflationary pressure resulting from the currency's slide this week. "The longer the central bank waits, the higher it'll need to hike," a trader said, adding even this intervention would only be a short-term panacea.  

The forint plunged against the euro Thursday in a move dealers said tested the central bank's patience, leaving a rate hike looking inevitable. The currency traded at HUF182.10 early Thursday, sliding to HUF182.60 by midday and to HUF285.00 by late in the day. This compared with HUF280.30 late Wednesday. The currency continued to weaken despite the boost to other regional currencies from the Slovak government's intervention. Zoltan J. Gal, state secretary at the prime minister's office, attributed the sharp weakening of the currency to regional factors. He refused to comment on whether the government had been in consultation with the National Bank of Hungary in the wake of Thursday's drastic weakening. Traders said the forint's weakness was also likely due to investor repositioning before the U.S. rate decision late Thursday, since comments pointing to further U.S. rate hikes from the Fed after its rate decision would be severely negative for Hungary. Hungary, which is struggling with the widest budget deficit in the European Union, could see a further deterioration in its currency and bonds if portfolio investors decide to withdraw from forint assets, traders said.  

THE CZECH KORUNA: Short term, the Czech central bank is expected to leave interest rates on hold, as it did Thursday. CIB Bank analysts predict the bank will next hike rates in the third quarter.  

The koruna weakened against the euro Thursday in the wake of the bank's decision to keep its key two-week repo rate unchanged at 2%, or 75 basis points below the European Central Bank's corresponding rate. The weakness was also driven by the weakness of the Hungarian forint and Slovak koruna against the euro. The Czech currency clawed back some losses late in the day after the Slovak government intervened to support the Slovak koruna. Late Thursday, the koruna traded at CZK28.520 to the euro, from CZK28.390 late Wednesday.  


 
FIXED INCOME 
   

POLISH BONDS are likely to react to the U.S. interest rate decision and accompanying statement in line with an expected rise in German bunds early Friday, traders said.  

Polish government bonds were little changed Thursday, weakening early in the session, before clawing back losses after the Slovak government intervened to support the Slovak koruna. Late Thursday, the yield on the two-year bond was at 5.07%, unchanged from late Wednesday. The five-year bond yield was also unchanged at 5.60%, while the 10-year bond yield was at 5.68%, from 5.73%.  

HUNGARIAN BONDS: U.S. Federal Reserve comments late Thursday are interpreted as favorable for emerging markets, and Hungarian bonds could recover Friday, a trader said.  

Hungarian government bonds weakened Thursday as the forint fell against the euro, making a Hungarian central bank rate hike look inevitable, the trader said. Yields on the short end of the curve rose between 20 and 25 basis points compared with late Wednesday, while yields on the long end rose between 15 and 20 basis points.  

CZECH BONDS: The 25 basis point U.S. interest rate hike Thursday should strengthen core bond markets including German bunds Friday, with the positive influence spilling over into trade of Czech paper, CSOB analyst Jan Cermak said.  

Czech government bonds were little changed Thursday. Trade was light until the Czech National Bank announced it was keeping its key interest rate on hold. Yields on the short end of the curve fell by between three and four basis points immediately after the bank's announcement, although they later crept back up. The Czech rate decision had little effect on the long end of the curve. Long-dated bonds tend not to move in tandem with those in core markets such as German bunds. "There seemed to be some bullishness on the steep end of the curve," Cermak said. Late Thursday, the average yield on the benchmark 10-year bond was at 4.11%, from 4.10% late Wednesday.

IN WARSAW: The market may bounce back Friday, with local funds likely to push the WIG20 index up to achieve a successful close to the end of the month, the quarter and the half-year period, a trader said. That is, "Unless we see some huge supply by foreign players after the Fed's (interest rate) decision," he said.  

The WIG20 ended down 0.3% at 2842.29 Thursday as some foreign investors took profits after the index's two-day rally. "Foreign sellers are the major culprits," the broker said. Among losers, TPSA ended down 2.7%, PKN down 2.7% and Prokom down 1.2%.  

IN BUDAPEST: Upward momentum is expected to last, even if the Fed decides to hike interest rates. "The sellers are still here, but they are not as strong as in the past weeks," an EIB trader said. Even if the market opens lower Friday - since Federal Reserve comments might be negative for emerging markets - Budapest stocks are set to rise further later in the day, he said..  

The BUX index ended up 1.1% at 20390.31 Thursday as buying interest returned after several weeks of heavy selling, mirroring a recovery by U.S. stocks, the trader said. Among gainers, OTP Bank ended up 2.6%, Magyar Telekom up 2.5% and Egis up 4.4%.  

IN PRAGUE: Further gains by CEZ shares is possible Friday, given the shares are proving attractive to foreign buyers this week, traders said.  

The PX index ended up 1.9% at 1346.3 Thursday, driven mainly by a rally by CEZ shares, which ended up 4.1% with a volume of almost CZK3 billion. "The only reason for the rise on the index was foreign buyers on CEZ," an Atlantik Financial Markets trader said. With the exception of Zentiva, which ended up 3.5%, most stocks were little changed. "Zentiva is the same story as CEZ - foreign buyers see opportunity," he said. Among stocks moving sideways in thin trade were Philip Morris, which ended up 0.6%, Komercni Banka, up 0.1%, and Cesky Telecom, up 0.7%. [ 06-30-06 0101ET ]  


OVERNIGHT NEWS 
   

The lower chamber of Czech parliament failed to elect a speaker Thursday, prolonging the political deadlock created by this month's general elections.  

Poland's premier asked former Finance Minister Zyta Gilowska to become his deputy Thursday, inviting her to rejoin the government after she resigned last week over allegations she collaborated with the country's communist-era secret police. Gilowska was seen as a leading advocate for fiscal responsibility in Prime Minister Kazimierz Marcinkiewicz's government and news of her departure triggered a sell-off of Polish zlotys and Treasury bonds. Markets quickly recovered, however, after Pawel Wojciechowski, a pro-market, U.S.-trained economist, was named as her replacement.  

Slovakia's Smer-Social Democracy Party and its two right-wing coalition partners have agreed on the distribution of ministerial seats in the country's new government, party leader Robert Fico said on Thursday.  

Romania's prime minister on Thursday proposed withdrawing his country's 890 troops from Iraq, citing security concerns and the operation's cost, but the president called the idea "unacceptable."  

Serbia's government is drafting an "action plan" to locate and capture top war crimes suspect Gen. Ratko Mladic, a senior government official said Thursday.

Investors fear a Smer government with the fringe parties, lukewarm to the 2009 euro entry plan, could loosen fiscal discipline and expand public deficits.

title: Slovak  crown stabilises after c.bank  intervention
text:
BRATISLAVA, June 22 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown weathered a bearish regional mood on Thursday better than its neighbours following supportive central bank intervention on Wednesday, dealers said. The crown ended at 38.230/250 to the euro, down from 38.190/220 late on Wednesday.  

Other central European currencies fell by more, with the Polish zloty losing 0.4 percent and the forint weakening by half a percent.  

Dealers said investors in the Slovak market were wary of approaching 38.550 per euro, the point where the central bank bought crowns directly on the market on Wednesday.  

Emerging markets are suffering because rising yields in major markets are drawing investors away.  

But even if the emerging markets stabilise, the Slovak crown will have little room to strengthen until the the next government is formed, traders say.  

"There wasn't much interest in the market today and that could last for weeks," said Boris Somorovsky, a trader at Tatra Banka. "In the meantime we'll probably follow regional swings, but within a narrow range."  

The leftist Smer party won a weekend election and it now leads negotiations to form a government. The market will be edgy as long as participation of two fringe parties in the ruling coalition remains a possible option.  

The crown fell to seven-month lows on Wednesday after Smer signalled it might rule with far-right nationalists and a party of former autocratic Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar.  

Smer has also held talks with two centre-right parties, the Christian Democrats and the ethnic Hungarians.  

Investors fear a Smer-led government with Meciar and the nationalists, will push up the fiscal deficit, scare off investors and postpone plans to adopt the euro in 2009.

title: UPDATE 3- Slovak  crown below ERM-2 parity, c.bank  intervenes
text:
(Adds central bank intervention)  

 BRATISLAVA, June 21 (Reuters) - Post-election jitters and a sour mood on emerging markets pushed the Slovak crown below its central rate in the ERM-2 exchange rate mechanism on Wednesday, prompting intervention by the central bank to support the currency.  

 The crown <EURSKK=> <SKK=> has weakened sharply since the leftist Smer party won a general election on Saturday and started talks on forming a government with two fringe parties, an option analysts have called the worst case scenario to emerge from the election.  

 On Wednesday the crown fell below its central rate of 38.455 to the euro in midday trading for the first time since the central European country entered the waiting room for the single European currency in November 2005.   

 The central bank (NBS) stepped in and bought crowns at around 38.550 to the euro, dealers said. The NBS confirmed it intervened, but declined to give any levels for its deals.  

 "The reason was a significant weakening of the crown in recent days, which we considered unjustified by economic fundamentals," NBS spokesman Igor Barat said. "We will remain ready to react if needed in the future."  

 The intervention pushed the crown to 38.300 per euro. Traders said the central bank continued to buy the crown on the market in several waves. The crown is now trading some 4.2 percent below its all-time highs of 36.925 it hit on March 1.  

 The currency fall comes after Smer leader Robert Fico said he did not see any major obstacles to forming a government with the centre-left HZDS party of former authoritarian Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar and the far-right nationalists.  

 EURO WORRIES  

 Investors worry a Smer-led government, especially if joined by the nationalists and Meciar, would raise spending, spook foreign companies and delay euro zone entry from 2009 as intended.  

 "The market got scared of the possibility of a Smer coalition with HZDS and the nationalists," said Lucia Steklacova, a senior analyst at ING Bank. "Such an alternative would probably mean looser fiscal policy, higher inflation and subsequently higher interest rates."  

 Smer will hold talks later on Wednesday with three centre-right parties that formed the previous government of Prime Minister Mikulas Dzurinda.  

 But the market reacted negatively to Fico's statements that ruling with Dzurinda's junior partners, the ethnic Hungarians and Christian Democrats, was not his most attractive option.  

 Such a government would be welcomed by the market as it was expected to have a more moderate economic agenda, analysts said.  

 Fico, whose party won a third of parliament's 150 seats, has pledged to cancel a business-friendly flat 19 percent tax rate and undo other reforms introduced by Dzurinda's cabinet to ease the pain of economic transformation from the past four years.  

 Analysts said the turmoil could last weeks as Fico faces tough talks to forge a viable coalition. Dzurinda could still stay in power if Smer fails to find enough allies among the six parties that have entered parliament.  

 "A combination of Smer, HZDS and the nationalists would quite possibly lead to a delay of euro adoption from the targeted year 2009, which would be negative for the market," said Slovenska Sporitelna analyst Michal Musak.

As inflation in Slovakia is rising, CSFB believes the Slovak central bank favors SKK-strength and probably hoped to engineer some currency appreciation with earlier-than-expected ERM2 adoption.

title: UPDATE 2- Slovak  c.bank  intervenes  to support falling crown
text:
(Writes through with analyst comments)  

BRATISLAVA, Oct 13 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened directly on the foreign exchange market on Thursday to support the ailing crown, with analysts saying the move was aimed at safeguarding inflation goals set for euro adoption.  

The Slovak crown has been under pressure in the past few weeks, hit by a domestic government crisis followed by economic and political turmoil in neighbouring central European states.  

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) stepped into the market on Thursday when its unit fell to 39.200 per euro, the weakest level since May. The intervention was the first central bank action designed to support the crown in more than five months.  

"The reason for the action was that the development of the exchange rate did not correspond with economic fundamentals," central bank spokesman Igor Barat said.  

"We have stated in the past that we will be ready to correct excessive movements which are not in line with developments of the economy, and this is still valid."  

The central bank's action brought the crown through the psychological level of 39.000 per euro, and the unit traded at 38.910/930 to the single currency in afternoon activity.  

The NBS last intervened to support the crown at the end of April when capital flight from emerging markets pushed central European currencies sharply down.  

The central bank had repeatedly intervened in the opposite direction in the first three months of the year when it fought hard to slow down the crown's rapid appreciation.  

INFLATION IN MIND  

The central bank did not elaborate on the reasons for the intervention, but analysts said the monetary body wanted to prevent risks to its inflation goals that could arise if the currency was too weak for too long.  

"The exchange rate channel has the fastest impact on inflation," said Maria Feherova, senior analyst at Slovakia's largest bank, Slovenska Sporitelna.  

The NBS has a target to keep inflation under 2.5 percent at the end of next year, which would be slowing price growth from the annual 4.3 percent expected in December in 2005.  

The end-2007 inflation limit is 2.0 percent, which the central bank expects will be enough to meet the euro adoption condition.  

Analysts have long expected the Slovak crown to firm as the new European Union member has shown fast economic growth and rising inflows of foreign direct investment in the past few years.  

Slovakia has also become the frontrunner for euro adoption among the four largest new EU members from central Europe as its neighbours struggle with ballooning fiscal deficits.  

But the crown is frequently influenced by capital flows on bigger markets in the region and it often follows movements of the Polish zloty or Hungarian forint.  

"The crown weakening did not come because of a worsening of Slovakia's economic picture," Feherova said. "The recent moves were caused solely by external factors."
