title: UPDATE 1- Slovak  cbank  intervenes  in  FX  to sell crowns again.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 12 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Monday for the second time in less than a week, renewing its fight against the appreciating crown currency.    

On Thursday the bank had staged its first direct market intervention since May 2003. Last week's action pulled the unit down by 0.7 percent to the euro, but the currency resumed firming on Monday, sparking the second intervention round.    

Central bank spokesman Igor Barat confirmed the intervention but declined to comment on details.    

Traders estimated the central bank might have bought around 200 million euros on Monday, a similar amount to Thursday's intervention.    

"The central bank was on the market.... It is paying from around 39.800 up to 39.900 (per euro)," one foreign bank dealer said.    

Monday's intervention round pushed the crown to 39.950 per euro, from slightly under 39.800 where the bank started to sell crowns on the market. The Slovak currency closed the session at 39.900-940 per euro, compared with 39.855/875 at the open.    

The Slovak central bank has been battling what it calls excessive firming of the crown for more than a year. It has repeatedly said the unit's advance was too quick and that it could hurt exporters in the new European Union member state.    

Despite its attempts, the crown has firmed by over three percent to the euro since the beginning of this year.    

The bank has repeatedly said the surge has been driven by inflows of speculative capital, but many analysts say foreign investors are attracted mainly by Slovakia's good economic fundamentals. Central bank officials have said there will be some room for crown firming in the long term, but they said the bank would continue using its monetary arsenal to prevent sharp market moves.    

Traders and analysts said the central bank might slow crown appreciation and keep the unit at weaker levels for some time, but they expected new firming pressure in the coming weeks on the back of more foreign capital inflow.

BRATISLAVA, July 12 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market on Monday to weaken the crown, dealers said.    

It is the second central bank intervention in less than a week as it continues to fight appreciation pressure on the crown. The bank conducted the first direct market intervenetion since last May on Thursday.    

Traders said they saw the central bank selling the crown on the market in a range of 39.800-39.900 per euro.

title: Slovakia - Factors To Watch on July 12.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 12 (Reuters) - Here are news stories, press reports and events to watch which may affect Slovak financial markets on Monday:    

 STATS OFFICE TO RELEASE MAY RETAIL SALES DATA    

 The Statistics Office will release retail sales and industrial wages data for May.    

 ECON MINISTER TO HOLD NEWS CONFERENCE    

 Economy Minister Pavol Rusko will hold a news conference on incentives contracts with car producers PSA Peugeot Citroen and Kia Motors.    

 CBANK WANTS TO REGULATE CROWN FIRMING    

 The Slovak central bank said its direct market intervention on Thursday to halt crown firming fulfilled the desired goal, adding that it was ready to continue correcting excessive market movements.    

 Karol Mrva, the member of the central bank's policy-making board in charge of foreign exchange policy, told Reuters the bank intervened because the crown had firmed too quickly since the start of the year.    

 JUNE INFLATION SLOWS IN LINE WITH FORECASTS    

 Slovak inflation slowed in June due to the fading impact of EU entry and the lower cost of oil and analysts said the data confirmed the benign nature of price growth in the country.    

 Inflation was 0.2 percent month-on-month in June, putting the annual rate of price growth at 8.1 percent, the Slovak Statistics Office said.    

 Core prices, which exclude the impact of administrative measures, such as increases in regulated prices and excise taxes, rose 0.3 percent on the month and 2.3 percent on the year. June inflation was in line with market expectations.    

 STATS OFFICE PUTS BACK MAY TRADE DATA RELEASE    

 The Slovak Statistics Office said it would release foreign trade data for May on July 15, instead of the originally scheduled date of July 12.    

 The office said it had pushed back the release of trade statistics because it needed more time than expected to process the data according to European Union's harmonised trade monitoring mechanism.

title: UPDATE 1-Slovak cbank says to keep fighting quick SKK gains.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 9 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said on Friday its direct market intervention on Thursday to halt crown firming fulfilled the desired goal, adding that it was ready to continue correcting excessive market movements.   

The central bank intervened directly in several waves on the foreign exchange market in the first such action since May last year, and dealers estimated it might have bought around 150-200 million euros.   

Karol Mrva, the member of the central bank's policy-making board in charge of foreign exchange policy, told Reuters the bank intervened because the crown had firmed too quickly since the start of the year.   

"It is premature to asses the result... In any case, we think that it fulfilled the purpose why we carried it out. And, of course, we stay prepared to continue," Mrva said.   

The monetary body has been fighting against crown appreciation for over a year, saying the currency's advance was not justified by fundamentals and that excessive gains could be dangerous for the small open economy that joined the EU in May.   

The central bank has said the rally is fuelled by hot-money inflows, but analysts said the main reason behind the rise were Slovakia's solid economic fundamentals, which would drive the unit to stronger levels again over the longer term.   

Mrva said there was "some room" for crown appreciation in the longer term, but he added the bank wanted to regulate the pace of the currency's movement.   

"In medium-term horizon, we see that the crown has tendency to strengthen... this is an attempt to regulate the pace," he said.   

"There will be some room for firming of the crown, but the pace since the beginning of the year was too quick. If it had continued for the rest of the year, it would have significantly exceed that room."   

Mrva did not comment how quickly was the central bank willing to let the crown appreciate.   

The crown has held between 39.900-40.000 per euro, its main reference currency, since the interventions, well off its record highs of 39.675 that it hit before the central bank bank stepped into the market on Thursday.

title: Emerging  FX -Slovak crown steadies, rand off highs.
text:
LONDON, July 9 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown steadied on Friday though the market was wary after Thursday's intervention from the central bank to weaken it, the South African rand shied away from multi-year highs hit earlier this week.  

The Slovak central bank intervened directly on the foreign exchange market on Thursday after the crown touched new record highs around 39.70 per euro , but the euro's recovery was capped at 40.  

Market sources said the intervention had been large by Slovak central bank standards, estimated to have been around 200 million euros.  

"(Thursday's) intervention was certainly aggressive, though I wouldn't rule out further action today given that the crown only weakened by 0.6 percent from its intra-day highs," said Caio Natividade, emerging markets strategist at Deutsche Bank.  

Another analyst said the central bank might be willing to buy up to 500 million euros to try and get the euro/crown rate back above 40 and create more of a two-way market.  

By 0905 GMT, the crown traded down 0.13 percent at 39.95 to the euro .  

The crown has been driven up over the past 12 months by strong foreign investment inflows helped by perceptions that the country is progressing faster down the path of economic reform than its peers in central Europe.  

The central bank has been trying to slow the pace of crown appreciation to maintain the country's competitiveness for over a year through a combination of interest rate cuts and market interventions.  

Slovak June consumer price inflation data on Friday had minimal market impact. The core rate was broadly in line with market forecasts rising 0.3 percent on the month for an annual rate of 2.3 percent.  

RAND RALLY PAUSES  

The South African nudged down from near five-year peaks hit on Thursday after the market failed to break under the six-per-dollar level.  

"There's a good amount of corporate interest to buy dollars around six and it's also significant that euro/dollar has come off its highs," said one UK bank dealer.  

The rand tends to track movements in the euro, the currency of its main trading partner, though it has also found strength from soaring gold prices this week. South Africa is the world's largest bullion producer.  

"People have done well profit-wise out of the rand this week and are taking the opportunity to lock in those gains."  

However, the dealer added that pullbacks were likely to be limited to the 6.15/20 level before the market makes another assault on the six level.  

The rand was down around 0.5 percent at 6.08 per dollar .  

The Russian rouble edged down, but the pace of its fall slowed after Thursday's sharp losses saw it hit six-month lows versus the dollar.  

Downward pressure has come on the back of growing concerns over the health of the banking sector. Earlier this week Guta bank, one of the country's largest by assets, had to stop paying out to depositors after running out of cash.  

It is now in talks for a takeover by the state-owned Venshtorgbank.  

Russia's biggest private bank, Alfa-bank, said on Thursday it was introducing a 10 percent commission for depositors who withdraw cash early.  

Local dealers said the rouble was finding support from a $200 million offer at 29.16 per dollar, suspected to be from the central bank, helping to contain the market in the face of strong dollar demand from households.  

The central bank has $88.3 billion in its reserves from which it can draw to support the rouble.  

Rouble for settlement in the next trading session traded at 29.1165 per dollar .

title: Slovak  crown weakens after c.bank  FX intervention .
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 8 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown weakened by
0.7 percent on Thursday after the central bank repeatedly
intervened directly on the market to stop the unit's rise,
dealers said.
    The crown firmed through a psychological level of 39.700 per
euro at around midday on buying by a foreign bank, hitting an
all-time high of 39.675.
 
    The jump pushed the central bank to buy euros on the market
in its first direct forex intervention since May last year.
    The bank carried out several waves of interventions, with
dealers saying they saw it selling crowns in a range of
39.700-39.950 per euro.
    "They are still in the market, they are trying to drive the
  

crown over 40.000. It is not working so far, but it does not  

seem that they are going to stop now," one foreign bank trader  

said.  

Dealers said the central bank action would keep the market  

more cautious in the coming days and they expected the crown to  

hover at around 39.900-40.000 per euro in the near future amid  

fears of new interventions.  

However, analysts viewed the current weakening as providing  

a good entry level for long-term players who expect more crown  

gains due to Slovakia's strong economic growth, government  

reforms and expectations of foreign direct investments.  

"Our long-term recommendation to buy SKK is still valid...  

In case of a second intervention wave, we recommend to further  

increase open positions," Komercni Banka said in a market note.

title: UPDATE 2- Slovak  c.bank  intervenes  to weaken crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 8 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank stepped up its fight against the firming of the crown on Thursday with several waves of direct intervention on the foreign exchange market, dealers said.   

The monetary body has been fighting against crown appreciation for over a year, saying the currency's advance was too quick and that excessive gains could be dangerous for the small open economy that entered the European Union in May.   

The central bank has said the rally is fuelled by hot-money inflows, but analysts said the main reason behind the rise were Slovakia's solid economic fundamentals, which would drive the unit to stronger levels again over the longer term.   

"The central bank was in the market, it was buying (euros) in waves... I would say they were buying in a range and that the top of the action was at around 39.900," one dealer at a foreign bank unit in Bratislava said.   

The crown firmed through a psychological level of 39.700 per euro at around midday on buying by a foreign bank.   

Some traders said they saw the crown's all-time high at 39.666 per euro, but one foreign bank said that rate was an off-market price and the real record high where deals were made was 39.675.   

Traders estimated the bank might have bought 150-200 million euros in its interventions.Central bank officials were not immediately available for comment.   

Thursday's intervention, the first direct action on the market since May last year, came after a series of verbal warnings that the bank would use all its tools to prevent unjustified crown jumps.   

The bank has cut rates by 150 basis points in three moves this year to make the crown less attractive for carry players taking advantage of higher interest rates compared with other markets. The two key week-repo rate is now 4.50 percent.   

CROWN DOWN, SEEN RISING AGAIN   

The direct market action weakened the crown to around 39.950 per euro in afternoon trading, and analysts expected investors to become more cautious in the next few days.   

"The intervention is typically designed to slow the pace of crown appreciation rather than reverse the trend. They may try and drive (euro/crown) up to 40.10, but after that they'll probably step back," said Koon Chow, emerging markets strategist at CSFB.   

"Equally the market may wait a bit before creeping back into long positions."   

However, dealers said the central bank might only slow the crown firming because it was based on Slovakia's strong economic growth - at 5.5 percent in the first quarter - improving trade balance and expectations of foreign direct investment projects.   

"This halts the firming for some time. It will not change the trend, and we might see new highs again, but it will not be as quick as recently," said ING Bank trader Jan Rafaj. (Additional reporting by James Thornhill in London).

title: Slovak  crown ticks up, eyes c.bank  intervention .
text:
BRATISLAVA, June 15 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown opened
slightly stronger in a nervous market on Tuesday with dealers
waiting to see whether the central bank would act against the
currency's rise.
    The crown hit an all-time high of 39.780 per euro on Monday
on the strength of the economy's performance and a government
victory in European Parliament election.
 
    But the central bank talked it lower again, suggesting it
could cut interest rates to  discourage inflows of hot money.
    "The market will test the central bank's patience with the
gradual shifting of the crown to stronger levels...  (But) we
continue to see risk of real intervention," Komercni Banka said
in a report.
    Komercni Banka said it did not expect the central bank to
step into the market as long as the crown traded at levels
weaker than 39.800 per euro.
    The main market-moving factor on Tuesday will be the central
bank's two-week repo tender.
    The central bank had used the repo auction, its main
  

monetary policy tool, in the past to discourage speculative  

capital inflows by leaving the money market in a liquidity  

surplus and effectively pushing the interbank rates down.

title: Slovak  crown flat, seen testing  intervention  levels.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown
  opened flat on Thursday, but dealers said the market
might test the new, lower levels at which they now think the
central bank might intervene to support the crown.
 
    The crown was at 40.980/41.010 at 0840 GMT versus the euro
compared to 40.990/41.000 at Wdnesday's close.
    The crown retreated from five-and-a-half month highs on
Wednesday as investors took profits and local companies shopped
for cheaper foreign currencies.
    Some traders said a near-term direction of the unit remains
  

unclear as sound economic fundamentals and market's belief that  

the central bank softened its resistance against crown firming  

were largely offset by political uncertainty.  

"The power is balanced on both sides... but interest in the  

crown still persists so we could test 40.900 (per euro) level,"  

said HVB Bank dealer Michal Baranek.  

He said the crown could break through the 40.900 mark before  

the 2004 state budget draft enters the key parliamentary reading  

later this month as some investors might be keen to test the  

central bank's sensitivity to crown appreciation.  

The central bank heavily intervened in May to knock the unit  

off its record highs of 40.800 per euro, arguing that excessive  

firming hurt exporters. The bank also cut 25 basis points from  

its interest rates in September to warn speculators.  

But some dealers said the budget debate would prevent sharp  

crown firming in the near future as the budget vote is seen as  

the key test of unity of fragile ruling coalition. The vote on  

the budget draft is expected in the first half of next month.

title: Slovak crown jumps to 5-1/2 mo highs, eyes cbank.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown
  jumped to five-and-half month highs against the euro on
Thursday after central bank comments eased market worries about
a near-term intervention to weaken the local unit, dealers said.
    The crown ended at 41.020/080 to the euro, its main
reference unit, after 41.100/160 late on Wednesday. It firmed to
a three-week high of 35.051/111 to the dollar, from 35.336/379.
    Central bank governor Marian Jusko reiterated on Thursday
the bank's position that the crown should firm only in the long
term and the move had to be justified by sound economic
fundamentals.
 Although it was not viewed as a policy shift, dealers said
the comments appeared to have partially lifted players' fears
the bank would take aggressive measures to prevent gradual crown
strengthening beyond 41.000 to the euro.
    "It does not look from the comments that the central bank
would like to intervene dramatically at the moment...
  


 it looks
we can get under 41.000 per euro level in the near future," CSOB
dealer Robert Hakszer said.
    The crown touched the 41.030 per euro level during the
session, nearing sensitive levels last seen in May when the
central bank knocked the unit off its all-time highs of 40.800
per euro.
    "The central bank's long-term expectations were reflected in
an immediate change of the exchange rate. It was an impulse
mainly for foreign players to buy Slovak crowns," Hakszer said.
    The bank intervened repeatedly in 2003 to prevent excessive
firming of the crown due worries that a strong currency could
hurt exporters. It also cut interest rates by 25 basis point in
September to show it might use this tool to fend off
speculators.
    But traders said the crown would probably not stay under
41.000 per euro for long as uncertainty in the market might
increase when parliament opens debate on the 2004 budget draft.
    On the secondary bond market, the yield on the benchmark
five-year bonds  shrank to 5.329/195 percent from
5.400/200, and the 10-year paper moved to 5.413/343 percent from
5.500/300 percent.

title: CORRECTED - Slovak cbank sold crowns in June to halt firming.
text:
In July 29 BRATISLAVA story headlined "Slovak cbank sold
crowns in June to halt firming" please read in first paragraph
"...bought 20 million euros in a direct deal..." instead of
"...bought 20 million crowns in a direct deal..." (changes


currency unit).


 A corrected version of the story follows. 

 BRATISLAVA, July 29 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said on Tuesday it bought 20 million euros in a direct deal with an unspecified commercial bank in June to curb the crown's strength. 

 The central bank intervened by buying over 400 million euros in May, both on the open foreign exchange market and in direct deals with banks, to knock down the crown which hit an all-time high of 40.770 per euro that month. 

 The bank said it did one deal and bought euros after being contacted by a commercial bank early in June "in order to stop strengthening of the crown exchange rate". 

 Apart from open market interventions, the Slovak central bank has invited commercial banks to approach it when they are about to sell or buy a larger amount of crowns to avoid volatility on the small Slovak foreign exchange market. 

 The central bank had repeatedly fought against crown firming fuelled by speculative capital inflow earlier this year, saying that too strong a currency would hurt Slovakia's export competitiveness and cause widening of the foreign trade deficit. 

 However, the crown has weakened over the past month, mainly because of turmoil on bigger central European markets and due to local political tensions. It closed 41.910/960 to the euro, its main reference currency, on Tuesday.

title: UPDATE 2-Slovak April trade gap worse than market forecasts.
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 29 (Reuters) - Slovakia's foreign trade deficit broke a six-month narrowing trend in April and widened on the year as imports outpaced slowing exports for the first time since October, data showed on Thursday. 

 The trade deficit of the future EU member's small, open economy grew to 6.985 billion crowns ($200.5 million) in April, its widest level this year, from a gap of 5.495 billion in the same month of 2002, the statistics office said. 

 The gap was bigger than market expectations for a 2.9 billion-crown shortfall. 

 "It was a surprise to us. We expected a much better number, and much more benign import figures due to (a fall in) the price of oil," said ING Bank chief economist Jan Toth. 

 The trade figures pushed the crown weaker, and analysts said the data, coupled with an absence of firming pressure on the currency, had relieved pressure on the central bank to cut interest rates at a policy meet on Friday. 

 A key reason behind the wider deficit was a deceleration in export growth, which slowed to 11.4 percent year-on-year in April from 24.4 percent in March. 

 Economists said the smaller export rise was mainly due to a high comparative base from last year, and that none of Slovakia's major export categories had underperformed in April. 

 Commerzbank analyst Radomir Jac said the base effect would play a significant role in the trade balance for most of the second half of 2003, but that soft domestic demand should still help narrow the full-year shortfall. 

 Imports were above analysts' expectations, as the predicted impact of low crude prices following the war in Iraq and the weak dollar had not shown up in Slovakia's April oil bill. 

 Imports grew 12.9 percent on the year, from 14.8 percent in the previous month, and the cumulative four-month trade gap totalled 13.546 billion crowns, down from 24.884 billion in the same period of 2002. 

 CROWN DOWN, RATES SEEN FLAT 

 The market had expected the data to provide room for a new inflow of foreign capital after a month of stagnation following a central bankintervention that knocked the Slovak currency off record highs in early May. 

 The crown, which has become an investor favourite among central European EU candidates due to its booming economy and high interest rates, weakened to 41.120/135 to the euro after the trade data, from 41.000/089 at the open. 

 Tatra Bank analysts Robert Prega said the wider trade deficit would probably reinforce the central bank's stance of fighting against crown firming. The bank is worried that too strong a crown will hit exporters and further deepen the external imbalance. 

 The central bank has repeatedly warned it could cut interest rates - the main two-week repo rate is now at 6.5 percent - to prevent hot money inflows, but analysts now see no imminent policy easing as the bank does not need to respond to speculative firming pressure. 

 "The likelihood of an interest rate cut is very low at tomorrow's central bank meeting, and I think there will be a correction of expectations on the money market as well," said CSOB Bank analyst Marek Gabris.

title: Emerging  FX -Slovak crown steadies after cb acts, lira dips.
text:
LONDON, May 6 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown steadied on Tuesday after central bank intervention saw it retreat from record highs against the euro on Monday while the Turkish lira eased ahead of new foreign currency auctions from the central bank. 

 Monday's intervention triggered a sharp reversal in the Slovak crown down to one-month lows against the euro, with the central bank saying its gains were not justified by economic fundamentals. 

Central bank governor Marian Jusko also said the bank was considering tougher measures to prevent the currency rising on speculative inflows. However, analysts remain sceptical the bank will succeed in reversing the crown's uptrend. "Jusko said he was looking to do more to weaken the currency, but the whole market is bullish so it's pretty much useless," said Juliette Declercq, emerging markets currency analyst at JPMorgan. 

 Local dealers said they expected overseas players to take any pullback as fresh opportunity to buy, though Declercq added a note of caution ahead of Slovakia's upcoming EU referendum. 

 "I still wouldn't recommend building up short euro/crown positions ahead of the EU referendum on May 16/17, but if that goes through the bank will have to buy a lot of euros and have a lot of rate cuts to control the crown," she added. 

 The Slovak's are widely expected to vote in favour of joining the EU in 2004, but the worry is that the turnout will be below the 50 percent required to make the result valid. 

 Declercq likened the Slovaks' dilemma with that experienced in the neighbouring Czech Republic two years ago. 

 "In that case, the Czech's only managed to reverse the trend when interest rates came down to euro zone levels." 

 Foreign investment inflows have been pouring into Slovakia this year as the country plays catch up with its neighbours on the path to economic convergence with the EU. 

 By 0930 GMT, the crown traded a shade down on the session at 41.16 per euro . 

 Elsewhere in the region, Hungarian central bank governor Zsigmond Jarai said on Tuesday that overshoots in the budget deficit could lead to euro zone entry being delayed until 2009/2010, from the current plan to join in 2007/2008. 

 LIRA DIPS 

 The lira's recent rally stuttered on Tuesday with the market running out of steam at five-month high levels against the dollar set on Monday. 

 The lira pullback coincided with the central bank resuming daily auctions to buy $20 million of foreign exchange to boost its reserves, though local dealers played down the material impact of the auctions on the market. 

 Analysts said the risk premium that hit the lira leading up to and during the war in neighbouring Iraq had now been almost fully unwound, making further gains harder to come by. 

 "Turkey is still a high inflation country and nominal gains are going to cause trouble...We've seen a rebound but ultimately the nominal level of the lira has to weaken again to keep competitiveness," said Adam Slater, emerging markets analyst at Credit Agricole Indosuez. 

 Turkish April consumer price data out on Saturday was better than expected, though the annual rate remains at 29.5 percent. 

 Slater added that in the near-term the high level of Turkish interest rates was likely to support the lira. 

 The lira traded at 1,536,500 on the interbank market  after ending Monday's session at 1,527,000.

title: Slovak cbank chief sees tough measures against SKK.
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 5 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) is considering taking tougher measures than direct market interventions to halt the firming of the Slovak crown currency, NBS Governor Marian Jusko said on Monday. Jusko told reporters NBS sold billions of crowns on the market on Monday to knock the crown from an all-time high of 40.770 to the euro . 

 He added that the crown firming was not justified by economic fundamentals, mainly by the wide current account deficit. 

 He declined to specify what measures the bank may take. Analysts have said the NBS would have to cut interest rates to fend off speculative capital inflows.

title: Slovak cbank says almost no room for crown firming.

title: UPDATE 1-Slovak cbank bought 200 mln euro from banks in Jan.
text:
BRATISLAVA, March 3 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank continued to intervene indirectly by buying euros from commercial banks in January to fight off speculative demand for the crown currency, it said on Monday. 

 "The central bank continued to use offers from commercial banks when it bought foreign currencies worth 200 million euros through individual deals in January," the bank said in its monthly monetary report. 

 The Slovak central bank was forced to buy hundreds of millions of euros in the last months of 2002 to fend off speculative capital inflows that had been boosting the crown to all-time highs of 41.100 against the euro. 

 The bank's current bias is to resist a firmer crown, fearing it could hurt exports. Besides intervening, it also slashed 175 basis points off its key interest rates last year to make the crown less attractive for speculators and prevent the unit form gaining unjustifiably. 

 After the crown initially retreated at the end of last year, an improving foreign trade balance in 2002 and a decision by French car maker PSA Peugeot Citroen (PEUP.PA) to build a 700-million-euro plant in Slovakia lent it a new firming impulse in early 2003, boosting it to 41.200 per euro in mid-January. 

 The central bank intervenes to influence the crown either openly on the foreign exchange market or by secret individual deals with commercial banks. 

 The banks may approach the central bank when they have a large order, and it then decides whether to make the conversion off the market to prevent the deal from affecting the crown. 

 The crown lost ground in February due to the massive retreat of foreign speculators from central European following heavy losses on the Hungarian market after they unsuccessfully tried to push the forint  out of its fluctuation band. 

 The unit has been trading between 41.750-42.000 per euro, its key reference unit, in the past few days, but traders see it firming in the longer term due to expected foreign investment inflows and because of an anticipated convergence with the EU. 

 Some analysts said data showing a sharp narrowing of the foreign trade deficit for January, released last week, could lift some of the central bank's opposition to crown firming in the coming months.

title: Slovak cbank bought 50 mln euro from banks in Dec.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 31 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank, battling to dampen demand for the local crown currency, said on Friday it had bought 50 million euros from commercial banks in December. 

 The central bank was forced to intervene in the last few months of 2002 as speculative capital inflows, attracted by high interest rates, pushed the crown to record highs against the single currency. 

 The bank, worried that too strong a currency would hit export comptitiveness and thus the country's trade balance, also intervened both on the open market and in discreet deals with banks in November to take the steam out of the crown's advance. 

 Individual deals with banks continued in December, the central bank's monetary report said on Friday. 

 Commercial banks may approach the central bank when they have large orders to avoid artificial influences on Slovakia's small foreign exchange market. 

 After a retreat at the end of last year, the crown resumed its rise early in 2003 and the bank repeatedly warned it would use all its tools - interventions and rate cuts - to prevent excessive gains. However, the crown fell sharply last week as speculators fled central Europe following heavy losses in Hungary when that country's central bank intervened and cut rates to knock the forint down. 

 The Slovak unit has stabilised this week, trading between 41.600-41.900 per euro, its key reference currency. 

 Analysts expect the crown to appreciate further this year as the country's economy converges with the European Union, which Slovakia will join in 2004. 

 A crown advance could prompt the Slovak central bank to cut interest rate by 50 to 100 basis points within the next six months in order to discourage speculators, they said.

title: UPDATE 1-INTERVIEW-Slovak cbank sees long fight with speculators.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Slovak Central Bank (NBS) Governor Marian Jusko said on Wednesday the bank would repeat drastic moves like the major cuts to interest rates it made in November if forced to do so by unjustified firming in the crown. 

 Jusko's comments coincided with a two-percent drop in the crown on Wednesday. 

 It has been hammered this week after Hungary's central bank fended off speculative capital causing unwanted firming in the forint with huge interest rate cuts and interventions. 

 In November, the Slovak central bank slashed interest rates by 150 basis points and bought around half a billion euros on the market to knock the crown lower after it hit all time highs of 41.100 against the single European unit. 

 "If the situation calls for drastic measures similar to those made in November, yes, the national bank will take these measures... We will not hesitate," Jusko said in an interview. 

 "Artificial strengthening in the Slovak crown pushed only by expectations would be harmful to the future development of the economy, and this factor is the most important thing in our present situation." 

 The central banks in Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary have fought firming pressure on their currencies since last year due to speculative plays by foreign investors hoping for fat returns as the countries near EU entry in 2004 and adoption of the euro, expected around four years later. 

 Jusko said the recent steps taken by his Hungarian counterparts, including slashing their key interest rates by 200 basis points over two days, were necessary to counter possible negative economic effects. 

 He said his and other central European central banks would likely have to continue fighting speculators until the region completes eurozone entry. 

 "I think it will last for the whole period, from now up until our entry into the EMU... The action by the Hungarian central bank was really very very drastic, but it was necessary as the forint was becoming stronger and stronger, and perhaps it didn't correspond to the fundamentals of the economy," he said. 

 "To have too strong a forint, or too strong a crown, could be hard for the further developments of our economies." 

 SEES CROWN GRADUALLY FIRMING 

 Jusko said Slovakia should join EMU before or at the same time as its neighbours in the region, but not after. 

 And if met, forecasts of increased exports, better state fiscal performance and heady growth should also allow the crown to firm gradually before Slovakia enters the ERM-2 exchange rate mechanism it must follow for two years before eurozone entry. 

 "It seems to me that the first possible date that Slovakia could enter the EMU will be 2008... And if our expectations materialise, the crown should be stronger," Jusko said. 

 The bank sees GDP up by four percent or more annually through 2006. 

 Slovakia's invitations to join the EU and NATO, and the election of a centre-right government that has pledged to reform state finances and cut spending are all positive economic factors, but the NBS will not allow market expectations to push the crown to a point outpacing real economic developments, Jusko said. 

 He added he expected December monthly and 2002 full-year foreign trade data, due out next week, to show improvements over 2001, while the troublesome foreign trade gap should also show an improvement this year on the back of lower domestic demand from the government's measures and higher exports. 

 Jusko said the bank would probably need several months to analyse the effects of the government's austerity measures and the potential improvement in foreign trade, before it judged whether a new trend had been established. He would not comment on the bank's possible future policy towards interest rates. 

 "We need to analyse the situation for two or three months at a minimum because the new (austerity) measures of the government have only just come into effect in January," Jusko said.

title: UPDATE 1-Slovak November trade gap lower than expected.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 3 (Reuters) - Slovakia's foreign trade deficit surprisingly narrowed in November 2002 on the back of renewed strong export growth and cheaper fuel imports, data showed on Friday. 

 The November trade shortfall totalled 9.737 billion crowns ($246 million), down from a 12.781 billion crown gap in the same month of 2001, the Slovak Statistics Office said. 

 The deficit was better than market expectations as a Reuters survey of analysts last month showed an average forecast for a 12.6 billion crown deficit in November. 

 "The data are better than expected.... What was surprising is the solid growth of exports after (a) worse performance in the previous few months," said Commerzbank analyst Radomir Jac. 

 Exports rose 11.3 percent year-on-year in November, outpacing a 4.5 percent annual rise in imports. 

 The statistics office also revised October monthly trade data to show a gap of 13.152 billion crowns, from an originally reported 13.003 billion. 

 The cumulative trade deficit for January-November of 2002 totalled 83.412 billion crowns, compared with 86.828 billion in the same period a year ago. 

 Analysts said the better-than-predicted trade balance was also partially affected by imports of fossil fuels, mainly Russian crude oil and natural gas, which were cheaper due to the strength of the Slovak crown against the dollar. 

 Raw materials, the second largest import category, totalled 99.163 billion crowns in the first 11 months of last year, down 8.4 percent year-on-year. 

 Economists said the improving trade balance would mean upward pressure on the crown currency, which rose immediately after the release of November trade data. 

 The crown traded at 41.230/260 to the euro, its key reference currency, as of 0830 GMT, from 41.335/395 at Thursday's close. It was hovering near four-year highs against the dollar at 39.799/838. 

 "The trade development is positive for the crown... We can expect pressure on strengthening, but, at the same time, the central bank is likely to act against the firming because it would probably still find it undesirable," Jac said. 

 The Slovak central bank repeatedly intervened on the foreign exchange market last year to attempt to stop the crown's rise, which it said was unjustified due to the trade balance deficit. ($1=39.51 Slovak crowns).

title: Slovak  cbank bought EUR583mln in Nov  interventions .
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 23 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said on Monday it had bought 583 million euros from commercial banks in total through discreet and direct deals in November, to halt the rise of the crown. 

 The bank's monthly monetary survey said it bought 55 million euros from commercial banks discreetly in individual deals at the beginning of the month, and the rest of the entire amount in direct interventions in three days beginning on November 12. The central bank's market operations were followed by a surprising 150-basis-point cut in key interest rates effective from November 18, aimed at lowering the interest rate differential with the euro zone and neighbouring markets and thus narrowing the room for speculation. 

 The Slovak crown's jump was sparked by the victory of centre-right, pro-reform parties in September elections. The crown rose by around one percent in October to 41.577 to the euro, its key reference currency. The bank bought 30 million euros in discreet deals in October when it began to fight the unit's firming. 

 However, the crown continued to firm in November, hitting an all-time high of 41.100 early in that month, as foreign funds poured into central European markets in the expectation of gains once the region joins the eurozone in around 2008. 

 The bank said it had started to intervene directly at the crown's level of around 41.190 per euro, and that the moves resulted in the unit's easing by 1.4 percent versus the euro and by 1.3 percent to the dollar over the month. 

 This month the crown has continued to ease due to a typical end-year mood, and is seen trading within the 41.750-950 per euro range this week.

title: Slovak cbank says covertly bought euros in Oct.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 2 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said on Monday it conducted covert interventions and bought hard currencies from commercial banks in October to halt the rise of the crown. 

 The bank's monetary survey said it bought 30 million euros ($29.8 million) in discrete deals in October when it began to fight the crown's firming. The unit's jump was sparked by the victory of pro-reform parties in September elections. 

 The crown rose by around one percent in October to 41.577 to the euro, its key reference currency. 

 It continued to firm in November, hitting an all-time high of 41.100 early in that month, as foreign funds poured into the central European markets in the expectation of gains once the region joins the eurozone in around 2008. 

 The rally sparked a new series of central bank's secret hard currency purchases, later combined with direct interventions on the foreign exchange market. 

 The bank had said it bought hundreds of millions of euros in November, but it will reveal the exact volume of that month's hard currency purchases in the next monetary survey at the end of December or early in January. 

 The interventions and a 150-basis-point interest rate cut on November 15 reversed the crown's rally, and the unit eased to trade at 41.810/890 per euro on Monday.

title: Slovak cbank gov pleased with crown level-agency.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Nov 27 (Reuters) - Slovak central bank Governor Marian Jusko is satisfied with the level of the Slovak crown, after the bank intervened and slashed interest rates to knock the unit down earlier this month, news agency TASR reported on Wednesday. 

 The crown had surged on bullishness towards central Europe as investors expecting fat returns once Slovakia and other ex-communist states join the eurozone in around 2007-2008 raced into the region in convergence deals. 

 The currency was also boosted by a September election win by centre-right parties who have pledged to lead Slovakia into the EU and NATO, slash spending, and make other reforms. But the central bank stopped the unit in its tracks with a number of policy steps, and Jusko said he was satisfied with the result. 

 "Since we managed to fulfil our short-term goal - to stop the strengthening of the crown - I'm satisfied," TASR quoted Jusko as saying. 

 Jusko said the bank's longer-term actions would continue to depend on developments on Slovakia's wide external imbalance: "The important thing will be if there is a gradual improvement in external developments, improvement in foreign trade." 

 The central bank began covertly intervening in the market to knock the crown lower, in mid-November, and then bought over 500 million euros with crowns in direct market intervention. 

 It followed the intervention with a shock 150-basis-point cut to its key two-week interest rate, bringing it to 6.5 percent, which has since chilled market enthusiasm. 

 The crown hit a six-week low to the euro on Wednesday, as crown selling from local and foreign banks set off a small wave of stop losses. Dealers generally expect the crown to ease slightly before the year-end, as investors repatriate profits abroad and banks close positions to square their books. 

 The central bank's policy making bank board is scheduled to meet on Friday, but analysts do not think the bank will further cut interest rates due to the now-subdued mood towards the crown.

title: Slovak crown falls on profit-taking.
text:

 fell against the euro on Tuesday along with other central
European currencies as profit-taking following a recent rally
coupled with corporate demand for hard currencies.

hard-currency purchases by corporate clients, which, some

profits by foreign firms operating in Slovakia.
    But the Slovak central bank, which intervened buying over
500 million euros in the market earlier this month and slashed
its key interest rate by 150 basis points to knock the crown
weaker, appears to have stabilised the currency's rate for the

title: Slovak crown ends slightly lower, trade thin.
text:

 closed marginally lower on Friday in quiet trade and

due to profit taking and the threat of intervention by the

title: Slovak cbank  forex  reserves jump to $8.9 bln.

title: Slovak crown slips on foreign profit taking.
text:

 closed slightly lower versus the euro on Thursday.

 Traders say the crown, which has gained around seven percent

title: Slovak  crown firms despite cbank  intervention .
text:
BRATISLAVA, Nov 14 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown
 closed stronger on Thursday despite a third straight day
of central bank intervention to weaken it, and dealers said
foreign buying will likely keep the unit under firming pressure.

 Thursday's intervention pushed the crown briefly lower to
around 41.800 per euro, but the unit recovered from the losses
after the bank disappeared from the market, dealers said, adding
they expected more firming pressure in the coming days.



    "Interest in buying crowns has not weakened at all... We are

foreign bank trader said.
    Dealers said the central bank would probably have to resort

speculative capital pouring into central European markets in
expectations of fat returns once the region joins the euro zone.

title: Emerging  FX - Intervention  sends  Slovak  crown lower.
text:
LONDON, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown fell to its lowest levels in almost a month against the euro on Wednesday as the central bankintervened to weaken it for the second day in a row. 

 However, the region as a whole got a boost after Moody's on Tuesday lifted its ratings on the foreign currency government bonds of the eight central European EU candidates. The South African rand also found support from a rating outlook upgrade. 

 Local dealers said the Slovak central bank re-entered the market to sell the crown at 41.47 per euro , sending it down a further half percent against the single currency. 

 The bank later confirmed it had been in the market again and said it was prepared to continue its efforts to knock the currency lower if it kept on firming. 

 "Intervention yesterday showed that the central bank can at least move the currency and the signs suggest they have been in again today," said one dealer in London. 

 "However, they can probably only smooth the up-trend given all the investment that's likely to come in," he added. 

 The dealer said in the short term the next upside targets in euro/crown were 41.9 and then 42.20. 

 Slovakia has enjoyed a surge of foreign investment after parliamentary elections in late September produced a reformist centre-right coalition government and following Ireland's approval of the Nice Treaty on enlargement in October. 

 At 1045 GMT, the crown traded down 0.51 percent against the euro from late Tuesday levels at 41.76. 

 Czech central bank vice-governor Oldrich Dedek said on Wednesday he thought Czech interventions to weaken the crown this year had been successful and that he still expected a short-term drop in the currency. 

 Dedek said the bank had sold crowns to buy 2.3 billion euros from the open market in this year's interventions, with an additional four billion euros taken directly into its reserves from state coffers from the privatisation of gas importer Transgas. 

 The crown traded down 0.23 percent to the euro at 30.73. 

 MARKETS MULL MOODY'S UPGRADE 

 Moody's took analysts by surprise on Tuesday with an across-the-board foreign currency ratings upgrade for the eight central European EU candidates. 

 Moody's said the move was to bring the ratings into line with local currency ratings now that financial integration with the EU is "virtually irreversible". 

 The market response to the upgrades was muted, with the region's main bond markets already seen as overbought, particularly at the long-end of the curve. 

 "In our view, the move is a premature one," said analysts at UBS Warburg, in a research note. 

 UBS said that while few doubt that the EU candidates will eventually become euro zone members, "the lack of certainty means a more gradual convergence between local and foreign currency ratings would have been more credible". 

 Moody's adopted a more gradualist approach to Greece's euro membership, even though it was already in the EU, UBS added. 

 However, others were more upbeat saying the move further underlined the attractions of the region as an investment destination. 

 "The Moody's upgrade didn't have much impact in local and external bonds, but it did offer more proof that investment should be headed into emerging Europe, rather than Latin America or Asia," said one dealer at a European bank in London. 

 Elsewhere, the South African rand opened strongly on Wednesday, finding support from S&P's decision the previous day to upgrade the country's foreign currency ratings outlook to positive. 

 South African Reserve Bank Governor Tito Mboweni said on Wednesday that the central bank would not struggle to fight against inflation at all costs. 

 His comments hinted at a pause in the tightening cycle, with the bank having hiked rates by 400 basis points this year in an effort to control surging inflation caused by the rand's sharp fall at the end of last year. 

 The bank has missed its three-to-six percent target for the CPIX inflation indicator for 11 months running. 

 The rand eased back later in the session to trade flat around 9.81 per dollar .

title: Slovak  cbank says prepared to continue  intervening .

 "It depends on the further devlopment of the exchange rate, so it's hard to say, but we are on the market, and we are still prepared to continue our effort to weaken the currency," Szulenyi told Reuters.

title: WRAPUP 1-Slovak cbank fights back to dent crown euphoria.
text:
(wraps Slovak cenbank intervention, Fitch/Moodys ratings 

 from London/New York) 

 By Michael Winfrey 

 BRATISLAVA, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Tuesday, sending the crown currency more than one percent lower in an attempt to dampen enthusiasm for the local unit which it believes is overvalued and could damage the country's economic health. 

 The bank's bid to tame the crown comes amid an increasingly buoyant mood in central European markets which have benefited from a constant inflow of foreign capital ahead of European Union enlargement. 

 Sweeping ratings upgrades by Moody's Investors Service for eight EU candidate countries and indications that a slight delay in EU expansion could help the mostly poor candidates save cash has also made the region look attractive to investors chasing higher yielding assets. 

 The Slovak central bank sold crowns in several waves to push the unit down from record highs where it had climbed in recent days along with other central European currencies in anticipation of EU entry in 2004. 

 The Slovak crown had jumped by nearly eight percent since July - also boosted by a victory by a reformist cabinet in September elections - as it took in its share of the steady stream of foreign funds flowing into central Europe. 

 The central bank had repeatedly warned in recent weeks that the unit was overvalued because of Slovakia's wide foreign trade gap and finally intervened on Tuesday after the crown touched another record high the previous session. 

 "We started intervening when the crown was at around 41.120 (to the euro)," central bank Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters shortly after the session opened. 

 Szulenyi declined to detail volumes used in the interventions, but market watchers said the central bank may have sold well over 250 million euros worth of crowns in a variety of operations throughout the day. 

 The crown, which hit a record high of 41.070/100 versus the euro on Monday, closed at 41.580/590. 

 BANK FACES BATTLE 

 Analysts said the intervention could be the start of a long-lasting battle against investors who have flocked to the crown and neighbouring currencies hoping to cash in on economic reforms and the convergence of candidates' interest rates with those in the West as the region creeps closer to accession. 

 "The Slovak crown has experienced a similar development as other regional currencies, the Hungarian forint, Polish zloty and the Czech crown, which have all been boosted by positive market sentiment," Commerzbank analyst Radomir Jac said. 

 "It can be expected that the positive mood towards the region will continue and the market will try to push the currencies stronger." 

 As evidence of the rosy mood towards central Europe, Moody's Investors Service boosted its ratings across the board for Slovakia and seven other EU applicants on Tuesday. 

 At the same time, EU Enlargement Commissioner Gunter Verheugen indicated entry for the candidates could come a few months after the originally planned January 1, 2004 deadline, which could save cash-strapped aspirants from paying billions in euros in contributions to the Union's coffers. 

 Moody's rival Fitch Ratings sounded a cautionary tone after the upgrades, however, saying several candidates still had fiscal problems that could hinder their EU entry. 

 Analysts said the upgrades had been largely priced in, as foreign capital had flooded bond and currency markets with speculative convergence plays and cross deals, but said it may have highlighted the strong positive mood toward the region. 

 "While it's helpful, it was fully priced in the convergence spreads on the eurobond market, and I don't see it having a large impact beyond augmenting the feel-good factor in the region," said IDEAglobal analyst John Davitte. 

 SLOVAK CBANK SEEN FORCED TO ACT FURTHER 

 Analysts said the Slovak central bank's attempt to weaken the crown may not last, as foreign banks were still hungry to buy the unit, and more action could be needed to prevent it from reaching fresh record levels. 

 "The central bank will fail in what it is doing now," said Jan Toth, ING's chief economist in Bratislava. 

 "Interventions at this level help close some positions foreign investors have in the crown, but after some time investors will realise they want some Slovak exposure, so they will buy Slovak crowns...and the currency will appreciate." 

 Analysts also said the Slovak central bank is likely to have to cut interest rates to stem inflows into the crown due to their high differential with the West, despite an expected surge in 2003 inflation. 

 "The acceleration of inflation will be... outside of the central bank influence... There will be a certain room to lower the rates, and the room will widen in line with the pace of the crown firming," said Jac.

title: Slovak  crown drops after  central bank intervention .

title: Emerging  FX - Intervention  dents  Slovak  crown, lira down on Iraq.
text:
LONDON, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened to weaken the crown on Tuesday, helping to bring it down from record highs hit the previous session, though analysts said the move was unlikely to break the uptrend. 

 Elsewhere, the Turkish lira extended its retreat from recent four-month highs against the dollar with the Iraqi parliament's rejection of a U.N. resolution on weapons inspections increasing nerves over a possible U.S.-led military attack. 

 Slovak central bank treasury director Frantisek Szylenyi confirmed that the bank bought euros against the crown at 41.12 , triggering a fall of almost one percent. He gave no indication of the amount bought. 

 "There may have been a shake-out of some crown long positions, but most people will probably just see it as an opportunity to get cheaper entry levels," said Koon Chow, central Europe currency analyst at CSFB. 

 Chow added that the intervention is likely to be the start of an ongoing process, but added that he was sceptical whether it would achieve anything other than to slow the pace of crown appreciation. 

 "The market could well be back at 41, if not lower in a week's time," Chow said. 

 September's election victory for reformist centre-right parties and progress towards EU enlargement after Ireland approved the Nice Treaty last month have powered the crown up to record highs in recent weeks. 

 Slovakia's high-yields - the main interest rate is at eight percent - have also been attracting inflows. 

 At 1030 GMT, the crown traded down 0.8 percent at 41.45 per euro . 

 In Hungary, October consumer prices rose a touch more than expected to an annual rate of 4.9 percent, up from 4.6 percent in September, providing backing for the central bank's hawkish stance on rates at its council meeting on Monday. 

 The central bank said that despite a stronger forint, inflation risks remained high and there was no scope to ease interest rates from the current 9.5 percent. 

 The numbers made little impression on the forint, with the country's high-yields seen lending it solid support in the face of deteriorating economic fundamentals. 

 The forint was little moved at 238.50 per euro . 

 LIRA, RAND RETREAT 

 The Turkish lira was on the backfoot on Tuesday as investors opted to lock in recent gains as nerves returned over Iraq. 

 The Iraqi parliament voted to reject a tough U.N. resolution on weapons inspections, but left the final decision down to President Saddam Hussein. 

 "The Iraq situation is part of the reason for the lira consolidation as it brings us potentially a little bit closer to conflict in the Middle East," said Dwyfor Evans, emerging markets analyst at Bank of America. 

 "But there's also been some reaction to (Monday's) rate cut. We got 200 basis points, but the market was hoping for 300 or 400 and there's been profit-taking on the back of that," he added. 

 The Turkish central bank cuts overnight interest rates by 200 basis points to 44 percent on Monday. 

 The lira traded at 1,640,000 versus the dollar on the interbank market from 1,617,000 at Monday's close. 

 Other high-yielding units were also in consolidation mode after recent gains, with fresh Iraqi tension prompting some investors to scale back their riskier positions. 

 Dealers said profit-taking took the rand lower early on, but it ran into support after ratings agency S&P upped its outlook on South Africa to positive, and affirmed the country's BBB-long-term foreign currency rating. 

 The rand traded around 9.82 to the dollar , broadly steady from late Monday levels. 

 The Polish zloty posted a bigger retracement, dropping back around 0.65 percent from recent four-and-a-half month highs under 3.93 to the euro .

title: Slovak  crown shoots lower on cbank  intervention .

    Another trader from an international bank in Bratislava
added: "The second wave pushed the crown from below 41.400 to
around 41.500."
    The central bank has repeatedly threatened to knock the
crown lower in the past few weeks, as it says that recent
firming on the currency is based solely on positive sentiment
but does not reflect the country's macroeconomic fundamentals.
    Dealers said that because the crown was not able to break
the level of 41.500 to the euro, the unit could stay in a range
of 41.200-500 in the nearest term, but it could go weaker if the
central bank continued aggressively intervening.
    Before the intervention, the crown had hit an all-time high
of 41.070/100 at midday on Monday, up around eight percent since
July on bullish sentiment tied to a win by rightist, pro-reform
forces in September elections and the increased likelihood of
Slovakia joining the EU and NATO in around 2004.

title: UPDATE 3- Slovak central bank intervenes  to weaken crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank made good on recent threats and intervened to knock down the surging crown on Tuesday in what dealers said was likely the start of a long-lasting battle against the strong bullish mood on the unit. 

 The central bank sold crowns in several waves to push the unit down from record highs where it had climbed along with other central European currencies on expectations of EU entry in 2004 and high rate differentials with western markets. 

 The crown had jumped by around five percent since September, when a pro-reform rightist coalition won parliamentary elections, sparking bullish sentiment and a strong inflow of foreign funds into the Slovak crown. 

 The central bank had repeatedly warned in recent weeks that the unit was overvalued because of Slovakia's wide foreign trade gap, and it finally intervened on Tuesday to push it weaker to around 41.580/600 by the afternoon. 

 "We started intervening when the crown was at around 41.120 (to the euro)," central bank Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters shortly after the session opened. 

 Szulenyi declined to detail volumes used in the interventions, but market watchers said the central bank may have sold between 200-250 million euros worth of crowns in a variety of operations throughout the day. 

 Analysts said the effect of the move might not last for long, as foreign banks were still interested in the currency, and more action could be needed to prevent it firming back in the direction of 41.070/100, the all-time high hit on Monday. 

 "The central bank will fail in what it is doing now," said Jan Toth, ING's chief economist in Bratislava. 

 "Interventions at this level help close some positions foreign investors have in the crown, but after some time investors will realise they want some Slovak exposure, so they will buy Slovak crowns...and the currency will appreciate." 

 LONDON STILL BULLISH ON REGION 

 Dealers said the central bank began intervening with off-market deals through London brokers just after the open, and then followed by more than two waves of crown selling on the automated trading system that London banks resisted with aggressive buying. 

 Sentiment in the region was also helped by ratings upgrades from Moody's Investors Service for Slovakia and seven other EU applicant countries due to economic restructuring in central Europe, but the markets' first reactions were muted. 

 Analysts said the upgrades had been largely priced in, as foreign capital, noting the candidates were creeping closer to eurozone entry, had flooded bond and currency markets with speculative convergence plays and cross deals. 

 "The Slovak crown has experienced a similar development as other regional currencies, the Hungarian forint, Polish zloty and the Czech crown, which have all been boosted by positive market sentiment," Commerzbank analyst Radomir Jac said. 

 "It can be expected that the positive mood towards the region will continue and the market will try to push the currencies stronger." 

 Analysts also said the Slovak central bank is likely to have to cut interest rates to stem inflows into the crown due to their high differential with the West, despite an expected surge in 2003 inflation to be caused by utility price and tax hikes. 

 "The acceleration of inflation will be caused by administrative measures, rather than by demand pressure, so it will be outside of the central bank influence... There will be a certain room to lower the rates, and the room will widen in line with the pace of the crown firming," said Jac. 

 The key two-week repo rate is now 8.00 percent, following a 25-basis point cut at the end of October.

title: Slovak crown in tight range, mkt eyeing trade data.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown
 ended little changed on Monday after moving in a narrow
range during a quiet session as investors awaited the release of

    "I see the crown moving between 41.400-41.700 to euro in the
next few days."
    However, dealers said an improvement in the trade gap could

title: Slovak c.bank knocks crown off record high.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Oct 23 (Reuters) - Verbal intervention by the
Slovak central bank pulled the crown down on
Wednesday from the record high versus the euro hit in the
previous session, dealers said.
    The crown closed at 41.580/620 to the euro, its key
reference currency, from 41.300/380 at Tuesday's close. It hit
all-time high of 41.270/330 per euro during Tuesday's session.
The unit was  at 42.620/670 to the dollar, after 42.270/360.
    Central bank governor Marian Jusko said the currency's
recent advance was not consistent with the country's wide trade
deficit and warned the bank was ready to act if the unit rose
further.
    Jusko's afternoon comment reinforced a similar statement by
the bank's monetary policy director Peter Sevcovic early in the
day, who said the crown's firming was a bubble.



    The crown and other central European currencies gained
sharply on Monday on the inflow of new foreign funds into the EU
candidate states after the Irish voted "yes" in a referendum on
the EU enlargement treaty.
    The crown has also been benefiting from plans of the new
Slovak government to introduce austerity measures designed to
curb the fiscal deficit.
    "The central bank statements were not much concrete, and
certainly not surprising... But mainly some foreign players took
it as a signal and started to buy (euros). The highest matched
deal was at 41.680 to the euro," said Slovenska Sporitelna
dealer Vladimir Gajdos.
 
    "Before the end of the session, however, we saw some selling
again, which sent the crown to the closing levels," Gajdos said.
    He added he expected the crown to trade within the 41.400



and 41.700 to the euro range in the near future.

title: UPDATE 2- Slovak  cbank verbally  intervenes  to stem crown rise.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Sept 25 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened verbally on Wednesday to stem the rise of the crown which has gained sharply this week following a victory by pro-reform parties in weekend elections. 

 The crown had jumped by more than three percent against its key reference currency, the euro, since Monday, but central bank governor Marian Jusko said the rise was too sharp, and was unjustified because of Slovakia's wide foreign trade gap. 

 "I am personally a little bit nervous about the development. There are some reasons for strengthening but what we have seen in the past two or three days is too quick, and too sharp," Jusko told journalists. 

 The crown started to firm on Monday on the back of news that four centre-right parties had gained a combined majority in weekend elections and had started talks on a coalition government. 

 Analysts said the new cabinet could be the most pro-reform administration among central European EU candidate countries and that it could move quickly to cut the fiscal deficit, which should keep investors bullish on the Slovak crown. 

 Jusko acknowledged that the foreign trade balance had shown signs of improvement in June and July, but said the still-wide trade shortfall did not justify such a sharp firming in the currency as had occurred over the past few days. 

 "I am quite optimistic about the trade balance outlook but what is going on on the foreign exchange market now is not justified," he said. 

 The trade gap - the main reason behind the bank's cautious monetary policy this year - narrowed slightly on an annual basis from January to July to 48.9 billion crowns, but the central bank still considers it too high. 

 MORE FIRMING SEEN 

 The crown moved slightly weaker on Jusko's comments trading at 41.954/42.004 per euro as of 1455 GMT, compared with a five-month high of 41.860/900 earlier in the day. 

 But traders expect the positive mood to continue in the coming days, and said the market could now try to test whether the central bank is willing to intervene directly to halt the crown's rise. 

 "I think the trend is for strengthening, and this will probably prevail, maybe with some corrections, in the coming days," said Slovenska Sporitelna trader Juraj Zabadal. 

 Jusko declined to disclose a range within which the central bank would like to see the crown moving, and he would not comment on possible direct interventions. 

 "We will analyse the situation, and we cannot base this just on developments over a few days," he said. 

 Some traders said the central bank could enter the market at around the crown's all-time high of 41.500 to the euro.

title: Slovak cbank sold 205 mln euro on  FX  mkt in June.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 26 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said on Friday it sold 205 million euros when it intervened in the market to support the ailing crown currency in June. 

 The bank said it intervened because of a sharp depreciation in the Slovak crown against the euro last month. It was its first intervention on the forex market since January 2001 

 It did not disclose intervention levels, but crown was trading at around 45.000 to the euro when the first wave of crown buying came. 

 The bank added it used only direct market intervention - as opposed to verbal intervention - in June and that for the first time it had conducted deals with foreign banks in the course of the action. 

 The crown was trading around 44.47 to the euro and 44.7 to the dollar at 1256 GMT.

title: Slovak crown firms, further strength seen limited.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 23 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 firmed on Tuesday, but dealers said further strengthening


 would be limited by political uncertainty ahead of September 

 elections and movements in other currency markets. 

     The crown was trading at 44.680/740 to its key reference 

currency the euro, at 0810 GMT, from 44.800/860 late on Monday. 

 It was at 45.090/150 to the dollar, from 44.510/580. 

     Dealers said the market could track the Czech crown 

  , which has eased recently after hitting all 

 time highs against the euro earlier this month. 

     "So far nothing significant has happened... If the Czech 

 crown stays in a negative mood... it should stop any significant 

 strengthening in the (Slovak) crown," said Tatra Banka dealer 

 Boris Somorovsky. 

     "Everything is in the hands of local customers. because of a 

 lack of impulses, it should stay in a range of 44.700-44.900 

 (per euro)." 

     The Czech crown weakened slightly against the euro early on 

 Tuesday on continued speculation over possible covert central 

 bank crown-selling intervention through selected banks. 

 Investors often trade the Czech and Slovak pair together. 

     Dealers said political uncertainty ahead of September 

 elections crucial to Slovakia's EU and NATO entry hopes would 

 remain the key driver behind the currency in the longer term. 

     Investors have retreated from crown positions just two 

 months ahead of the vote due to worries that the 

 opinion-poll-leading HZDS party of autocratic ex-Prime Minister 

 Vladimir Mecir could return to power. 

     Meciar was criticised by the West during his 1994-1998 

 administration as undemocratic, corrupt, and chauvinist, and 

 diplomats have said his return would torpedo Slovakia's 

 accession aims. 

     "We should focus more on polls being released about possible 

 partners for a coalition after the elections in September," said 

 Somorovsky. 

     Meciar is expected to win the most votes in the September 

 20-21 polls, but opinion surveys indicate that other parties who 

 have said they will not cooperate with him can block him from 

 forming a government if they join forces.

title: Slovak crown opens weaker, seen calm, rangebound.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 19 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 was a touch weaker against the euro early on Friday,


 mainly on domestic client activity, and dealers said they 

 expected it to trade calmly but to remain under pressure. 

     The crown was at 44.700/740 to the euro at 0740 GMT, 

 compared with 44.680/730 late on Thursday. It was stronger 

 against the dollar, at the midpoint of 44.040, from 44.385/440. 

     The crown hit a three-year low of 44.940 per euro early on 

 Thursday on heavy hard currency buying by domestic banks, but it 

 later rebounded as foreign banks took profits from their short 

 crown positions. 

     "We eased a bit early today as a result of a strong 

 overnight euro/dollar performance... Mainly domestic clients 

 were buying (cheap dollars) and some foreign subjects could be 

 seen too," said Slovenska Sporitelna dealer Juraj Zabadal. 

     Zabadal said the crown remained under pressure, but he did 

 not expect huge jumps throughout the day. 

     "The downward trend continues, but I don't think we'll see 

 big jumps. I think the crown will stay within the 44.600/800 

 to-the-euro range today. But we might test the 45.000 level 

 quite soon, maybe within a few days," he said. 

 The Slovak unit is now at levels where the central bank

intervened to support it in June. But dealers do not expect the 

 bank to step into the market again as current price movements do 

 not appear to be fuelled by speculative selling. 

     Zabadal also said he did not expect central bank action if 

 the currency continued weakening at its current, slow pace. 

     The central bank has said a range of 44.000-45.000 crowns to 

 the euro is justified by economic fundamentals, but it also 

 warned earlier this week that it was monitoring the unit's 

 movements and would be ready to act in case of sharp jumps. 

 The crown is expected to gradually weaken as Slovakia 

 approaches September elections that will decide whether the 

 country will be invited to join the EU and NATO. 

 The nationalist HZDS party of autocratic ex-premier Vladimir 

 Meciar - which is unacceptable to the EU and NATO - is 

 currently ahead in the polls. But analysts say it increasingly 

 unlikely that it will be able to find partners to form a 

 government.

title: Slovak crown eases, seen weaker on cheaper dollar.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 16 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 eased slightly against the euro in moderate Tuesday


 morning activity, and dealers said the unit could weaken further 

 as local corporate clients seemed eager to buy cheaper dollars. 

     The crown was quoted at 44.570/600 to its key reference 

currency, the euro, as of 0730 GMT, compared with 44.539/589 

 late on Monday. It was stronger to the dollar, at 44.310/350 

 from 44.325/365. 

     The crown weakened on Monday as domestic companies snapped 

 cheaper dollars following the euro's rise over parity with the 

 greenback. 

     "We see quite strong bids, and interest in buying hard 

currencies, so we might move towards 44.700 (per euro)," said 

 Slovenska Sporitelna trader Juraj Zabadal. 

     Dealers said the crown could be also influenced by the Czech 

 unit's moves as the two neighbouring currencies often move in 

 tandem. 

     The Czech crown was slightly stronger versus the euro on 

 Tuesday morning, at 29.300/330, but the market was expected to 

 be volatile as players would keep eyes on the central bank for a 

 possible intervention against the unit's strength. 

     Traders see the Slovak crown moving between 44.500-44.700 

 per euro on Tuesday, and they do not expect the Slovak central 

 bank to step into the market and prop up the unit even though it 

 trades near last intervention levels from end-June. 

     They added the central bank could intervene to stop the 

 crown weakening if it fell quickly to around 45.000 per euro.

title: Slovak crown up but seen weak as polls approach.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 12 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 firmed slightly on Friday and was seen following the


 neighbouring Czech unit, but dealers said room for significant 

 strengthening ahead of September 20-21 elections was limited. 

     The market also played down $2.7 billion the government 

 received on Thursday for the sale of a controlling stake in gas 

 monopoly SPP, as the central bank has agreed to keep the funds 

 off the market in a special account to avoid rocking the crown. 

     Players said although the crown has weakened to near levels 

 that sparked central bank intervention to prop up the currency

 last month, they did not expect further action by the bank 

 unless there was a sharp move weaker. 

     The crown was trading at 44.579/629 to its key reference 

currency, the euro, at 0745 GMT, from 44.630/670 late on 

 Thursday. It was at 45.090/129 to the dollar, from 45.550/850. 

     "We could be influenced by moves on the euro/Czech. At the 

 moment I think we are in a (easing) channel," said Tatra Banka 

 dealer Boris Somorovsky. 

     "There are more and more signals coming from abroad that the 

 elections will be crucial, so I think at the moment it is not 

 the time to invest in the Slovak crown, because we don't really 

 know what the next government will look like." 

     Foreign investors have approached the crown with caution 

 ahead of the general elections due to worries that autocratic 

 ex-Premier Vladimir Meciar's HZDS party could retake power, 

 which would sink Slovakia's aim of NATO and EU entry. 

     Meciar currently leads opinion polls with around 25 percent 

 support, but he could be blocked from forming a government if 

 other parties -- who have almost unanimously rejected working 

 with him in power -- join together to create a cabinet. 

     Dealers expected the crown to stay in a tight range from 

 44.500-45.850 in the near term, and they did not expect the 

central bank to intervene unless the weak support level was 

 broken quickly. 

     "We don't see the central bank coming into the market unless 

 we move very quickly towards 45.000 (crowns to the euro)... this 

 may depend on euro/Czech moves," Somorovsky said. 

     The Slovak central bank intervened in several rounds last 

 month to support its unit, which was under pressure due to 

 political and macroeconomic risks, starting to buy crowns at 

 around 44.900 per euro and then continuing propping it up at 

 stronger levels. 

     The Czech central bank said on Thursday that it was ready to 

 act to drive its currency down from recent record highs. The 

 Czech and Slovak currencies often move in tandem.

title: Slovak crown flat in quiet trade, expected to ease.
