BRATISLAVA, June 21 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 was virtually flat at the open with no activity on


 Friday, and dealers said it could ease in the near term but were 

 carefully watching the for potential central bank action. 

     The crown was quoted at 44.349/399 at 0755 GMT to its key 

 reference currency, the euro, from 44.366/416 late on Thursday. 

 It was at 45.887/997 to the dollar, from 45.998/032. 

     The crown has eased in recent months due to worries over the 

 fiscal gap and upcoming elections expected to decide whether 

 Slovakia joins NATO and the EU in around 2004. 

     It dropped to three year low to the euro of 44.92 on Monday, 

 sparking intervention by the central bank. The bank came into 

 the market again on Tuesday in a series of interventions that 

 ended with the bank buying crowns at around 44.400 to the euro. 

 "It's unchanged, no activity... We expect that we will stay 

 in a range of 44.300-44.600, and we could move towards a weaker 

 crown because of demand for forex, which is quite strong," said 

 Tatra Banka dealer Boris Somorovsky. 

     "I don't think the crown should break the 44.300 level and 

 strengthen, I would rather expect it to stay in this range until 

 new impulses or new facts the market can use for further 

 trading." 

     The bank has said an exchange rate of between 44.000 and 

 45.000 to the euro reflects the performance of the Slovak

 economy, and dealers said they did not expect further 

intervention if weakening came at a slow rate in that range. 

     "If the weakening is not dramatic, and if it is more or less 

 slow, I don't expect them to intervene. But if it is very 

 illiquid... and there are aggressive moves, they should step in 

 to help the crown," said Somorovsky.

title: Slovak  crown firms on another cbank  intervention .
text:

 firmed against the euro on Tuesday, after the central

     The crown closed at 44.35/40 to its key reference currency,

 in a week. The bank started to support the crown on June 11 with

  The market expects the crown to remain under pressure, as

     The Slovak unit is expected to see higher volatility with a 

 prevailing weakening tendency ahead of September general 

 elections, which are considered as crucial for deciding whether

title: Emerging  FX - Slovak intervention  buoys crown, zloty dips.
text:
LONDON, June 18 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown forged higher against the euro on Tuesday as the central bank intervened to support it for the second day running. 

 Elsewhere, the zloty slipped on market caution ahead of a meeting between the Polish President and central bank members to discuss monetary policy, while the Israeli shekel fell after another Palestinian suicide bomb attack. 

 The Slovak National Bank intervened to defend the crown on Monday and was in the market again on Tuesday, selling euros around the 44.70 crown level . 

 "We started at around 44.70. I will not say to what level we will continue...(but) we've said we find the 44.50 level as favoured," central bank Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters. 

 Analysts were sceptical on whether the intervention would have any more than a short-term impact on the market. "The one thing in (the central bank's) favour is that the crown is not a widely followed or traded market," said one London analyst. 

 That has helped the crown avoid being targeted for attack by speculators, despite Slovakia running large current account and fiscal deficits, the analyst said. 

 However, pressure on the crown is likely to increase as political uncertainty mounts heading into September's national elections. 

 "People going to take it very cautiously ahead of the poll...no-one is going to be getting into the market, while people already there will be hedging," said Michael Every, emerging markets analyst at Royal Bank of Canada. 

 The nationalist HZDS party, led by the autocratic former Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar are currently ahead in the polls ahead of the September vote. 

 At 0935 GMT, the crown traded at 44.4250 to the euro from 44.52 late on Tuesday and at 46.913 to the dollar from 47.17. 

 ZLOTY EASES 

 The zloty drifted lower ahead of a meeting between Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski and top central bankers at 1330 GMT to discuss the ongoing dispute between the central bank and the government over interest rates and foreign exchange policy. 

 Kwasniewski has said he would block any attempt by the leftist government to try and dilute the bank's independence, but has also said he sees room for a further rate cut. 

 Another ultra-benign Polish inflation reading on Monday further increased the pressure on the Monetary Policy Council to cut rates again. 

 Polish consumer prices rose 1.9 percent year-on-year in May - a new post-communist record low and down from three percent in April. "We've seen local corporates pretty active buying euros against the zloty in the past week," said one London trader. 

 "They're not so much worried about a change in the foreign exchange regime, but from intervention or at least stronger words from central bankers." he added. 

 The zloty traded at 3.8276 to the euro from 3.817 and at 4.044 to the dollar from 4.048. 

 The Israeli shekel fell off recent highs against the dollar after a Palestinian suicide bomber blew himself up on a bus in Jerusalem killing at least 17 people. 

 Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon vowed to fight "Palestinian terror" on a visit to the scene. 

 The shekel traded at 4.9320 to the dollar from 4.9240.

title: UPDATE 2- Slovak  cbank  intervenes  again to boost crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, June 18 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) intervened on the foreign exchange market for the third time in a week on Tuesday, boosting the crown by almost one percent and said it was ready to act again if necessary. 

 The Slovak unit has been under pressure since end-April due to concerns about the government overshooting its budget deficit target and uncertainty ahead of general elections in September. 

 The bank started to support the crown on June 11 with its first direct intervention since January 2001, boosting the currency from around 44.800. 

 It did so again on Monday at 44.920 crowns to the euro, a three-year low and more than eight percent off near all-time highs hit in April, but Tuesday's intervention still appeared to have surprised the market. 

 "We started at around 44.700. I will not say to what level we will continue," Central bank Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters shortly after the intervention began. 

 Traders said the bank had fought against the continuing downward draught by buying crowns until it managed to push the unit up to around 44.300. The crown traded at 44.430/470 by 1150 GMT, two hours after the last intervention. 

 "We keep watching (the market) and we're ready to act accordingly to developments," said Szulenyi. He declined to give a desired exchange rate level but earlier said 44.5 per euro was a "favoured level". 

 The central bank also declined to say how much of its hard currency reserves it had spent to support the crown but dealers estimate the amount to be up to 150 million euros spread over the three interventions. 

 Szulenyi also rejected market speculation that the central bank had been defending the 45.000 level against the euro. 

 The bank has in the past said it has an internal range within which it wants the currency to move, saying the range could move according to economic performance, mainly in the external balance. 

 MORE INTERVENTION SEEN AHEAD 

 Analysts said the NBS would likely be forced to continue intervening to fight off the speculators as September's general elections approach. 

 "I think they will have to keep acting for maybe another week, if they really want to support the current levels and to beat the speculators. But I don't see it a huge problem, as the market volumes are low," said CSOB dealer Richard Brza. 

 Some dealers expect the crown will breach the psychological 45.000 support level ahead of the September 20-21 ballot. 

 The vote will be crucial to Slovakia's hopes to join the European Union and NATO. A victory by autocratic ex-Premier Vladimir Meciar, currently leading in the polls, could hinder Slovakia's integration chances. 

 American and EU officials have repeatedly warned that Meciar's return to power would jeopardise Slovakia's chances for entry into the two institutions. 

 Meciar was accused of backsliding on democratic and economic reforms while he was in power and Slovakia was overlooked when NATO expanded into post-Communist Europe in 1999.

title: Slovak  c.bank  intervenes  again to boost crown.
text:

title: Slovak  crown firms after cbank  intervention .
text:

 higher against the euro on Monday, after the central bank's

 earlier in the day.

currency, the euro, from 44.680/740 at Friday's close. It was at

 dealer said, adding he saw a short-term trading range for the

 elections, which are considered as crucial for deciding whether

title: Slovak  cbank confirms  intervening  to support crown.

title: Slovak crown firms on better-than-expected Q1 GDP.
text:
BRATISLAVA, June 13 (Reuters) - Better-then-expected 

 Slovakian economic growth data for the first quarter of 2002 

 helped the Slovak crown to firm versus the euro 

 early on Thursday, but dealers said the outlook remained 

 uncertain. 

     The crown, which has been under pressure due to fiscal and 

 trade balance risks, was at 44.480/520 to its key reference 

currency, the euro, at around 0840 GMT, from 44.510/570 late on 

 Wednesday. 

     It was at 47.150/200 against the dollar, from 47.130/200. 

     The Slovak central bank directly intervened to support the 

 crown on Tuesday after the unit hit 44.800 per euro, its weakest 

 level since summer 1999. 

     The intervention boosted the currency, but dealers said 

 afterwards they saw persistent pressure -- mainly from domestic 

 corporate clients -- which threatened to push the unit back to 

 weaker levels soon. 

     Early on Thursday, the Slovak Statistics Office said the 

 country's GDP grew a real 3.9 percent, year-on-year, in the 

 January-March period, the same annual rise as in the last 

 quarter of 2001. 

     A Reuters survey of analysts earlier this week showed the 

 market predicting a real annual increase of 3.4 percent. 

     "The GDP data were good and perhaps it helped to boost the 

 crown a bit. We were about to go to around 44.600 (to the euro) 

 early in the morning, but then the trend turned around, to the 

 current levels," said Slovenska Sporitelna dealer Miroslav 

 Morhac. 

     Morhac said the unit was boosted by both domestic and 

 foreign players. 

     "Domestic clients appear to show some confidence to the 

 crown again, as they were already also selling (foreign 

 exchange)," he said.

 current bullish mood was. The Slovak unit has been widely 

 expected to come under pressure again as the country moves 

 closer to general elections, scheduled for September.

title: Emerging  FX -Turk Lira at new 2002 lows,Slovak crown calms.
text:
LONDON, June 12 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira took another hit on Wednesday, dropping to new seven month lows against the dollar on growing fears that Turkey's governing coalition is in danger of collapse. 

 Elsewhere, the Slovak crown steadied at higher levels after intervention-inspired gains on Tuesday, with the main emerging European currencies generally trading with a subdued tone. 

 The lira fell around one-and-a-half percent against the greenback following comments from nationalist Deputy Prime Minister Devlet Bahceli on Tuesday, in which he renewed his warning that the government could collapse. 

 "The key question is whether all these political manoeuvrings undermine the IMF (International Monetary Fund) programme," said Gregory Kronsten, emerging markets analyst at WestLB. 

 "On the face of it they don't, but if market confidence evaporates and everyone heads for the door then it could cause problems," he added. 

 Bahceli's main gripe is over sensitive political reforms aimed at meeting European Union entrance criteria. He accused his two coalition partners of portraying his party (the MHP) as a force blocking the country's progress towards EU entry. 

 But the biggest threat to the coalition remains the health of Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit. Analysts fear that if he is forced to stand down it could be the trigger for early elections. 

 Ecevit appeared in public on Sunday, for the first time in over a week, but said he still needed a few more weeks to recover from the string of ailments that hospitalised him last month. 

 At 1000 GMT, the lira traded at 1,529,000 to the dollar on the interbank market from 1,510,000 at Tuesday's close. 

 SLOVAK CROWN CALMER 

 The Slovak crown settled at higher levels after Tuesday's intervention-inspired gains, with local dealers saying the central bank's action was likely to set a floor for the crown in the near term. 

 The crown traded at 44.54 to the euro up from Tuesday's intervention level of 44.80. 

 Meanwhile, tension between politicians and central banks in the region continued to simmer. 

 In Hungary, the central bank said a government plan to set up a supervisory body at the bank was at odds with its independence and EU practice. 

 The new cabinet, which took power last month, submitted a proposal to parliament on Tuesday to amend the central bank law and set up a committee to supervise its operations, but not monetary policy. 

 "It's not so much the supervisory body as the government's interference on exchange rate policy that really concerns the central bank," said Natalia Gurushina, emerging markets analyst at Deutsche Bank. 

 "The worry is that (the committee) will be used as a conductor through which the government can influence policy," she added. 

 The bank has been at odds with the new government on inflation and exchange rate policy, with the latter keen to dampen forint strength that it believes is dragging on exports and growth. 

 A similar debate is going on in Poland, where the government has called for a shift in exchange rate policy in order to weaken the zloty. 

 So far Poland's central bank has stood firm in opposing a shift - policy cannot be changed without its approval. 

 Bank Governor Leszek Balcerowicz believes lax fiscal policy lies at the root of zloty strength, with a bloated budget deficit drawing in portfolio capital. 

 He repeated on Wednesday his call for the government to curb the budget deficit next year to help cap the Polish unit's strength.

title: Slovak  crown up as cbank  intervenes , seen stable.
text:
BRATISLAVA, June 11 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 reversed a six-week decline on Tuesday after the central


 bank intervened to support the ailing currency and dealers said

 the crown's sharp decline earlier on Tuesday. 

     He would not disclose the amount of hard currency used in 

 the intervention but traders estimated the total volume was 

 around 50 million euros. 

     "The strongest point was 44.250, but part of the move was 

 caused by stop-losses of those who were playing on further 

 weakening... Domestic importers then bought relatively cheaper 

 hard currencies," said Robert Hakszer of CSOB bank. 

     Dealers said the central bank's intervention should put a 

 near-term floor on the crown but most market watchers predict a 

 gradual depreciation in longer term, mainly due to the expected 

 uncertainty ahead of important general elections in September. 

 The central bank has in the past said it has an internal 

 corridor within which it wants the crown to move, saying the 

 range could move according to economic development, mainly in 

 the external balance. 

 Dealers said the central bank had now shown that the lower

title: Emerging  FX - Intervention  boosts  Slovak  crown, shekel soft.
text:
LONDON, June 11 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened to defend the crown on Tuesday, acting on recent verbal warnings that its recent fall had been too rapid. 

 Elsewhere, the Israeli shekel dropped back close to last week's record lows against the dollar as Israeli forces extended their forays into Palestinian areas in the West Bank. 

 The Slovak central bank confirmed it had entered the market to bolster the weak crown at the 44.80 level to the euro , triggering a jump of around 0.7 percent. 

 "Its not a huge surprise because they warned verbally last week, but whether it will prove that successful is another question," said Adam Slater, emerging markets analyst at Credit Agricole Indosuez. 

 The central bank's Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters last Thursday that the bank would react if the crown continued to show daily falls of one percent or more. 

 "Its a thin market and the central bank has traditionally been able to exercise some control. But the fundamentals still look pretty weak...I suspect this may not be the way to burst the speculative bubble that has developed," said Slater. 

 Other analysts said they were surprised the intervention came this week, with volatility not as great as it had been the previous week. 

 "I think it would be dangerous for the bank to be targeting a specific level with elections coming up, it would be better to stick to the line that it is volatility that worries them," said Jeff Gable, emerging markets analyst at Deutsche Bank. 

 Gable said intervention was a high-risk game given the danger of speculative outflows in the run up to national elections in September. 

 Investors are worried about the prospect of authoritarian ex-Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar's HZDS party winning power - they currently lead in the polls. 

 At 0940 GMT the crown traded at 44.34 to the euro from 44.67 late on Monday and at 46.86 to the dollar from 47.16. 

 SHEKEL RESUMES SLIDE 

 Fresh Israeli raids in the West Bank kept up the tension in the region and helped put the shekel back on the defensive on Tuesday, after it bounced the previous day following a Bank of Israel rate hike. 

 Analysts said the central bank looked to be trying to halt the shekel's slide at around the five level against the dollar and did not rule out another near-term rate hike. 

 "The clear interpretation is that the central bank has drawn a line in the sand at five and is prepared to respond with further intra-meeting moves if required," said Alex Garrard, emerging markets analyst at UBS Warburg. 

 "There was no data between the last two rate hikes, but its likely that the central bank had some insight into how inflation was shaping up for May," he added. 

 The bank is worried about the inflationary implications of the shekel's fall over 11 percent so far this year. 

 Consumer prices jumped by 1.5 percentage points in April, for a cumulative rise of 3.9 percent since the start of the year - already above the government's target of two-to-three percent for the year. 

 The shekel traded at 4.9720 to the dollar from 4.9550 late on Monday. 

 Elsewhere, the forint showed little reaction to another positive inflation reading. Hungarian May consumer price inflation eased to an annual rate of 5.6 percent, from 6.1 percent in April, in line with expectations.

title: UPDATE 2- Slovak  cbank  intervenes  to prop up crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, June 11 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market to support its hard-pressed currency for the first in more than a year on Tuesday, driving the crown up against the euro. 

 The market expects the central bank's action to stabilise the crown in the medium term, but dealers were quick to say that the unit was still likely to come under pressure in the run-up to a crucial general election in September. 

 The central bank made good on its threat last week to directly intervene, stepping into the market by selling euros when the crown fell to 44.800 to the single currency, its lowest level since the summer of 1999. 

 The bank's Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters the intervention, the first since January 2001, was triggered by the crown's sharp decline earlier in the session. 

 He refused to comment on market speculation that the bank would not let the crown drop below 45.000 versus the euro. 

 "I said sometime ago that we will act if the crown continues to weaken sharply... today's move was too quick, there were some deals done at 44.900," Szulenyi said. 

 He would not disclose the amount of hard currency used in the intervention but traders estimated the total volume was around 50 million euros. 

 "The bank wanted to prevent the crown from testing 45.000, which seemed likely after morning stop-losses. I think we should see stabilisation now, between 44.300-44.600," said Tatra Banka trader Boris Somorovsky. 

 The crown has been on a downward path since the end of April when concerns about widening fiscal and trade gaps knocked it off all-time highs of 41.400 versus the single currency. 

 By 1300 GMT the crown was trading at 44.470/525 against the euro compared with Tuesday's 44.280/330. 

 PRE-ELECTION PRESSURE 

 The bank's intervention should put a near-term floor on the crown but most market watchers expect a gradual depreciation in longer term. 

 The central bank has in the past said it has an internal corridor within which it wants the crown to move, saying the range could move according to economic development, mainly in the external balance. 

 "The macroeconomic situation has not changed, so the market will wait for more data, like foreign trade, to judge the fundamentals," said a Bratislava-based trader at a foreign bank. "The central bank showed its target now, so 44.800-45.500 per (euro) would be considered as intervention level for some time. But, we will check the 45.000-per-euro level again before the elections," he said. 

 September elections will be crucial for deciding on Slovakia's invitation to join the European Union and NATO, as a victory of autocratic ex-Premier Vladimir Meciar, currently leading the polls, is likely to impede integration chances. 

 United States and EU officials have repeatedly warned that Meciar's return to power would jeopardise Slovakia's chances for entry into the NATO and the EU because of undemocratic policies he pursued during his previous term as prime minister which ended in 1998.

title: UPDATE 2-Slovak cbank says will act if crown falls further.
text:
BRATISLAVA, June 6 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened verbally on Thursday to prevent further falls in the edgy crown and said it would step directly into the market to support the currency if its recent sharp decline went on. 

 Unlike other east European currencies which have gained on foreign inflows linked to confidence in their joining the EU, the Slovak crown has weakened due to worries over widening budget and foreign trade gaps and political uncertainty. The crown's decline accelerated on Wednesday and Thursday, with the unit hitting 18-month lows. 

Central Bank Governor Marian Jusko's comments on Wednesday that he welcomed the recent shift to weakening from an uptrend earlier in the year sparked a sell-off. 

 The unit briefly rebounded on Thursday after the bank's treasurer said the market's reaction was overdone and that more depreciation would not be justified by economic fundamentals. 

 "If this continues, and we see more daily falls of, say, one percent, then we will obviously react. But I will not say any concrete level," Central Bank's Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters in a brief telephone interview. 

 Market players said the central bank may soon need to make good on its direct intervention threat if it wanted to hold the crown steady. The currency is expected to remain nervous and prone to slide ahead of key September elections. 

 On Thursday Slovakia set September 20-21 as the date for the general election which will effectively decide if the country enters NATO and the European Union alongside its neighbours and if economic reform continues or stalls. 

 A return to power by authoritarian ex-premier Vladimir Meciar, whose party leads in the polls, would scupper Slovak chances of winning a NATO membership invitation at the Prague summit in November and leave the country isolated. 

 DOWNSIDE PRESSURE 

 The crown traded at around 44.43/47 to its key reference currency, the euro, shortly before Szulenyi's comments, compared with levels of 43.86/92 before Wednesday's statements by Jusko. 

 "The current level of the crown corresponds to economic fundamentals, and to the performance of the economy... I think the crown should now stabilise at around the present rates," Szulenyi said. 

 "It looks like we will go higher again (crown easing). The market might try to push it further, and we can soon test 44.50 (per euro)," said Slovenska Sporitelna trader Vladimir Gajdos. 

 Some foreign players would be tempted to try to find the central bank's intervention level by pushing the crown weaker. "The trend is clear. I don't think that anyone will come to this atmosphere and build crown positions," one foreign bank dealer said. 

 "The elections are coming, and the uncertainty is the reasons for buying (hard currencies). We are in a completely different situation from the Czechs," he added. 

 Analysts said the central bank might have wanted a weaker crown but it underestimated the market's sensitivity and may need to spend some reserves to prevent further decline. 

 "Everybody was expecting crown weakening before elections. But this is not the elections, this looks like a wish of the central bank, though executed in a little bit unfortunate way," said VUB bank analyst Pavol Popp. 

 A falling crown could help Slovakia's trade deficit, which was one of the reasons given for a rate hike in April. Some analysts also said that a weaker currency will mean more crown income from privatisation deals.

title: Slovak crown opens flat, may ease later.
text:

 was flat early on Monday, with dealers saying the unit


 might rather ease later in the day, on the expected slide of the

     "We're closely watching the Czech (unit), which at the

     However, Tatar said no trading could have been seen on the 

 Slovak market since the open. 

  "The market is pretty flat. There are some bids hanging at 

 around 41.45 (to the euro), but no movement was seen so far." 

     He added he saw the crown trading within a range of between 

 41.45 and 41.51 to the euro throughout the day. 

     Last week, the Slovak crown hit its all-time highs, driven 

 by the bullish Czech currency, but retreated from the levels on 

 Friday. 

     The crown briefly touched 41.33/37 to the euro early on 

 Friday, but some investors took profit from the crown's recent

     The Slovak crown, which has gained over three percent this 

 year, has followed the neighbouring Czech crown as some

 The Czech central bank intervened twice in as many weeks to

 Dealers do not expect the Slovak central bank to step into

title: Emerging  FX -Venezuelan bolivar steady on Chavez ousting.
text:
LONDON, April 12 (Reuters) - The Venezuelan bolivar showed held steady in Europe after Friday's confirmation that president Hugo Chavez had resigned, having jumped against the dollar on Thursday as the pressure on him mounted. 

 Elsewhere, the Czech crown fell from record high levels against the euro following verbal intervention from the central bank governor, while the Turkish lira hit new nine-month highs versus the dollar on growing optimism on the domestic economy. 

 The bond market cheered Chavez's departure but dealers say it may not be an unequivocal positive for the currency given it is also likely to bring oil prices down, one of Venezuela's main revenue sources. 

 The bolivar hit two-month highs against the dollar on Thursday as another mass anti-Chavez demonstration upped the pressure on the unpopular president. 

 Venezuela's armed forces chief Lucas Rincon appeared on national television on Friday to confirm that Chavez had resigned following the demonstration in Caracas, in which at least 10 people died and over 80 were injured. 

 "There's almost a sense of euphoria in the markets, with the view taking hold that Venezuela is now back in the real world and can move forward," said Peter West, chief Latin American economist at BBVA Securities in London. 

 "However, once that euphoria dies down we are likely to enter a period of reflection and it's far from clear what comes next," he added. 

 One of the main factors keeping Chavez in office was the lack of a clear alternative and analysts said that a period of uncertainty was now likely to ensue until elections can be held. 

 Pedro Carmona, the head of Venezuela's leading business association, Fedecamaras, said he would head a transition government that would lead to free elections. 

 Dealers in London said there had been little trade in the bolivar despite the news, the unit is sparsely traded in Europe. 

 The recent rally in crude prices had been inspired in part by a six-week oil workers' strike in Venezuela, and prices immediately came under pressure as news of Chavez's ousting emerged. 

 At 0925 GMT the bolivar traded at 850 to the dollar . 

 VERBAL INTERVENTION DENTS CROWN 

 The Czech crown was brought down from earlier record highs below 30 to the euro as Czech National Bank governor Zdenek Tuma pledged to continue efforts to weaken the currency. 

 The crown eased as the market latched on to an opinion article in the business daily Hospodarske Noviny, in which Tuma said the bank's policy would aim to deflate what he called an "exchange rate bubble" that could be dangerous for the country's economic stability. 

 However, dealers increasingly see the central bank as losing credibility in its efforts to slow down the crown's appreciation, with two interventions within a week failing to stop the currency hitting fresh record highs. 

 "The central bank is out the picture. They say there is no fundamental reason for the crown to be here, but if you look at the amount of portfolio inflows there is a every reason," said one London dealer. 

 "I would say there are good fundamental reasons why people want to buy Czech companies," he added. 

 The dealer said the market was probably now getting over-stretched on the upside and that players would be looking to take profits. However, he added that any weakness was likely to be short-lived. 

 The crown traded at 30.11 to the euro from 30.04 and at 34.195 to the dollar from 33.97. The Slovak crown followed its Czech counterpart to record highs against the euro around early on, before being pegged back. 

 Strong foreign investment inflows are also buoying the Slovak unit, but the central bank has been more relaxed about its rise. 

 Slovak central bank Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters on Thursday that the bank had no plans to intervene at current levels. 

 The Slovak crown traded at 41.442 to the euro from 41.42 and at 47.08 to the dollar from 46.94. 

 The Turkish lira extended its rally up to nine-month peaks against the dollar on growing optimism over the domestic economic outlook. 

 An upbeat central bank survey on Thursday raised hopes that an annual inflation target of 35 percent for 2002 would be met, and boosted hopes for further rate cuts. 

 The lira traded at 1,282,500 to the dollar on the interbank market from 1,292,000 at Thursday's close.

title: Slovak crown hits record highs, c.bank unmoved.
text:

 matched an all-time high against the euro on Thursday,


 and dealers said its path following the strong Czech crown could 

 possibly lead to further gains in the near term. 

     They added that comments from the Slovak central bank (NBS)

     "We are still following the Czech crown. There was an 

 all-time high on the Czech crown (against the euro), and the 

 reaction on the Slovak was the same," said CSOB dealer Richard 

 Brza. 

     "I thought that 41.5 (Slovak crowns per euro) was a good 

 support, but it broke... I don't know where the bottom could be, 

 but 41.2 or 41.3 could be a good support. 

     Dealers said the Slovak crown could range between 41.3-41.8 

 to the euro in the near term. 

Central bank Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told 

 Reuters on Thursday the bank had no plans to intervene against 

 the crown at current levels, despite a battle in the 

 neighbouring Czech foreign exchange market, where that country's 

central bank has so far unsuccessfully tried to knock its unit 

 off of record highs. 

 Althought the Czech central bank has intervened against the 

 Czech crown twice in the last two weeks, the currency broke 

 through the 30.0 per euro level for the first time in Thursday's 

 session. 

 The Slovak central bank does not see the Slovak crown's 

 strength as having negative effects on the economy at present, 

 partially due to its relative weakness against the very strong 

 Czech unit, which is what is used to pay for a large part of 

 Slovak exports. 

 The two currencies often move in tandem as dealers hedge 

 euro positions through the Czech/Slovak pair.

title: Slovak crown slightly up, seen testing key level.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 11 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 opened slightly firmer, moving closer to all-time


 highs against the euro on Thursday morning, with dealers saying 

 it could test a key resistance level soon. 

     The crown traded at 41.50/53 to the euro as of 0730 GMT, 

 after 41.54/59 late on Wednesday. It was at 47.13/19 to the 

 dollar, from 47.24/28. 

     The Slovak crown has been influenced mainly the Czech 

currency in the past few weeks, which had repeatedly jumped to 

 new record highs before the Czech central bank intervened last 

 week and on Wednesday to knock the unit weaker. 

     "The Slovak crown's reaction to yesterday's (Czech) 

intervention was not so strong, so it looks that people think 

 the Slovak could firm further," said one foreign bank trader. 

     "The 41.50 (Slovak/euro) level will be a strong level, but I 

 think it could break eventually." 

     Some traders said the market will watch whether the Slovak 

central bank takes some action against the crown when it moves 

 closer to the all-time high of around 41.45 to the euro. 

     However, several dealers said the central bank's comments on 

 Tuesday that the crown's strength was not hurting the economy 

 could indicate that the bank did not intend to step into the 

 market.

title: Slovak crown steady, seen testing stronger levels.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 10 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 hovered near two-year highs against the euro on


 Wednesday morning, with dealers saying the unit could test 

 slightly stronger levels if the Czech crown firms further. 

     The Slovak crown was at 41.52/57 to the euro as of 0730 GMT, 

 slightly stronger from 41.54/59 late on Tuesday. It stood at 

 47.06/12 to the dollar, after 47.37/44. 

     The Slovak crown has in the past few weeks mostly followed 

 the neighbouring Czech currency, which trades around all-time 

 highs of around 30.10 per euro, as investors tend to hedge their 

 euro exposure through the Czech/Slovak pair. 

     "I think we could test 41.50 (per euro) if the Czech central 

 bank does not take any action and the Czech crown firms 

 further," said a bank trader in Bratislava. 

     "But I don't think any further firming (of the Slovak crown) 

 should be either very fast or significant, as we have already 

 seen what appeared to have been client orders to buy euros when 

 it (the Slovak crown) was at around 41.49/54." 

     The Czech central bank intervened to weaken its surging 

currency last week and dealers said further intervention, or 

 lack of it, will also set the direction for the Slovak crown in 

 the near future. 

     Dealers said they did not expect the Slovak central bank to 

intervene on the market to slow the crown's appreciation given 

 comments on Tuesday that the present strength of the currency

 was not hurting the economy. 

     The  Slovak central bank has repeatedly said it will only 

 step into the market if it sees sharp volatility rather than 

intervene against specific crown levels.

title: Slovak crown at two-year high, upside seen tight.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 9 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 firmed to two-year highs on Tuesday on the back of


 record highs reached by the neighbouring Czech crown and 

 positive comments from the Slovak central bank, dealers said. 

 But the market sees limited room for further gains as it 

 expects local clients to begin picking up cheap euros at 

 slightly stronger levels. 

     The crown was trading at 41.54/59 late on Tuesday to its key 

 reference currency, the euro, from 41.67/70 late on Monday. It 

 was at 47.37/44 to the dollar, from 47.65/79. 

     "The Slovak crown strengthened. The main impetus for this 

 was a strong firming in the Czech crown against the euro. It 

 reached its highest level against the euro ever," said Tatra 

 Banka dealer Boris Somorovsky. 

     "We are approaching an all-time high, which is around 41.5 

 (Slovak crowns to the euro). There might be tries in the next 

 session, maybe tomorrow, to test this level, but if the crown 

 strengthens past that, it would be just for a short time, and I 

 would expect orders to buy cheap euros above these levels." 

     The Czech crown hit an all-time high of 30.05/08 to the euro 

 before retreating on Tuesday to close lower, erasing the impact 

 of intervention by that country's central bank last week. The 

Slovak crown often tracks its more-heavily-traded neighbour. 

     The Slovak crown last touched 41.5 to the euro in early 

 2000, prompting repeated intervention from the Slovak central 

 bank (NBS) to knock it weaker. 

     But dealers said they were now not worried about central 

 bank action after NBS Vice Governor Elena Kohutikova said 

 earlier in the day that the strong crown was not hurting the 

 economy. 

     Traders also said such a move at this level would be very 

 expensive for the central bank which would have to expect much 

 more room to firm to justify buying crowns. 

     "To buy such expensive crowns would mean the expectations of 

 strengthening is much stronger than the 41.500 (to the euro) 

 level," Somorovsky said.

title: Slovak cbank says strong crown not hurting economy.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 9 (Reuters) - Slovak central bank (NBS) Vice Governor Elena Kohutikova said on Tuesday that the recent firming of the crown currency, which is near two-year highs, would not hurt the economy, now burdened by a wide trade gap. 

 "We are seeing a market trend for crown strengthening, rather than weakening at the moment... but the strengthening is not such that would endanger the performance of the economy," Kohutikova told a conference in Bratislava. 

 The Slovak crown firmed slightly to 41.60/66 against its key reference currency, the euro, on Tuesday, nearing the two-year high level of 41.5 crowns. In May 2000 the Slovak central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market and sold the crown when it touched the 41.5 level versus the single currency.

title: Slovak crown up slightly, seen in range.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 9 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 edged up on Tuesday in quiet trade and dealers said it


 would likely remain in a near-term tight range as investors kept 

 an eye on the Czech crown. 

 The Czech and Slovak currencies often move in tandem, as 

 dealers hedge euro exposure through the Czech/Slovak pair. 

     By 0725 GMT the Slovak crown was trading at 41.63/69 versus 

 its key reference currency, the euro, from 41.67/70 late on 

 Monday. It was at 47.63/68 against the dollar from 47.65/79. 

     "The Slovak crown strengthened a little bit. We broke the 

 41.70 (crowns to the euro) support level. We've only seen some 

 local banks selling euro against the crown and the move was not 

 sharp or quick," said CSOB dealer Richard Brza.. 

     "It's been quiet trading for the last few weeks. I think the 

 next support could be around 41.50, but I don't think we'll go 

 there for the next week. The top for the next few weeks will be 

 41.80." 

     Dealers said that the Slovak crown would probably ease if 

 the Czech central bank intervened to dampen demand for that 

currency again, as it did last week, to prevent it from pushing 

 too high. 

     They added any medium-term advance by Slovak crown was seen 

 limited as foreign players were expected to remain cautious 

 ahead of September elections seen crucial to Slovakia's entry 

 into the European Union and NATO.

title: Slovak crown steady in calm trading, eyes on Czech.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 8 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 was only slightly changed in listless trading on


 Monday, and a lack of domestic impulses left the Czech unit's 

 developments the only moving factor for the Slovak currency. 

     The Slovak crown was quoted at 41.67/70 to its key reference 

currency, the euro, late on Monday, after 41.69/75 at Friday's 

 close. It was at 47.65/79 to the dollar, from 47.40/47.

 in the past few weeks as investors like to hedge their euro 

 exposure through the Czech/Slovak pair. 

     The Czech central bank intervened on the forex market to 

 knock its currency off record highs last week and dealers said 

 the market was now divided on whether to try and push it 

 stronger again. The Czech crown was at 30.76/78 to the euro late 

 on Monday 

     The Slovak crown did not react to Monday's release of 

 better-than-expected consumer price inflation data, which showed 

 the annual core and headline rates at 2.7 and 3.6 percent, 

 respectively, both all-time lows. 

     Dealers said the Slovak corporate flows appeared to be well 

 balanced at present, and they predicted the Slovak crown to move 

 in a tight range of 41.65-41.75 for the near future, barring any 

 unexpected large company order.

title: Slovak crown opens flat, seen following Czech.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 8 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 opened flat on Monday, shrugging off


 better-than-expected inflation data, as investors kept an eye on 

 the neighbouring Czech crown for further direction, dealers 

 said. 

    They said the Slovak market was closely watching to see 

 whether the Czech central bank (CNB) would continue to intervene

 to knock that country's currency lower, as it did last Thursday 

 after the Czech crown reached all-time high levels versus the 

 euro. 

     By 0740 GMT the Slovak crown was quoted at 41.70/75 versus 

 its key reference currency, the euro, from 41.69/75 late on 

 Friday. It was at 47.52/59 against the dollar from 47.40/47.

 has not been a move. I expect that we should stay at this level, 

 or maybe the Slovak crown could weaken, but it will depend on 

 the Czech crown," said Slovenska Sporitelna dealer Vladimir 

 Gajdos. 

     "Slovak inflation figures were very good, but we have seen 

 no move yet on the market. There has only been price checking." 

     The Czech crown has been the strongest influence on the 

 Slovak unit in the past few weeks. The two often move in tandem 

 because investors tend to hedge their euro exposure through the 

 Czech/Slovak pair. 

 On Friday, analysts said the CNB would probably have to 

intervene more forcefully to stop the Czech crown strengthening 

 to firmer-than-desired levels. 

 Data released earlier in the day also showed Slovak core 

 inflation, the central bank's key monetary goal, was flat month 

 on month for an all-time-low annual rate of 2.7 percent. 

 Headline inflation was also flat on the month for an annual 

 rate of 3.6 percent. Both figures were well under market 

 expectations. 

 Dealers said they expected the Slovak crown to stick to a 

 tight range between 41.65-41.85 versus the euro, barring any 

 major move on the Czech market. 

 "A possibility of intervention of the CNB against the Czech 

 crown remains high after a not very successful intervention

 (last Thursday). If the central bank intervenes again, the 

Slovak crown will weaken," Volksbank said in a report.

title: Slovak crown end slightly higher, in tight range.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 5 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown



 ended a touch higher on Friday but trading activity


 was light as investors remained cautious after the neighbouring

 Thursday.

 had benefited from the Czech unit's recent rapid firming.

 trades were matched," said Tatra Banka dealer Boris Somorovsky.

 the euro/Czech market was stabilised after yesterday's 

intervention. I expect us to stay in 41.65-41.90 range in the 

 near term and we'll see what happens." 

     February inflation data, due to be released at around 0700 

 GMT on Monday, was expected to have little if any impact on the 

 Slovak crown, dealers said. 

     Market players were now awaiting upcoming sales of 49 

 percent stakes in Slovakia's three regional energy utilities, 

 which are expected to earn the government hundreds of millions 

 of euros. 

     "This is the thing that might bring some potential pressure 

 for crown strengthening, but we aren't sure about the timing of 

 this deal," said Somorovsky.

 April 12 and the state is expected to evaluate the offers early 

 the following week.

title: Slovak crown seen stable in technical trading.

title: Slovak  crown falls on Czech  intervention .

title: Slovak crown up, following Czech unit.

title: Slovak crown closes flat, eyeing Czech unit.

title: Emerging  FX -Zloty lower on Polish  central bank  concerns.
text:
LONDON, March 1 (Reuters) - The zloty edged down to two and half week lows against the euro on Friday amid renewed concerns over the independence of the Polish central bank. 

 In the neighbouring Czech Republic, the central bank was also in focus. Thursday's meeting of the Czech central bank surprised markets by the absence of any hardline comment aimed at talking down the ever resilient crown. 

 Dealers said they expected appreciation pressure on the Czech currency but were mindful of the central bank's proven readiness to intervene in order to prevent any sharp firming. 

 Hungarian growth figures had little effect on the forint with market attention directed towards forthcoming elections. 

 Elsewhere, the Russian rouble continued to hover just below 31 to the dollar and the South African rand firmed slightly on central bank comments and the affirmation of the country's credit ratings by Standard & Poors. 

 POLISH CENTRAL BANK INDEPENDENCE 

 The zloty edged lower to 3.6720 to the euro as the issue of central bank independence dominated concerns. 

 The Polish parliament on Friday resumes discussions over a resolution scolding the central bank for damaging the economy with high interest rates. 

 The move follows Wednesday's controversial decision by the central bank to leave rates on hold. The main Polish market rate stands at 10 percent, 6.5 percentage points above inflation. 

 "This is not going to help the zloty but I don't think it will crush it either unless they do something really drastic with the central bank's independence," said one trader. 

 Investors are waiting to see if the resolution will be followed by a bill, proposed by junior goverment coalition members, aimed at watering down the central bank's inflation fighting mandate and adding more dovish members to the 10-seat rate-setting panel. 

 Dealers said worse-than-expected current account deficit figures for January, which showed the monthly shortfall widening to $826 million from $500 million in December, also weighed on the Polish unit on Friday. 

 The Czech crown opened steady versus the euro but analysts said they expected the 31.50 level to be tested within the next few days after the central bank maintained a stony silence on the robustness of the crown. 

 The Czech currency set a two-month high just shy of 31.5 on Thursday after the central bank left interest rates unchanged and kept the market guessing as to if and when it might intervene to weaken what it says is an overvalued crown. 

 "That was a surprise. I get the feeling everyone was expecting them to talk down the crown," said Dwyfor Evans, emerging market economist at Bank of America. 

Central bank and government officials are concerned that a stronger crown - the currency has already hit all time highs against the euro in recent months - would undermine the country's economic recovery. 

 Vice-Governor Ludek Niedermayer said after the bank's monetary policy meeting on Thursday the bank was not overly concerned about day to day market volatility and stuck to the standard policy line the bank can intervene if and when needed. 

 "The central bank has gone in directly or verbally in the last three or four months. The market knows that should euro/Czech fall below 31.50 there's likely to be some form of intervention," said Evans. 

 The Slovak crown fell off highs early on Friday as the market reacted negatively to Thursday's news that there was only one bid for gas company SPP in Slovakia's biggest ever privatisation. 

 The crown was quoted at 41.75/80 to its key reference currency, the euro. On Thursday, the Slovak government received a sole bid for 49 percent and management control over SPP from a consortium of Gaz de France , Russian Gazprom and Germany's Ruhrgas. 

 A source close to the deal said the offered price was below, but close to, analysts' valuation of the deal of $3.0 billion. 

 Having recoverd a little from month and a half lows against the euro on Wednesday the Hungarian forint was again looking a little weaker. It was trading around 245.90 to the euro . 

 Hungary's gross domestic product (GDP) growth slowed to 3.8 percent in 2001 according to preliminary data, from 5.2 percent in the previous year, according to figures out on Friday. 

 The rand firmed about three cents to the dollar at 11.37, heartened by the central bank's confirmation that its net open forward position (NOFP), a measure of its uncovered foreign exchange liabilities, had fallen to $2.99 billion from $4.8 billion in December. 

 The unit was also supported by rating agency Standard & Poor's affirmation of the country's BBB-minus/A-3 foreign currency sovereign credit rating.

title: Emerging  FX -Czech, Slovak crowns probe higher.
text:
LONDON, Feb 22 (Reuters) - The Czech crown hit its highest levels in a week against the euro on Friday on reports of good foreign demand and receding nerves over possible central bank intervention. 

 Elsewhere, the Slovak crown rose alongside its Czech counterpart, buoyed by good news on the privatisation front earlier in the week. 

 The crown has drifted steadily higher this week despite a stern warning against excessive strength from Czech central bank governor Oldrich Dedek in a Reuters interview last week. 

 Dedek said the crown should fall to around 33 to the euro and warned that the bank was prepared to fight currency strength with all means available to it, including intervention and rate cuts. 

 However, one dealer in London said he didn't expect the central bank to step in around current levels. 

 "I still think we are some way from intervention, I don't see them coming in ahead of the 31.50 level," the dealer said. 

 Czech January trade data added to the mildly positive tone, with the deficit coming in a shade below expectations at 6.57 billion crowns. 

 Technical analysts are cautious on the near-term outlook for the euro/crown rate, saying the bias remains to the downside for the euro. 

 "It could be that we're hammering out a bottom, but I wouldn't say I'm bullish - we're still in a downward sloping trend channel," said Steve Wesiak, technical analyst at ABN Amro in Amsterdam. 

 Wesiak said key support lies around 31.46 crowns per euro, but that the market needed to take out resistance around 32.675 and then just below 33 to turn the outlook more positive. 

 At 1045 GMT, the crown traded at 31.735 to the euro from 31.79 and at 36.457 to the dollar from 36.465. 

 SLOVAK CROWN BUOYANT 

 The Slovak crown was also on the up, continuing to attract demand after good news earlier in the week on the government's plans to sell a 49 percent stake in gas monopoly SPP. 

 The leftist SDL, a member of the coalition government, had been pushing for the stake to be cut to 24 percent, but withdrew its objection to the sale without the reduction. 

 Final bids for the stake, which could rake in as much as $3 billion, are due by February 28, with France's TotalFinaElf seen as one of six likely bidders. 

 However, analysts don't see the crown's current strength giving the authorities as much cause for concern as in the Czech case. 

 "I don't think the break of 42 (crowns per euro) is likely to prompt verbal intervention and there are lots of things that could take the heat out the currency," said Stephen Gilmore, emerging markets currency strategist at Morgan Stanley. 

 Gilmore said a possible deterioration in Slovakia's current account position and nerves ahead of September elections were potential negatives for the crown, but he added that the bank remained positive on the currency over the long term. 

 The crown traded at 41.90 to the euro from 42.11 and at 48.24 to the dollar from 48.38.

intervention would lead to weakening of the SKK versus the

title: Emerging  FX -Shekel slides, politics hurts Slovak crown.
text:
LONDON, Feb 11 (Reuters) - The Israeli shekel slid to record lows against the dollar on Monday as the market bet that the central bank would not intervene to stem its decline. 

 Elsewhere, the Slovak crown eased on domestic political worries ahead of a no confidence vote in a leading government economic reformers on Wednesday, and worries over possible military moves against Iraq continued to dog the Turkish lira. 

 Dealers reported sales from local mutual funds fuelling the shekel's latest descent, with few players worried that the central bank will do anything to cushion its fall. 

 "The central bank will be concerned about a further depreciation of the shekel, but as long as it isn't reflected in an adjustment of inflation expectations I don't expect them to act," said Ousmene Mandeng, emerging markets analyst at CSFB. 

 Mutual funds have been seen as consistent shekel sellers this year after an aggressive two percent interest rate cut from the Bank of Israel last December substantially reduced their willingness to hold Israeli assets. 

 Adding to the shekel's woes was a fresh escalation of violence in the region. Israel's missiles struck the main security complex in Palestinian-ruled Gaza City on Monday, while its tanks rolled into another Palestinian enclave at Nablus. 

 The moves were a retaliation after two Palestinians sprayed gunfire at a cafe near an Israeli army base in southern Israel on Sunday, killing two women soldiers before being shot dead themselves. 

 Analysts often play down the influence of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict on shekel moves, but Mandeng at CSFB said that it was hampering the recovery of the local economy. 

 "We've had no progress on the security front and that is affecting the real economy. As long as these factors do not change, it's difficult to see the upside in the shekel," he said. 

 At 1115 GMT, the shekel traded at 4.7370 to the dollar from 4.6610 late on Friday. 

 POLITICS WEIGHS ON SLOVAK CROWN 

 The Slovak crown slipped on political worries ahead of a parliamentary no-confidence motion on Wednesday against the reformist deputy premier for the economy Ivan Miklos, moved by opposition deputies. 

 If Miklos were to go, it would be seen as a blow to the country's aspirations to join the EU in the first enlargement wave. 

 However, a senior official in the coalition-member leftist SDL party said on Friday that he did not expect his party to join the opposition move. 

 The SDL was instrumental in forcing the resignation of another leading reformer, the former finance minister Brigita Schmognerova, last month. 

 "The movements in the crown have been pretty mild as it it isn't surprising news. This isn't the first time that Miklos has faced calls for his head," said Jeff Gable, emerging markets analyst at Deutsche Bank. 

 However, Gable noted that the ruling coalition parties are tentatively scheduled to meet on Tuesday to discuss the SDL's proposals to alter the sale of the gas monopoly SPP. 

 "Its unlikely that the SDL's demands will be met and that may darken their mood somewhat. That is the risk," said Gable. 

 The Slovak crown traded at 42.50 to the euro from 42.35 and at 48.47 to the dollar from 48.45. 

 The Turkish lira fell briefly below 1.4 million to the dollar early on Monday with nerves over possible military action against Iraq still dogging sentiment. 

 Turkish president Bulent Ecevit said on Friday that Iraqi president Saddam Hussain had indicated no change of position on allowing U.N. arms inspection teams into Iraq, in response to an appeal from Turkey last week. 

 However, the local press released what it claimed were the contents of Saddam's reply over the weekend, containing none of the aggressive rhetoric rumoured in the market last week. 

 The lira traded at 1,385,000 to the dollar on the interbank market from 1,376,000 at Friday's close.

title: Slovak crown flat, strengthening seen in near term.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 4 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown was flat in narrow trade on Monday but dealers said it may strengthen in the near future if the Czech central bank (CNB) refrains from intervening against the strong Czech crown. 

 The Slovak crown closed at 42.39/50 to its key reference currency, the euro, flat from Friday's close. It was at 48.92/98 versus the dollar from 49.22/29. 

 Dealers said client orders weakened the crown earlier in the day but a major Czech bank reversed the trend at the end of the session. 

 "We expect that we could reach 42.0 crowns to the euro in the near future and I see a support level there if there is no intervention against the Czech crown or any political chaos here," said CSOB dealer Andrej Zeman. 

 The CNB has cut interest rates twice within the last 10 days and intervened on the market in an attempt to weaken the Czech crown which is now trading near all-time highs. 

 The Czech and Slovak currencies often trade in tandem.

title: Slovak crown edges down, mkt still watching cbank.

title: Slovak  cbank confirms  intervened  on Wednesday.
text:

 Dealers told Reuters one day earlier they had seen the NBS in the market when the crown weakened past the level of 44.0 to the euro and said the volumes sold were likely around 10 to 15 million euros. 

 The move was the third intervention from the central bank this year. It also entered the market twice in the first week of January at the same level, saying the crown's weakness did not reflect Slovakia's macroeconomic position. 

 Sevcovic said the bank was still watching the currency but would not specify at which level the bank would protect the crown. "Yesterday the intervention was very close to 44.0, but of course (the figure) could float," he said.

title: Slovak  crown flat, propped by cbank  intervention .

title: Emerging  FX -Euro moves main driver for Europe,rand.
text:
LONDON, Jan 5 (Reuters) - Emerging currencies in Europe recovered some ground against the euro on Friday but remained under its spell as the single currency rose across the board amid expectations that euro-zone growth will outpace the U.S. 

 The euro's push to a fresh six-month high against the dollar provided the backbone for the single currency's rise to a 2-1/2 month peak against the Czech crown, a one-month top against the zloty and a lifetime high against the South African rand. 

 However, emerging currencies held firm against the dollar which has seen its support fade as concerns over the U.S. economy's health overshadowed the stock market-led rally that followed Wednesday's surprise U.S. interest rate cut. 

 "It's still the euro and dollar that's guiding emerging currencies at the moment. It's a good environment for traders but it's still too frothy to pull in more long-term investors," said one U.S. bank emerging market analyst. 

 The Polish zloty was trading at 4.0850 per dollar to the dollar from 4.1151 late on Thursday. Against the euro, the zloty stood at 3.8976 after earlier touching a one-month low of 3.9259. 

 The Czech crown slipped to 35.34 per euro, its weakest point against the single currency since October 19. Against the dollar, the crown stood at 36.94 after earlier touching a new nine-month peak around 36.67. 

 Both Czech and Polish bond prices extended their gains amid ongoing expectations of slowing inflation and forthcoming interest rate cuts. 

 The Slovak crown edged lower against the euro but dealers said the threat of central bank intervention to support the crown on one side and a market short of euros on the other would likely keep the currency in a tight range. 

 The Slovak central bank directly intervened selling hard currency on Tuesday and Wednesday to keep the crown from slipping past the 44 per euro level, saying its weakness did not reflect Slovakia's macroeconomic position. 

 The crown stood at 43.85/90 to the euro from 43.77/85 late on Thursday. 

 The rand was last bid at 7.48 per dollar, still shy of this week's two month highs but bolstered by gains made by the euro - the currency of South Africa's major trading partners - against the dollar. 

 However, dealers said the rand's drop to a new record low against the buoyant euro would keep dollar/rand gains in check until there was more foreign investment in South African assets. 

 So far, foreigners have been wary of jumping into South Africa despite South African bond yields hitting their lowest level in seven years amid expectations that domestic interest rates could be cut early this year. 

 Local banks and institutions piled into government debt, sending yields - which move in the opposite direction to prices - on the benchmark R150 bond, due February 2005, to 11.82 percent, its lowest point since January 1994. 

 A combination of lower bond yields, a firm rand and easing oil prices have boosted chances that the Reserve Bank could cut rates when its interest-rate setting Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) starts a two-day meeting on January 18, traders said.

title: UPDATE 1- Slovak  cbank  intervenes  to prop up crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, JAN 3 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) intervened on the foreign exchange market selling hard currency for the second day running on Wednesday to support the Slovak crown at the level of 44 crowns to the euro. 

 When asked if the central bank had been in the market after reports of intervention from dealers, NBS dealer Vladimir Polhorsky said, "Yes, we were." He confirmed that the level of the intervention was at 44 crowns to the euro. 

 NBS Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi added, "According to the latest macroeconomic indicators, the NBS doesn't think that a (crown) rate above 44 crowns to the euro is appropriate, so we supported the direct intervention." 

 The NBS would not reveal the volumes of the intervention. 

 The crown firmed to 43.87/94 to the euro, from bid at 44.0 before the news and 43.93/02 late on Tuesday. The crown traded at 46.12/23 to the dollar, from 46.41/51 on Tuesday.

 Dealers say the recent easing in the crown has been a result of the appreciation of the euro against the dollar and a generally short euro market. 

 The Slovak unit has lost more than three percent since mid-November, when it traded at around 42.5 to the euro.

title: Slovak crown ends flat, mkt sees more cbank action.

title: Emerging  FX -E.Europe extends rally on soft dollar.
text:
LONDON, Jan 2 (Reuters) - Emerging currencies in Europe started the new year strongly against the dollar on Tuesday as the U.S. currency fell to a five-month low against a broadly stronger euro. 

 The zloty extended December's rally and hit an 8-1/2 month high against the dollar while the Czech crown rallied to an eight month peak and the South African rand also posted gains. 

 However, the buoyant euro, boosted by expectations the euro zone economy will be relative strong while there is a sharp slowdown in the United States and Japan, rose against the rand and emerging currencies in Europe. 

 The stronger euro prompted the Slovak central bank (NBS) to intervene in support of the crown , buying crowns from the 44 per euro level. The crown was trading at 43.87/95 to the euro. 

 The central bank said it was satisfied with the outcome of the intervention but did not reveal the volume of hard currency offered by the bank. 

 Recent European data have reinforced the view that euro-zone growth remains relatively robust and it is well placed to withstand a period of slower global growth. This has provided a key support for emerging Europe which sends most of its exports to the euro zone. 

 The zloty stood at 4.1000 per dollar from 4.145 late on Friday and at 3.8753 to the euro against 3.852. 

 Dealers said the market was awaiting the release of Polish current account data at 1500 GMT. A Reuters consensus poll conducted at the start of December showed analysts expecting the current account gap to fall some some $800 million in November from $1.05 billion in October. 

 The Czech crown rose to its highest level against the dollar since March 28 last year but edged lower against the euro, trading at 35.11 to the euro after briefly firming to 34.95. 

 The crown stood at 37.14/17 per dollar from 37.60/63 on Friday.

title: UPDATE 1- Slovak  cbank ready to  intervene  to support crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Oct 3 (Reuters) - Slovak central bank (NBS) Governor Marian Jusko said on Tuesday that the bank was ready to intervene to support the crown if it continued to weaken against the euro. 

 "The crown has depreciated against the euro by 3.3 percent since the beginning of the year... In case of continued weakening of the crown, we are ready to intervene on the interbank foreign exchange market," Jusko told a news conference. 

 NBS Vice Governor Elena Kohutikova said the bank had intervened with 45 million euros on currency markets last month to support the crown. 

 "It was a so-called 'discreet' type of intervention," she added without elaborating. 

 The crown has declined to lows not seen in nearly a year, following the announcement of a November 11 referendum on whether to hold early general elections. 

 It traded at 43.94/02 to the euro on Tuesday morning, from 43.88/94 late on Monday and bid at around 42.60 in mid-September. 

 "We will intervene when the crown exchange rate development does not reflect the macroeconomic indicators... which are favourable at the moment," Jusko said. 

 Jusko also said that the bank would consider cutting interest rates further, following a reduction at the end of August, only after next year's budget had been set. The NBS board decided on September 29 to leave interest rates unchanged. On August 30, the central bank cut its key overnight rate for sterilising operations to 6.5 percent from 7.0 percent and its refinancing repo rate to 9.5 percent from 10.0 percent. 

 "The last time the bank board decided to keep interest rates unchanged, one of the reasons was uncertainty over next year's public finance," NBS Governor Marian Jusko told a news conference. 

 "When the budget is set, and if the stable macroeconomic developments continue, then we may decide to lower interest rates... but it certainly won't be as much as last time," he added. 

 The government has agreed to set the 2001 state budget so that the overall public finance deficit does not exceed 4.0 percent of gross domestic product. 

 The cabinet plans to vote on the budget draft on October 4 and to submit it to the parliament for the final discussion by October 15.

title: INTERVIEW-Slovak c.bank vicegov happy with  fx  rate.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Sept 20 (Reuters) - The Vice Governor of the Slovak central bank (NBS) Elena Kohutikova said on Wednesday that the NBS is satisfied with the exchange rate of the Slovak crown to the euro this year. 

  "In the first half of the year and now...I consider the 

  performance (of the crown) as very stable...any fluctuations 

  have been short-term...we do not have any indication that it 

 should be otherwise," Kohutikova told Reuters in an interview. 

 "The crown-dollar exchange rate is not that positive for us, but that is outside the influence of the NBS," Kohutikova said. 

 She stressed that the central bank was ready to intervene if needed. 

 "We are watching the non-economic factors, and we are ready to intervene if necessary." 

 The Slovak crown has been sliding since President Rudolf Schuster called a referendum on early elections two weeks ago following an opposition-initiated citizen petition. 

 Kohutikova said the central bank does not have strict targets for intervention. 

 "We always evaluate the performance of the crown on the background of the economy." 

 Recently, the crown has been consistently shaking off macroeconomic data. 

 "Apart from non-economic influences...the crown is mostly sensitive to capital and financial account," Kohutikova said. 

 She said the central bank is ready to assuage any impact from privatisation proceeds on Slovak financial markets. 

 "The (state privatisation agency) National Property Fund (NPF) has an account at the central bank, and NPF is the recepient of the privatisation proceeds...so we can release the proceeds gradually."

title: UPDATE 2-Slovak Deputy PM says economic stability reached.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 27 (Reuters) - Deputy Prime Minister for the Economy Ivan Miklos said on Thursday that Slovakia had reached economic stability and that he expected inflation to fall below 10 percent soon. 

 He said continued reforms could lead to Slovakia's credit ratings to be upgraded to investment grade in the first half of next year. 

 "All the economic indicators are showing that we have managed to reach macroeconomic stabilisation after a year since we introduced a package of measures aiming to that effect," Miklos told a news conference. 

 "Inflation will soon be under the level of 10 percent, and a further downward trend will continue in the first months of next year." 

 Slovak consumer prices fell 0.1 percent in June from May, taking year-on-year inflation to 15.4 percent. Core inflation, which excluded the effect of regulated prices and tax changes, came in at 5.8 percent year-on-year in June. 

 "The exchange rate of the crown can be seen at present as stabilised," Miklos said. 

 "The (crown's) rate since October 1998 has decreased only against the American dollar, but this movement is caused by a significant strengthening of the American currency against the euro over the last year." 

 Earlier this year the Slovak central bank was forced for the first time to intervene against the crown currency to prevent its unwanted firming. 

 Miklos said that he expected the country's corporate sphere to revive, boosted by a significant decrease in Slovak interbank market rates and subsequently also in commercial loan rates. 

 "While the average loan interest rate was at 23.5 percent in October 1998, in June 2000 it was only 10.8 percent," Miklos said in a prepared statement distributed at the conference. 

 "We expect lower financial costs (for loans) to help the corporate sphere to revive," he said. "This should, with some delay, increase also the state budget income from tax payments." 

 Miklos also said Slovakia's ratings with international agencies could return to investment grade, from where they fell in 1998. 

 "In continuing reforms, we can expect improving of ratings and moving Slovakia into the investment range again in the first half of 2001," the statement said. 

 Miklos said, however, that next year would be "quite difficult" in fiscal terms. 

 Among other factors, the cancellation of an import surcharge, currently at three percent, and lower individual income taxes and a 10 percent increase in pensions will cause fiscal pressure next year. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  cbank says no need to  intervene  on crown.

BRATISLAVA, June 16 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank's head of foreign exchange policy, Frantisek Szulenyi, said on Friday he saw no need for the bank to intervene on the foreign exchange market despite a continued weakening of the currency. 

 "I don't see any reason for us to intervene," Szulenyi told Reuters. The crown was quoted at 42.264/364 at 1122 GMT on Friday after opening quotes of around 42.07/15. Dealers say the weakening reflected continued bearish sentiment following Thursday's release of worse than expected first quarter gross domestic product figures. 

 GDP growth in the first quarter came in at 1.5 percent, well below market expectations of a 2.78 percent year-on-year rise. 

 The crown was trading at 41.900/980 to the euro just after the GDP figures were released compared with 41.850/920 at Wednesday's close. ((Robin Shepherd, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: UPDATE 1-Slovak CPI beats expectations, boosts crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 12 (Reuters) - Slovakia's headline inflation rate for April came in below market expectations on Friday giving relief to the crown currency which edged up to 42.8 against the euro after 43.15 at the open. 

 The statistical office said April inflation was 0.0 percent on a month-on-month basis and 15.9 percent year-on-year. A Reuters poll of analysts had predicted an average monthly inflation figure of 0.3 percent and 16.4 percent on an annualised basis. 

 "It was mainly foreign banks who were buying crowns since the market opened but this trend was visibly boosted by favourable economic indicators," Marek Senkovic a foreign exchange dealer at Istrobank said. 

 The crown has weakened in the last week prompting central bank intervention to stem the fall. The decline began at around 41.7 to the euro on May 4, driven, analysts say, by fears over the stability of the coalition government. 

 The central bank said the depreciation was not based on economic fundamentals, and its interventions were designed to counter volatility. 

Slovak central bank Vice Governor Elena Kohutikova said on Thursday she believed headline inflation had peaked at current levels and that it would decline to reach 10 percent by the end of the year. 

 The statistical office also said on Friday that core inflation - headline inflation stripped of the effects of regulated price and indirect tax changes - was minus 0.1 percent month-on-month compared with a 0.3 percent rise in March and 6.4 percent year-on-year after 7.0 percent in March. 

 Industrial production was 8.5 percent year-on-year in March compared with a downwardly revised 8.0 percent increase in February and construction output fell 16.1 percent year-on-year after an 11.7 percent decline in February. ((Robin Shepherd, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: CORRECTED - IMF urges Slovakia to cut spending, curb  currency .
text:
In BRATISLAVA story 'IMF urges Slovakia to cut spending, curb currency' 

 please read in fifth paragraph '...with GDP itself seen growing at 2.5 percent.' 

 This corrects GDP figure. 

 (The Slovak finance ministry, which issued the report, corrected the figure which, 

 due to a software problem, was improperly transcribed from the IMF). 

 A corrected repetition follows. 

 By Robin Shepherd 

 BRATISLAVA, May 12 (Reuters) - The International Monetary Fund (IMF) released a report on the strengths and weaknesses of the Slovak economy on Monday, highlighting recommendations to avoid a big appreciation in the crown and curb public spending. 

 The IMF report comes after several days of depreciation pressure on the Slovak currency and two rounds of central bank intervention to stem volatility. 

 The report praised the government's privatisation programme and also plans to sterilise foreign direct investment inflows through special accounts at the central bank. 

 "...A sustained and significant appreciation of the exchange rate would not be desirable at this juncture as it could adversely affect external competitiveness and result in a widening of the external current account deficit," the IMF said. 

 The IMF added it expected the current account deficit to be around 5.0 percent of GDP in 2000 with GDP itself seen growing at 2.5 percent. 

 The IMF's main concerns centred on public spending, particularly increased expenditure financed by privatisation proceeds. 

 "The mission is concerned about plans to increase government expenditure, contingent on financing from privatisation proceeds." 

 "It now appears that the deficit of the general government - excluding planned additional expenditure associated with privatisation proceeds - could approach four percent of GDP in 2000." 

 The report added that this figure could rise to around five percent unless such planned expenditures were reversed or offsetting spending measures were adopted. 

 Privatisation proceeds would be well used, the IMF said, if they were employed to retire foreign debt and postpone the need for further foreign debt issuance. 

 The IMF said that a public sector deficit of closer to three percent of GDP would be preferable because it would help build credibility among potential foreign investors and it would relieve spending pressures future years. 

 However, a rise in the fiscal deficit of one percent of GDP would be acceptable if funds were used to effect banking system reform which the IMF said was a crucial aspect of overall structural reform. 

 The mission was postive on Slovakia's inflation prospects. 

 "The mission does not see any significant inflationary pressures ahead, as long as wage settlements are moderate and the public finances remain under control." 

 "In these circumstances, there may be room for further, moderate interest rate cuts." 

 Unemployment had peaked at around the current level - 19.3 percent in March - but it was likely to remain high. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  cbank  intervenes  to halt crown weakening.
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 5 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market on Friday to prevent a further weakening of the crown, the head of the bank's foreign currency trading department said. 

 "We intervened when the crown was over 42.500 and since then it went significantly down (stronger)...We think the intervention was successful," Karol Mrva told Reuters. 

 "We still don't have any concrete level which we would want to protect...Our aim is to smooth out turbulence which was beginning to be unacceptable," he added. 

 The crown traded at a year low against the euro of 42.680 on Friday. After the intervention it firmed to around 42.1. 

 The central bank also intervend on Thursday to prevent the crown weakening. It does not generally disclose the volumes used in its interventions. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).
