title: Slovak  cbank says  intervened  to halt crown fall.
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 4 (Reuters) - The chief dealer at the Slovak central bank, Vladimir Polhorsky, told Reuters the central bank had intervened directly on the foreign exchange market on Thursday after the crown weakened sharply against the euro. 

 The Slovak currency opened at 41.7 to the euro but rapidly declined as the morning session got underway, briefly hitting levels of around 42.45. 

 "Today's weakening was too extensive so we intervened in favour of the crown to reduce volatility and calm down the market," Polhorsky said. He added the intervention came in the form of direct calls to selected banks with whom trades were conducted. 

 He would not disclose the volume of the intervention or the level at which it came but a dealer at a local bank who requested anonymity said he believed interventions began at about 42.2 to the euro and estimated the volume at around 30 million euros. It was quoted at 42.045/130 at 1053 GMT. 

 Polhorsky said that according to his sources at commercial banks, the weakening of the crown was driven by foreign institutions closing crown positions. The reason for the weakening was not clear but local media reported earlier in the day that two big privatisation projects would be delayed. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: INTERVIEW-Slovak c.bank says fighting volatility.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 19 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank's discreet interventions against crown strength are aimed at curbing volatility rather than defending a specific exchange rate, Vice-governor Elena Kohutikova said on Wednesday. 

 She added, in an interview with Reuters, that interest rates would not become a significant instrument in the management of the exchange rate. The overnight repo rate stands at 7.5 percent for sterilisation operations and 10.5 percent for refinancing. 

 "We see that the interest rates are at an acceptable level at present...We cannot subordinate interest rate policy to exchange rate policy," she said. 

 The central bank has used the equivalent of over $400 million this year to buy foreign currency directly from local banks. The bank has voiced concerns that trade performance could be hurt if the currency firmed too much. 

 "The interventions are designed to prevent certain volumes of forex from moving the exchange rate significantly for a few days," Kohutikova told Reuters in an interview. 

 When asked whether the bank was defending any particular crowns levels, she said: "No, we are intervening to prevent volatility in the market." 

 She added there was no need at present for different forms of intervention: "Of course, it's a matter for the bank board to decide, but for now we do not see a reason to use a different procedure." 

 Interest in the Slovak crown soared in December after the European Union formally invited the country to open accession talks. The pressure has been kept up due to expectations of large privatisations planned by the government for this year and next. 

 "Too much crown strengthening having to do with the capital account...would not be very good for the economy, so we have prepared some instruments to eliminate this effect," she said, referring to plans to set up special privatisation accounts from which forex inflows would be dissolved in the economy gradually. 

 "Negotiations are going on right now and there seems to be general support for the idea...The funds would be spread out to minimise the pressure on the crown," she said. 

 Kohutikova said the central bank also remained prepared to sterilise the crown market as needed, regardless of costs. "We are sterilising huge amounts of money and are ready to sterilise enough to maintain currency stability." ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Emerging  FX -Nasdaq takes shine off zloty.
text:
LONDON, April 11 (Reuters) - East European currencies were mostly firm on Tuesday in thin trade apart from the Polish zloty which slid in response to a drop in Wall Street's tech-heavy Nasdaq index overnight. 

 Poland, which has the largest concentration of technology, media and telecom stocks of any East European bourse, and is also the largest regional market, saw the zloty slide to 5.29 percent above parity against its basket of euros and dollars from close to six percent on Monday. 

 "The capital account has shown a lot more portfolio flows, it is just a sentiment thing, people feel the zloty is more exposed globally," said Tim Ash, analyst at West LB. 

 The zloty was trading at 3.9925 bid to the euro by 0958 GMT, compared with 3.9965 at the open and 3.9769 at Monday's close. 

 Ash believes zloty weakness should be used by investors as an entry point. 

 "You are still getting 600-700 basis points for Polish paper over Hungary," he said. 

 The Hungarian forint was quiet on Tuesday, with more positive news on the economy outweighing a reports in a local newspaper that National Bank of Hungary Gyorgy Suranyi had tendered his resignation which had been turned down by the government. 

 Although Suranyi's departure is a perennial in the markets, analysts and traders said it would certainly be received badly, given Hungary's sometimes fractious government coalition. 

 "If he did go, it would be important. He has often been the last man standing in terms of the foreign exchange regime," said West LB's Ash. 

 The forint was trading at 258.29 bid compared with 258.10 on Monday, with investors continuing to fall out of love with East Europe's most succesful economy. 

 Data on Tuesday showed Hungary's March headline consumer prices rose 9.6 percent rise year-on-year and one percent month-on-month. 

 Core inflation was 8.6 percent year-on-year and 0.4 percent month-on-month. 

 In the Czech Republic, the release of the central bank's monetary meeting notes opened the possibility of another interest rate cut, with comments that the continuation of the strengthening of the crown "could lead to an unwanted tightening of monetary conditions". 

 The Czech crown was trading at 36.438 bid to the euro moderately lower than 36.21 bid on Monday. 

 In Slovakia, the central bank continued to keep investors on their toes, with comments that it was "intervening discreetly" in the market. 

 The Slovak crown was at 41.526 bid to the euro, little changed from 41.525 on Monday. ((David Chance, London Capital Markets +44 171 542 6784 email david.chance@reuters.com)).

title: WRAPUP 1-Slovak  central bank  battles on with strong crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 11 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank continues to combat crown strength with market intervention and is ready to keep expected privatisation inflows from boosting the currency, Vice-Governor Elena Kohutikova said on Tuesday. 

 Between December and mid-February the central bank intervened directly on the foreign exchange market, buying euros to prevent the crown from firming. 

 The recently appointed vice-governor told a management conference the bank was still intervening, albeit less overtly. 

 "We are intervening discreetly in the market... continuously," she said, adding that the bank had so far bought the equivalent of $400 million in interventions in 2000. 

 These covert interventions involved directly buying large volumes of foreign currency from local banks. 

 The crown came under appreciation pressure in December when Slovakia received a formal invitation to open European Union accession talks. 

 Officials say they do not want it to strengthen in a way that could hit Slovakia's export-led growth and falling current account deficit, although they have allowed it to firm a little after stronger trade data. 

 Kohutikova said the bank was facing mounting pressure in its efforts to sterilise crown liquidity arising from the conversion of forex inflows. 

 "I expect the sterilisation position (the amount currently borrowed by the bank from the crown market) could reach as much as 60 billion crowns ($1.4 billion) this year." Kohutikova said the figure currently stood at around 25 billion crowns. 

 Appreciation pressure on the crown has increased ahead of an extensive programme of sales of government holdings in banks and enterprises, expected to bring in tens of billions of crowns from foreign investors in the next two years. 

 "Towards the end of the year I expect the actual bank privatisation to begin, not only in state-owned banks but in smaller banks where the state has a share," Kohutikova said, adding that she expected the main privatisation wave next year. 

 "We are negotiating with the FNM (state privatisation agency) and the finance ministry on opening special accounts for these capital inflows...to stabilise these funds at the central bank and gradually dissolve them into the economy." 

 Kohutikova said the central bank believed the 2000 current account deficit might come in lower than the 5.3 percent of GDP targeted. She forecast the deficit at 4.1 percent of GDP in 2001, 3.7 percent in 2002, 3.2 percent in 2003 and 2.8 percent in 2004. $=43.1 Slovak crowns ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  cbank says no  intervention  at current rate.
text:
BRATISLAVA, March 7 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said on Tuesday it would not intervene to cap crown strength at the current rate of around 41.61 to the euro. 

 "At these levels we are not entering into the market yet," Frantisek Szulenyi, the head of the foreign currency assets department at the central bank, told Reuters. 

 Szulenyi also said that the central bank still had a secret level at which it would intervene to prevent a firming of the currency. 

 Since the central bank allowed the crown to firm through the 42.3 level - where it had intervened on several occasions - and subsequently the 42.0 to the euro levels - which many dealers believed could have been the new intervention level - some analysts suggested that the bank may no longer have a firm idea of when it would intervene again. 

 Specifically asked whether the central bank still had a level at which the market should expect an intervention, Szulenyi said: 

 "Of course, we have a certain internal level."In keeping with central bank practice, he would not be drawn on what that level was. 

 Finance Minister Brigita Schmognerova said on Monday that the rate of the crown to the euro was "appropriate" at levels reached last Friday when the crown was trading at around 41.75 to the euro. 

 Szulenyi said he had no comment to make on the minister's remarks.

 "I don't know of anyone from the central bank who said 42.000 was some level at which we would intervene," Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters.

 The central bank had intervened on several occassions since mid December to stop the crown breaking through 42.3 to the euro but allowed the currency to firm through that level last week.

title: Market mixed on Slovak rate move at cbank meeting.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 24 (Reuters) - Slovak dealers gave mixed views on Thursday at the liklehood of a repo rate change after Friday's central bank board meeting. 

 The central bank launched a new automatic repo system at the beginning of February setting the overnight rate for refinanicng at 12 percent and the sterilisation repo rate at 8.0 percent. 

 Dalibor Cernicka, managing director of Money Market Brokers in Bratislava, said a change in rates was unlikely precisely because the central bank had only just introduced the new system. 

 "They could indicate the direction of rates but I think they would wait at least two months (for a change)," he said. 

 Miroslav Nespala from CSOB bank agreed. 

 "I would appreciate it if they narowed the spread to 8.5/11.5 but I don't expect the central bank will do it tomorrow as it's only less than a month since they started this system," he said. 

 But others gave a different view. Rastislav Zivor, of ING Barings, said the central bank may cut the sterilisation rate by 50-100 basis points. 

 "This would support the operations which the central bank has been doing on foreign exchange until now. And it would make it cheaper to sterilise the market (after spending money on interventions)," he said. 

 The Slovak currency firmed slightly earlier this week, after the central bank broke with recent policy and allowed the crown to strengthen through the 42.3 to the euro level. It had intervened on several occassions to stop the crown firming over 42.3 since mid-December. 

 On Thursday the currency was traded between 42.14 and 42.2 to the euro. 

 ING's chief economist in Slovakia, Jan Toth, said a 50-100 basis point cut from 8.0 percent may come because the country's improved export performance lessened the central bank's need to keep the crown weak. 

 Foreign trade figures for January will be released on Friday morning. The finance and economy ministries have both said the figure will be slightly better than the 2.9 billion deficit recorded in January 1999. 

 The SITA news agency quoted central bank monetary policy head Elena Kohutikova on Thursday as saying Slovakia's current account deficit should fall to 5.6 percent of gross domestic product for 1999, 5.3 percent for 2000 and 4.1 percent of GDP in 2001. 

 ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  cbank says may still  intervene .

 "It is not excluded that we will enter the market, that we will intervene maybe at other levels...We may intervene in future but maybe not at the 42.300 level," Frantisek Szulenyi, the head of the central bank's foreign exchange assets department told Reuters.

title: Slovak  crown steady near c.bank  intervention  level.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 14 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown	



was calm in quiet Monday morning trading, hovering near the


 levels where the central bank has been repeatedly intervening to 

 prevent a firming, dealers said. 

     The crown was quoted at 42.30/32 to the euro at 0840 GMT, 

 unchanged from Friday's close. 

     The central bank has repeatedly intervened since 

 mid-December at around 42.3 to the euro to prevent the currency

 from strengthening. 

     "We have seen only very passive trading so far today," said 

 VUB Bank's Ladislav Benedek. "Should demand for crowns 

 strengthen the crown over 42.3 (to the euro), the central bank

 is very likely to intervene again," he added. 

 The central bank has said economic fundamentals do not 

 warrant a crown firmer than 42.3 to the euro at present. But the 

 bank has said its intervention level could change at any time if 

 fundamentals change. 

 The crown was quoted at 42.78/83 to the dollar at 0840 GMT. 

 ((Andrej Salner, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 

 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 2000.

title: Slovak  crown calm after cbank  intervened  Wednesday.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 10 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown	



was trading calmly on Thursday morning with dealers saying that


 Wednesday's central bank intervention to weaken the crown had 

 ushered in stability. 

     The crown was quoted at 42.30/32 to the euro at 0840 GMT, 

 little moved from opening levels. 

     "The market is very calm, since yesterday's intervention

 removed some excess foreign currency," said Juraj Zabadal, a 

 trader at Slovenska Sporitelna. "We are not expecting any major 

 moves and the central bank is unlikely to have to intervene

 again today," he added. 

 The Slovak central bank (NBS) intervened in the foreign 

 exchange market on Wednesday to prevent the crown from firming 

 over 42.3 to the euro. The bank has been intervening around 

 these levels since mid-December. 

 Frantisek Szulenyi, the head of the NBS's foreign currency

 assets department, said on Wednesday he saw no need to change 

 the bank's intervention levels at the moment. 

 The crown was quoted at 42.57/61 to the dollar at 0840 GMT. 

 ((Andrej Salner, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 

 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  cbank confirms  intervention  to weaken crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 10 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank confirmed earlier reports by local dealers on Thursday that it had intervened to weaken the crown at around 42.3 to the euro. 

 "I can confirm that we have intervened at the usual levels," Frantisek Szulenyi, the head of the central bank's foreign currency assets department told Reuters. 

 Szulenyi said the bank placed its bids on electronic broker 

 systems and actively matched offers by other players. "To us, 

 the midpoint of where the crown is quoted matters...We wanted to 

 bring it above 42.300 (to the euro)," he said. 

 The central bank has repeatedly intervened since mid-December at around 42.3 to the euro to prevent the crown from firming. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  c.bank  intervenes  to cap crown strength.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 10 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market to keep the crown from firming, buying euros for crowns around 42.300-42.315 to the euro, dealers said. 

 The central bank intervened around the same levels on Wednesday and has been doing so repeatedly since mid-December. 

 "The central bank has been active right above 42.300 (to the euro)," one dealer, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters. Another forex dealer at a local bank added: "Yes, the central bank is in the market again." 

 Dealers said the central bank actively paid offers just above 42.300 to the euro on electronic broker systems. 

 The crown weakened slightly right after the intervention to 42.310/315 at 1037 GMT from about 42.285/300 just before the intervention. 

 Officials at the central bank were not immediately available to confirm dealer reports. ((Andrej Salner, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  c.bank confirms  intervened  to cap crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 9 (Reuters) - The head of the Slovak central bank's foreign currency assets department Frantisek Szulenyi said that the central bank had intervened to prevent the crown from firming over 42.3 to the euro on Wednesday. 

 Earlier in the day local dealers reported they had seen central bank activity in the foreign exchange market. "I can confirm we have intervened at around 42.30 (to the euro)," Szulenyi told Reuters. 

 Szulenyi said the bank (NBS) had placed bids in the market over electronic broker systems, as well as actively paid offers, to bring the midpoint of the level where the crown was quoted above the 42.3 to the euro intervention level. 

 The NBS has intervened at this level repeatedly since mid-December to prevent a firming. 

 "At the moment the situation is unchanged, it depends on macroeconomic indicators, mainly the trade balance and the balance of payments," Szulenyi said. "I see no reason at the moment to change it (the intervention level)." 

 The bank has said its intervention level could change at any time if economic fundamentals change. ((Andrej Salner, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Sloval cbank  intervenes  to weaken crown - dealers.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 9 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) intervened selling crowns on the foreign exchange market on Wednesday at the level of 42.30 crowns to the euro, dealers said. 

 "We've seen the NBS at 42.30 (to the euro)," a dealer at a foreign bank said. Another dealer at a local bank also said he had seen the central bank intervene at the same levels. 

 The central bank has intervened to weaken the crown on many occasions since December of last year. 

 NBS Governor Marian Jusko has said the bank does not intervene to counter trends but that it had a secret preferred range for the crown's exchange rate, which can fluctuate according to changing fundamentals. 

 The NBS last intervened to weaken the crown on February 1 at at levels between 42.29 and 42.3 crowns to the euro. After the intervention news on Wednesday, the crown was trading virtually unchanged at 42.26/34 to the euro. ((Bratislava newsroom, +421-7-5341-8402, fax +421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

 The crown was trading at 35.798 bid to the euro, slightly

title: Slovak  cenbank confirms crown  intervention .
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 1 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said on Tuesday it had intervened to weaken the crown at levels around 42.3 to the euro, confirming dealers' sightings of the bank earlier in the session. 

 "We have intervened...We began somewhere below 42.3 and continued up to that level," said Frantisek Szulenyi, the head of the central bank's foreign currency assets department. 

 The central bank has intervened to keep the crown from strengthening over 42.3 to the euro repeatedly since mid-December, saying a firmer crown could hurt the economy. Last week, the central bank said it remained committed to defending the 42.3 level for the time being. 

 However, on Monday afternoon the crown traded at levels firmer than 42.3 without the central bank stepping in. 

 Local dealers said prior to Tuesday's intervention they expected the central bank to appear on the market to weaken the crown. 

 After the intervention, around 0900 GMT, the crown was quoted at 42.310/350 to the euro from 42.270/295 at the open. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  cbank  intervenes  to weaken crown-dealers.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 1 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank reappeared on the foreign exchange market on Tuesday, intervening to weaken the crown at levels between 42.29 and 42.3 to the euro, dealers said. 

 "Finally the National Bank is on the market again," said one dealer who refused to be named. 

 The central bank has intervened to weaken the crown at these levels on several occasions since December last year. 

 Governor Marian Jusko has said the bank does not intervene to counter trends but that it has a secret preferred range, which can move along with changes to fundamentals, within which it wants to see the crown. 

 In a recent interview with Reuters, however, he said economic fundamentals themselves were affected by the rate of the crown. 

 ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Emerging  FX -Stronger, awaiting Polish c/a data.
text:
LONDON, Feb 1 (Reuters) - The Czech and Slovak crowns gained on Tuesday, at one point prompting the Slovak central bank to intervene again, as investors bet long term capital inflows would continue to boost the currencies. 

 Poland's zloty also opened firmer ahead of key current account data due at 1300 GMT that analysts will scour for signs of an export recovery. 

 But the rand hovered at 6.300 per dollar, near recent lows, despite credit growth numbers that showed South Africa's long-awaited economic recovery was not yet stoking inflation. 

 "Everyone's waiting for the Polish number. Until we get a good one, markets are going to remain cautious on Poland. It all hangs off exports," West LB economist Tim Ash said. 

 Analysts expect a December current account deficit of around $1.2 billion, after $1.15 billion in November, but a smaller number will be rewarded with strong zloty gains. 

 At 1015 GMT, the zloty rose to 2.75 percent above the central bank's parity rate from 2.48 percent on Monday. 

 FLAT POSTIONS AHEAD OF THE FED 

 Analysts and traders said most investors had flat positions going into the U.S. Federal Reserve's two day policy meeting, which starts today, with a 25 basis point hike widely expected. 

 The European Central Bank, which meets on Thursday, is also expected to raise rates by 25 bp. A mirror rates rise should help stem some of the recent volatility that has rattled emerging currencies pegged to dollar/euro baskets. 

 Still, flat investor positions did not stop Slovakia's central bank from intervening at around 42.3 crowns to the euro to stop the currency appreciating and choking off growth. At 1030 GMT, the unit stood at 42.32. 

 "The bank keeps on coming in at that level, but while people still see some long term upside there's more caution," Ash said. 

 The Czech crown also reversed some of Monday's losses that were prompted by news the government would set up an offshore account to deposit privatisation revenues that might otherwise be repatriated and boost the currency. 

 ((John Paul Rathbone, London Capital Markets unit, tel 44 171 542 5110, fax 542 5285, john.rathbone@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 2000.

title: Slovak  cbank says still ready to  intervene .
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 27 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said on Thursday it remained ready to prevent the crown from firming over the 42.3 to the euro level at which it has repeatedly intervened since mid-December. 

 "For the moment we do not see a reason for any change in the level at which we intervened the last time - 42.3 to the euro," Frantisek Szulenyi, the head of the central bank's foreign currency assets department, told Reuters. 

 When asked specifically whether the bank was prepared to prevent a firming over 42.3 to the euro, Szulenyi said: "For now yes." 

 He added that the bank had not intervened on the foreign exchange market in recent days since the crown was trading steadily above the 42.3 level. 

 At 0855 GMT, the crown was quoted at 42.320/345. 

 The central bank has long said that it has a preferred range within which it wants to see the crown. It does not publish this range, however, but says it can move according to economic fundamentals, such as the trade situation. 

 The Slovak Statistical Office said on Tuesday that a surge in exports had slashed Slovakia's 1999 trade deficit to 45.7 billion crowns in 1999 after an 82.9 billion crown deficit the year before. 

 But the December deficit, at 7.6 billion crowns, was the second highest monthly deficit of the year. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax, 421-7-5341-8403 bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  crown calm, near earlier  intervention  level.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 26 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown was calm on Wednesday morning, but dealers said they expected the currency to again approach 42.3 to the euro, the level at which the central bank had been intervening to prevent a firming. 

 The crown was quoted at 42.335/375 to the euro at 0815 GMT, unmoved from opening levels. 

 The central bank has repeatedly intervened since mid-December to keep the crown from strengthening beyond 42.3 to the euro. The bank has said, however, the intervention level could change at any time depending on economic fundamentals. 

 "Banks are long in foreign currency, so we will probably approach 42.3 to the euro again in the near future," said Juraj Zabadal, a trader at Slovenska Sporitelna. "The question now is whether or not the intervention level has been moved after Tuesday's foreign trade figures." 

 On Tuesday the Slovak Statistical Office said that Slovakia's trade deficit in 1999 reached 45.7 billion crowns compared with 82.9 billion crowns in the previous year. 

 The crown was quoted at 42.29/35 to the dollar at 0815 GMT. ((Andrej Salner, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: INTERVIEW -  Slovak  cbank can afford more  intervention .
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 13 (Reuters) - Slovak central bank governor Marian Jusko said on Thursday he had been surprised that the bank had needed to intervene to weaken the crown so often this year but added it could afford more interventions against any excessive firming. 

 "The amount of intervention in the past 13 days of this year quite surpised me. We did not expect such a sharp start but it is all still in accordance and within the framework set out by the monetary programme," he told Reuters in an interview. 

 Deputy Premier for the Economy Ivan Miklos said on Wednesday that interventions were justified at present but that in the longer term the finances of the central bank should be taken into account. 

 The bank has intervened several times since mid-December to prevent the crown, which was floated in October 1998, from firming through 42.3 to the euro. Dealers said they had seen another intervention on Thursday, the fourth session in a row. 

 While the central bank has also often said that the currency should reflect fundamentals, the governor pointed out that the rate of the crown could itself influence those fundamentals. 

 "Excessive strengthening of the crown could threaten our aims to further improve macroeconomic results, mainly in foreign trade," he said. 

 Asked how long the central bank could afford to continue intervening, Jusko said: 

 "Monetary policy is not determined by the financial results of the central bank. I think the bank has enough reserves to incur certain expenses to maintain a monetary situation corresponding with the state and development needs of our economy." 

 Analysts expect that major privatisations in 2000 will attract a big inflow of funds, further complicating central bank efforts to keep the crown from rising. Jusko said the bank was ready to sterilise such inflows. 

 "There will be costs and they are significant but the bank has large assets so we can bear these costs." 

 The central bank declined to give any figures as to its current level of reserves or how much it has spent so far during its market interventions. 

 Jusko acknowledged that he was not running a purely free floating exchange rate regime for the crown. 

 "Of course it could be argued that there is not a clean float here - I also think there isn't - and that there is here some form of managed float," he said. 

Central bank officials have repeatedly stressed that intervention is not designed to counter trends. Jusko, however, pushed a softer line. "If someone thinks that our policy is a managed float or that we are intervening on trends or the amount of fluctuation, I'll be glad to listen to these discussions but I think that what really matters for the economy is (central bank) transparency." 

 Turning to wider aspects of monetary policy, Jusko said interest rates lower than headline inflation could be satisfactory if inflation was being driven by adminstrative measures such as price deregulations. 

 "We could say that in the second half of (last) year the interest rate level was too low compared to inflation at that time. Since we know (the cause was) a one time measure whose effect will pass, that these were administrative measures, I think it is necessary to express satisfaction with the current level of interest rates." 

 Statistical office figures released on Wednesday put inflation in December at 14.2 percent year-on-year. One year interest rates were quoted on the interbank market on Thursday at 10.30/11.00 percent. 

 The central bank has targeted core inflation at 4.5 to 5.8 percent for end-December 2000 but many analysts say central bank warnings of a credit crunch this year suggest that monetary policy may not be adjusted to achieving this aim at all costs. 

 When this point was put to Jusko he said: 

 "On the one hand monetary policy cannot be too inward looking, exclusively following monetary aims regardless of the real state of the economy...We don't want to achieve the best possible monetary results at the expense of development opportunities for the real economy." "On the other hand monetary policy should not be too relaxed...We want to avoid the mistakes of conditions being such that access to credit is too easy and there is a great possibility in our situation that credits would be given that wouldn't be repaid." 

 He concluded the interview by saying that the central bank had no major differences with the finance minstry and that communication between the two was good. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax, 421-7-5341-8403 bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS-Slovak Dec inflation hits top end of target.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Slovakia's end year inflation rate came in at the top end of the central bank's target range on Wednesday, with consumer prices rising by 0.4 percent month-on-month in December and 14.2 percent year-on-year. 

 A Reuters poll of analysts conducted on Tuesday gave a mean average prediction of 0.33 percent for the month with annualised December inflation seen at 14.0 percent. 

 Prior to the release of the data, the Slovak central bank again intervened to prevent the crown firming through 42.3 to the euro but traders said the inflation figures were unlikely to move the market even at such a sensitive time. 

 "These data had no influence on market developments," said Branislav Matusek, a forex trader at ING Barings. 

 "Since the central bank has declared it is watching foreign trade data closely in determining the crown level it desires, the market's attention is likely to focus more on these figures ... The market will note other indicators, but they are unlikely to have an impact." 

 Jan Toth, chief economist at ING Barings in Bratislava, said the figures were a touch higher than expected and had been boosted by food and fuel prices. 

 These components of the inflation basket had probably been affected by seasonal and world pricing factors, however, rather than the amount of money circulating in the Slovak economy. 

 "So I would not expect monetary policy to tighten because of this," he told Reuters. 

 The central bank has targeted core inflation at 4.5 to 5.8 percent for end-December 2000 but analysts said central bank warnings of a credit crunch this year suggested that monetary policy may not be adjusted to achieving this aim at all costs. 

 "I believe there is a will in the central bank to significantly reduce interest rates this year in order to avoid the situation which arose in the Czech Republic in the last two years," said Milos Bozek of J&T Securities. 

 "This would also be a tool for fighting an overvalued crown." 

 Bozek said many analysts partly attributed the recent deep recession in the Czech Republic to a failure of the Czech central bank to begin cutting interest rates soon enough. 

 "Even if inflation is a bit above target they will not tighten because of the potential for a credit crunch," added Toth. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax, 421-7-5341-8403 bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Emerging  FX -Steady in Europe, ignoring bond falls.
text:
LONDON, Jan 12 (Reuters) - Emerging market currencies were little changed to weaker in Europe on Wednesday, showing no clear reaction to interest rate fears that sent international bond yields to their highest levels since 1997. 


Weakness in Polish Treasury bills, amid a rise in German Bund yields to more than two-year highs, had some impact on the zloty	  in early trade, said Jan Pudil, trader at West LB. But the unit later firmed to stand little changed despite reduced hopes that the currency will be fully floated soon.


 The zloty surged to near five-month highs ahead of a meeting between the central bank and the finance ministry on a float, but fell on Tuesday after the government did not discuss the issue at its weekly meeting. 

 Deputy Finance Minister Jaroslaw Bauc said a period of stabilisation was needed before a decision would be made. 

 "Despite all this, we remain inclined to believe that the zloty will be floated during 1H2000 and that the PLN/EUR exchange rate will become the exchange rate on which markets will focus," said Deutsche Bank analyst Laura Papi in a daily note. 

 Papi and Pudil said the currency was effectively free floating anyway as it can move in a 30 percent band. 


The zloty	     was bid around three percent stronger than the central bank's parity level, firmer than Tuesday's 2.9 percent, and at 4.1890 against the euro versus 4.1950.



SOUTH AFRICA MULLS RATES



South Africa's rand	  was little changed as the central bank began a two-day meeting that may lower interest rates for the first time since November.



Economists are divided on whether the Reserve Bank will free the repo rate, which it fixed at 12 percent on November 25, now that the millennium rollover has passed without problem. Some think it will leave the rate on hold because of evidence of mounting growth and rising rates elsewhere in the world.



The Bank said its Monetary Policy Committee would issue a statement on interest rates Thursday afternoon. The rand traded at 6.076 bid compared with 6.07 late on Tuesday.



The Israeli shekel	  was also steady despite losses in U.S. stocks and signs that Prime Minister Ehud Barak may have problems winning cabinet approval for his nominated central bank governor David Klein.



The currency set its strongest levels since July on Tuesday, continuing to gain on expectations Klein would not cut interest rates drastically.



But local dealers said the market was now following the direction of U.S. equities, whose strength has sent Israeli shares soaring. U.S. stocks fell on Tuesday, with technology issues suffering particularly heavy losses.



Reports that the cabinet was divided on Klein's appointment may also weigh on the shekel, which was bid around 4.1151 to the dollar compared with 4.1102 late on Tuesday.



The Slovak crown	  was little changed as the central bank intervened for a third day running, buying euros for crowns at around 42.3 to the euro. The currency	     was recently bid near 42.235 to the euro.
The Czech crown			continued to trade around the 36 to the euro level, weakening to 35.975 bid from 35.93 on Tuesday.

title: Slovak  cbank says  intervened  around 42.3 to euro.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 11 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank on Tuesday confirmed that it had intervened to weaken the crown at around 42.3 to the euro. 

 "Yes we have intervened close to the same levels (as yesterday). The 42.3 (intervention) level is the same," Frantisek Szulenyi, the head of the central bank's foreign currency assets department told Reuters. 

 Dealers said the Slovak central bank had intervened on the currency market, buying euros at around 42.29 to the crown, at around 0755 GMT. 

 The bank has intervened to prevent the crown from firming at or around the 42.300 to the euro level several times in December, and again on January 3 and January 10. 

 The central bank's monetary programme calls for intervention to prevent excess volatility, but not to counter trends. NBS Monetary Department Director Elena Kohutikova said last week the bank had intervened, as pressures for a crown firming were of a one-time character. 

 Kohutikova said the central bank intervention level may easily change at any time, depending on developments of economic fundamentals. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Emerging  FX -Central Europe firm, picture positive.
text:
LONDON, Jan 11 (Reuters) - Central European currencies were mostly firmer on Tuesday with the Polish zloty showing strength despite a delay in a decision to float the currency at a meeting of the central bank and finance ministry. 

 Traders and analysts said that trading volumes had improved from last week, although they were not back up to pre-Christmas levels. 

 "We expect a decision on the zloty to be taken in the second quarter. Obviously strong privatisation inflows will drive the zloty stronger," said Stefan Kolek, currency strategist at HypoVereinsbank. 

 By 1111 GMT, the zloty was trading at 4.174 bid to the euro little changed from the close of 4.1725. It was at 3.34 percent on the strong side of parity against its basket of dollars and euros. 

 Poland's Finance Ministry and the central bank's Monetary Policy Council on Monday concluded their meeting with no word on the flotation of the zloty when many had been expecting a decision or at least a timeframe for one. 

 The zloty currently trades in a 30 percent wide trading range and is devalued at 0.3 percent a month. 

 Elsewhere in Central Europe, the Slovak central bank continued to intervene, at around 42.3 to the euro and the crown was trading at 42.219 bid in mid-morning trade. 

 "The fact of intervention is marginal," said Kolek. "They cannot do anything in the long run." 

 Slovak bond yields dipped ahead of a 3.0 billion crown T-bond offering, ahead of strong anticipated demand. 

 The Czech crown was little changed after Monday's release of December consumer price inflation, which came in higher than expected at 0.5 percent month on month. 

 The crown was at 35.972 bid to the euro, marginally weaker than 35.97 at Monday's close. 

 Czech central bank (CNB) Vice-governor Zdenek Tuma said his bias on monetary policy remained neutral despite stronger-than-expected inflation in December, the daily Hospodarske Noviny said on Tuesday. In Hungary, the main news of the day was the addition of 200 million euros to a floating rate issue for a total of 600 million euros. 

 The forint was trading at compared 254.54 bid to the euro, little changed from 254.63 at Monday's close. 

 In South Africa, the rand was firmer as the market braces for central bank meetings on Wednesday and Thursday this week, at which a further cut in interest rates is expected. 

 The rand was at 6.0710 bid to the dollar, little changed from late-Monday trade. 

 The Israeli shekel continued to rally against the dollar to its highest level in 4-1/2 months with the appointment of David Klein as central bank chief.

title: Emerging  FX -Zloty, shekel lead Europe higher.
text:
LONDON, Jan 10 (Reuters) - Hopes that the Polish authorities will agree to a full float of the zloty	  lifted the currency to four-month highs on Monday in a busy European session for emerging market currencies.
Israel's shekel	  rallied as the market welcomed the nomination of a tough central bank chief, while the Czech crown	  gained after robust inflation data reinforced expectations of higher interest rates.



The zloty surged to 3.52 percent bid above the central bank's parity level from 3.0 percent on Friday, buoyed by hopes that the finance minister will agree at a 1500 GMT meeting with the central bank to fully float the currency.


 Analysts say such a move would show the authorities were confident in the zloty and would give a psychological boost to the currency, which is already allowed to fluctuate in a band of 15 percent on either side of the parity rate. 

 The latest firming of the currency came after a ministry adviser said the central bank should pledge to intervene against the zloty to protect Poland's current account if the floated unit rose sharply. 

 "That seemed to trigger quite a bit of zloty buying," said Bank of America currency strategist Juliet Sampson, adding that she was surprised at the market's reaction. "It looks like there's still going to be a lot of volatility, which has to be taken as a negative." 


The zloty	     was trading at 4.1538 to the euro compared with 4.1935 on Friday, around levels not seen since late August.



ISRAEL RISKS POLICY CLASH



Prime Minister Ehud Barak's choice of David Klein to succeed Jacob Frenkel as Bank of Israel governor, announced on Friday, boosted the shekel on expectations Klein will stick to a tough monetary policy.



"Klein is clearly a hawk, perhaps more hawkish that Frenkel, and that should be taken well by the markets," said Sampson. But the likelihood that Klein would clash more with the finance ministry, which wants lower interest rates, could destabilise economic policy, she said.



The shekel strengthened to 4.119 to the dollar from 4.1390 on Friday.



The Czech crown firmed slightly to around three-week highs against the euro after higher-than-expected inflation figures bolstered the view that a long series of interest rate cuts was over.



Consumer prices in December grew 0.5 percent on the month by the headline measure and 0.6 percent at the net level, against market expectations for a 0.3 percent increase on both counts.



The crown	     was bid at 35.98 to the euro from about 36.00 ahead of the data and 36.02 late on Friday.
The Slovak crown	  was little changed after the central bank again intervened to cap its strength around 42.3 to the euro.



The bank has intervened to prevent the crown from firming around that level level several times in December and again in January.

title: Emerging  FX -Zloty calm after Polish telecom delay.
text:
LONDON, Dec 23 (Reuters) - Failure to agree a price for the sale of a stake in Polish telecommunications company TPSA did not make much a of a dent in the zloty as trading was slim ahead of the extended Christmas and millennium break. 

 "It had an effect, but so many people are happy to have their positions through to the New Year," said Nick Douch currency strategist at Barclays Capital. 

 By 1140 GMT the zloty was trading at 4.165 bid to the euro, marginally higher than at the close of trade in New York, but slightly weaker than the 4.16 bid of morning trade on Wednesday. Against its basket of euros and dollars the zloty was 2.33 percent on the strong side of parity. 

 Poland on Wednesday rejected an offer by France Telecom  for a strategic stake in local phone group TPSA  and said it would call for fresh bids in the largest privatisation deal in the country's history. 

 Polish treasury minister Emil Wasacz said the French offer for a 25-35 percent stake in state-controlled TPSA had not met his expectations and that a fresh tender would be announced early in the New Year. 

 France Telecom, the sole bidder after U.S. SBC Communications  backed out in November due to a lack of clarity in market regulations, was believed to have offered $3.5 billion for a 30 percent stake, close to treasury demands. 

 The deal was said to have collapsed not so much because of the price, but due to the French firm's demands for full management control and 'get-out' clauses should a new telecoms law damage future profits. 

 Merrill Lynch said that while the bad news was evident in a six month delay there was a silver lining. 

 The cancellation clears the way for a new list of investors who came too late the first time or where circumstances have changed, Merrill said in a report. 

 "We believe Deutsche Telekom will undoubtedly be first on any advisors' wish list given their less than satisfactory position in PTC," Merrill said. The seasonal torpor in markets extended throughout emerging Europe, with the extent of Slovak intervention to halt the rise in the value of the crown becoming clear after central bank foreign exchange reserves rose to $3.4 billion as of December 21 from $2.9 billion as of December 15. "The Slovaks have got to think what they will do. The problem with intervention as they are practising it is that they are selling their own currency which adds to the money supply," said Douch. 

 The crown was little changed at 42.454 bid to the euro. 

 In South Africa, the prospect of bond markets closing until after the New Year limited appetite for rand trade. 

 The rand was at 6.1450 bid to the dollar.

title: Slovak  cbank says  intervening , buying euros.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 22 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said it intervened on the market on Wednesday, buying euros to prevent the crown from firming over 42.3 to the euro. 

 "I can confirm that a trade did take place...I don't think there is a rational reason for the exchange rate to move beyond 42.300 in the long term," Frantisek Szulenyi, the head of the central bank's foreign currency assets department, told Reuters. 

 The central bank intervened on Tuesday this week and on Tuesday and Wednesday last week to prevent the crown strengthening above the 42.3 level. 

 The bank, which will outline its 2000 monetary policy at a news conference at 1300 GMT, has long said it has a range within which it wants the crown to be but has not disclosed what that range is. 

 Although the central bank says it only intervenes to prevent volatility which does not refelect economic fundamentals, Karol Mrva, the head of the bank's monetary policy department told Reuters last week that volatility was now taken to mean a "significant strengthening" of the currency. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax, 421-7-5341-8403 bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS -  Slovak  cbank  intervention  seen light.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 21 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said on Tuesday it had intervened in the currency market and dealers said the bank had capped crown gains at 42.300 to the euro. 

 Dealers here said the intervention was light and made sense after intervention on Tuesday and Wednesday last week when NBS governor Marian Jusko said it was to prevent the crown from strengthing above 42.300 to the euro. 

 Only two dealers said they had seen the central bank act on Tuesday while others said any intervention must have been in very small volume. 

 The dealers that saw intervention said the central bank bid the currency from around 42.27 to the 42.3 level. 

 "It all happened pretty quietly...The NBS hung its bid on the trading system and only when some bank applied to it, it became clear it had been the central bank," Marek Senkovic, a forex trader at Istrobanka told Reuters. 

 "My estimate is that it (volume) could be only 3-4 million euros...Certainly not 10 (million) or more," Senkovic said. 

 The central bank declined to give the actual amount involved in its intervention. 

 Xenia Eacups from Tatra Banka said she had seen the crown peak at 42.260/300 to the euro earlier on Tuesday and this was probably the level at which the central bank had stepped in. 

 "In my view...the intervention came at the moment when the midpoint of the crown rate-spread was lower than 42.300 (to the euro)," Eacups said. "We can say it was only symbolic intervention...slightly stronger than just a verbal one," she said. 

 Referring to governor Jusko's remarks last week about the 42.3 level, Senkovic said: 

 "I think this is exactly what we saw today. I don't think the central bank would come up with a bid of some 42.400 or so, as it has been only checking the 42.300 level in recent days." 

Central bank foreign exchange department head Karol Mrva also said last week that central bank intervention would be used to check volatility. He said the bank now understood volatility to mean a "significant strengthening" of the currency. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  c.bank confirms crown  intervention .
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 21 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank told Reuters on Tuesday that it had intervened on the market earlier in the day to weaken the crown against the euro.

title: Emerging  FX -Slovak crown unmoved by bank sale.
text:
LONDON, Dec 20 (Reuters) - The sale of the Slovak government's 24 percent stake in Czech bank CSOB for 400 million euros had been widely anticipated by the foreign exchange market and did not renew upward pressure on the Slovak crown. 

 However, currency strategists said that the prospect of larger privatisations and a deepening of Slovak debt markets would add to upward pressures on the currency in the coming year. 

 "Volumes in the market are slim. The sale of CSOB had been expected," said Stefan Kolek, currency strategist at HypoVereinsbank. 

 The Slovak crown was trading 42.323 bid to the euro by 1102 GMT, slightly weaker from the New York close Friday of 42.27 to the euro and little changed from early morning levels. 

 The Slovak central bank has been intervening in the market in an attempt to halt the rise in the value of the crown, to the extent that foreign exchange reserves rose $39 million last week, reflecting purchases of foreign currencies. 

 Strategists say that given limited foreign participation in the Slovak crown markets, the central bank's task has been relatively easy so far, but that could change in 2000. 

 Privatisations such as that for bank Slovenska Sporitelna should also keep the crown strong. 

 "There will be more Slovak Eurobond issues, liquidity will be improved and the finance ministry wants to start a tapping system similar to the Hungarians," said Kolek. 

 Elsewhere, markets were quiet in the run-up to Christmas. 

 There was little movement in the Czech crown ahead of Tuesday's central bank meeting, with most analysts saying that a rate cut is unlikely. 

 The crown was trading at 35.981 bid to the euro, slightly weaker than 3.59 at the New York close. 

 The Hungarian forint was steady at 253.79 bid to the euro, compared with 253.97 on Friday, after the central bank cut its key two week rate by 25 basis points to 14.25 percent. 

 The only Hungarian data due for release this week is October retail sales. 

 The Polish zloty was stronger at 4.1940 bid to the euro, up from 4.21 bid at the New York close after more details emerged of the country's proposed sterilisation account for privatisation inflows. 

Central bank Governor Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said on Monday that 40 percent of next year's privatisation inflows should be kept on a special hard currency account to facilitate sovereign debt financing.

title: Slovak crown opens firmer, further upside seen.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 17 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown	     firmed slightly in moderate trading on Friday morning and had the potential to strengthen further on domestic client activity, dealers said.

 "There is some pressure from selling of forex into crowns by domestic clients," said Katarina Sevcikova, a trader at VUB Bank. "I would expect it to head for the 42.300 level again today." 

 On Tuesday and Wednesday this week, the Slovak central bank (NBS) intervened repeatedly to cap crown strength at the 42.300 to the euro level. NBS Governor Marian Jusko said on Thursday the crown would not firm beyond that level due to central bank intervention. 

 The crown was quoted at 41.43/51 to the dollar at 0755 GMT.

title: Emerging  FX -Weaker in Europe on  intervention  talk.
text:
LONDON, Dec 16 (Reuters) - Talk of crown sales by the Czech central bank enlivened quiet emerging European currency trade on Thursday, weakening the crown	  from 10-week highs against the euro despite a denial from the bank that it was intervening.
Local dealers said the central bank sold crowns	     at around 35.80 to the euro, but the central bank said it was not active in the market.



The currency weakened to 36.005 to the euro after the initial report from 35.725 in early trade and 35.80 late on Wednesday. Even after the denial the crown remained weaker on the day, at 35.855.


 Analysts have been expecting for weeks that the central bank would intervene, saying it would be worried a strong currency would hurt the fragile economic recovery. 

 "Thirty-five point eight is getting to quite strong levels. When they started to intervene last time (in October) it was at these levels and then it went all the way up to 37," said Jan Pudil, trader at West LB. 

 The central bank said soon after the intervention reports that it would not discuss monetary policy at a regular board meeting underway. 

Intervention was also a focus for the Slovak crown	 , which was softer after two days of central bank action to stop its appreciation.
The crown	     was quoted at 42.36 to the euro compared with 42.28 late on Wednesday and 1999 highs of 42.087 reached before the central bank began making weaker bids for its currency.


Central bank governor Marian Jusko said on Thursday the intervention meant the crown would not firm over 42.3 to the euro, Czech news agency CTK reported.



The zloty	  strengthened to 0.85 percent above the central bank's parity level from 0.67 percent on Wednesday ahead of the release later in the day of key industrial output data for November.



HypoVereinsbank said it expected output to have increased 13 percent from the previous year, which should keep the zloty above parity.



The zloty	     was trading at 4.234 to the euro, against 4.2260 on Wednesday, when the central bank left interest rates unchanged.

title: Slovak  cbank  intervenes , bidding at 42.3 to euro.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 15 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened on Wednesday to weaken the crown, bidding at 42.3 to the euro, dealers told Reuters. 

 "They are bidding at 42.300 to the euro. It seems foreign banks are trying to test the NBS resolve," a dealer, who requested anonymity, told Reuters. 

 The central bank said just prior to the intervention that rumours it had intervened earlier in the morning were untrue. It added, however, that it remained prepared to intervene should the need arise. 

 The head of the central bank's foreign exchange department Karol Mrva said the bank would intervene against volatility. 

 He said volatility was now understood to mean a significant strengthening of the crown. 

 On Tuesday, the bank bid down the crown to 42.15 to the euro and in mid-afternoon to 42.3 after the currency in early trade hit its strongest level since the creation of the euro, at 42.087 according to Reuters data. 

 The central bank said on Tuesday it had intervened to dampen down the crown, whose gains it attributed to Slovakia's invitation to begin membership talks with the European Union and end of year position closing.

title: Emerging  FX -Czech crown gains, Slovaks  intervene .
text:
LONDON, Dec 15 (Reuters) - The Czech crown	  strengthened to fresh 10-week highs against the euro on Wednesday following news of an acceleration of economic growth, while reports of a second day of central bank intervention held the Slovak crown	  below its 1999 highs.
Other emerging market currencies in the region were little changed, with Poland's zloty	  and Israel's shekel	  steady before the release of inflation data.



Although Czech third-quarter gross domestic product data was widely leaked on Tuesday, confirmation that the fragile economy was making a mild recovery gave the crown a slight boost that took it to its firmest rate against the euro since early October.


 GDP grew by 0.8 percent year-on-year in the third quarter, compared with forecasts for 0.5-0.7 percent and growth of 0.4 percent in the second quarter. But retail sales data released at the same time was less encouraging, showing an annual fall of 1.6 percent in October. 


The crown	     was bid around 35.829 to the euro, off its strongest levels of the day at 35.790 but still stronger than 35.86 late on Tuesday.



Analysts expected worries that the central bank may intervene to weaken the crown to cap its appreciation.


SLOVAK INTERVENTION NOTED



Across the border in Slovakia, dealers reported the central bank was intervening for a second day to keep the crown	     at the weaker levels it orchestrated on Tuesday.



They said the bank was bidding for the crown at 42.3 to the euro, similar to the rates it bid on Tuesday in its first ever intervention to weaken the currency.



"The market's so thin at the moment they (the central bank) can probably do what they want and get away with it," said Nick Douch, emerging market currency strategist at Barclays Capital.



The crown was trading at 42.288 after the reported intervention, compared with 42.32 late on Tuesday and 1999 highs of 42.087 early that day.



The focus in the zloty	     market was the release later in the day of inflation figures for November, expected to show a one percent monthly rise in consumer prices.



Ahead of the figures the zloty was little changed at 0.51 percent stronger than the central bank's parity level versus Tuesday's close of 0.59 percent. It was bid at 4.230 to the euro against 4.237.



The shekel was little changed near four-month highs following strong gains on Monday and Tuesday, which were triggered by historic peace talks with Syria and improved international sentiment on Israel's credit rating and stocks.



Inflation data to be published later in the day was expected to show consumer prices rose by as much as 0.2 percent in November. The shekel was trading at 4.1846 to the dollar versus 4.1856 late on Tuesday.



Hungary's forint			was little changed at 2.24 percent above parity, at the strong end of its trading band.



News on Tuesday that the central bank will reduce its monthly devaluation rate in the first half of next year, with another cut possible in the second half, meant the exchange rate mechanism would remain broadly unchanged in 2000, Deutsche Bank said.



Romania's leu	  strengthened against the dollar as the market remained undisturbed by the ousting of Prime Minister Radu Vasile on Monday. The leu was quoted at 17,860 to the dollar against around 17,900 at Tuesday's close.

title: FOCUS -  Slovak  cbank resumes  intervention .
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 15 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said on Wednesday it had again intervened to cap crown strength, with dealers seeing intervention on the bid at 42.300 to the euro for most of the day. 

 The bank said the intervention had been on a much smaller scale than Tuesday but central bank spokesman Ivan Paska told Reuters "When it will be necessary the central bank is ready to intervene again." 

 Market players estimated the central bank intervened to the tune of around 30 million euros on Tuesday. 

 Dealers reported that the bank had first entered the market on Wednesday when the crown touched 42.27 to the euro in mid-morning and bid it back to 42.3. 

 The currency has been trading above 42.3 throughout the afternoon and at 1517 GMT was quoted at 42.28/36 to the euro. The crown had opened at 42.32/40. 

 Dealers said the central bank move maintained stability in the crown market. 

 "The whole day has been relatively quiet thanks to a stable bid at 42.300 which the central bank seems to have owned up to," said Mario Mika, a trader at VUB Bank. "Their intervention was a success because it did prevent extreme volatility." 

 Wednesday's central bank activity followed several rounds of intervention on Tuesday to dampen down the currency which the central bank said had picked up strength because of Slovakia's invitation to join European Union accession talks on Friday and end of year position closing. 

 Prior to the crown's strengthening in the early part of this week, 42.300 had represented the currency's year high and dealers said this appeared to be the strongest level the central bank was prepared to accept. 

 The central bank has a target range for the currency but keeps it a closely guarded secret. 

 Before Wednesday's intervention, the head of the Slovak central bank's foreign exchange department, Karol Mrva, said the bank remained prepared to move if the crown firmed sharply. 

 He added that intervention would be used to check volatility. "These days, of course, volatility is viewed as a significant strengthening." ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax, 421-7-5341-8403 bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Emerging  FX -Weaker amid  Slovak intervention .
text:
LONDON, Dec 14 (Reuters) - Emerging European currencies were slightly weaker on Tuesday as intervention by the central bank of Slovakia drew more attention than the dismissal of the Romanian prime minister. 


The Slovak crown	 , boosted to record highs against the euro amid hopes for increased foreign investment next year, eased only a touch after dealers said the central bank intervened to weaken the currency.
The bank bid down the crown	     to 42.15 to the euro and then 42.20 after the currency in early trade hit its strongest level since the creation of the euro, at 42.087 according to Reuters data.


 Soon after the intervention it was bid at 42.168 compared with 42.10 late on Monday. 

 "I'm not sure how great a success they're going to have given the euro's broad-based weakness," said Jake Moore, emerging market currency analyst at Barclays Capital. "It (the intervention) will only be of limited impact." 

 The central bank's moves came despite Finance Minister Brigita Schmognerova saying on Monday she would prefer the central bank did not intervene before the end of the year as it could complicate exchange rate risks for companies. 

 Her comments boosted the crown to record levels, adding fuel to a rally driven in recent days by expectations the European Union's invitation for membership talks will boost foreign business investment in Slovakia. 

 ROMANIAN DISMISSAL 


The central bank of Romania was also expected to intervene after resuming dollar purchases on Monday to prevent an appreciation of the leu	 .



That prospect weakened the currency against the dollar and overshadowed the dismissal late on Monday of Prime Minister Radu Vasile.



Vasile was ousted following a revolt in his Christian Democrat party over slow economic reform and hopes that fresh leadership would speed admission to the EU.



The leu was bid weaker at 17,935 to the dollar from 17,895 on Monday.



The zloty	  continued to weaken amid dampened hopes for a fast decision on a full float of the zloty.



The currency fell to 1.08 percent stronger than the central bank's parity level, compared with 1.44 percent on Monday and more than two percent after comments by the finance minister last week triggered hopes for a quick move to a float.



Against the euro	     the zloty was bid at 4.221 to the euro from 4.212.



The focus is likely to shift to inflation on Wednesday, when consumer price data is expected to show annual inflation accelerated to 9.25 percent in November from 8.7 percent in October.



Czech third-quarter gross domestic product figures are also due on Wednesday, and expected to show about 0.7 percent growth from a year earlier.



The crown			was in the meantime little changed, bid at 35.86 to the euro against 35.88 on Monday.
Hungary's forint	  showed little reaction to news consumer prices rose 10.6 percent year-on-year and 0.4 percent month-on-month in November, broadly in line with market expectations.



The currency was bid at 2.22 percent above parity, just off Monday's close at the 2.25 percent strong end of the central bank's intervention band.

title: Slovak  deputy PM praises cbank crown  intervention .
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 14 (Reuters) - Slovak Deputy Prime Minister for the Economy Ivan Miklos said Tuesday's central bank intervention to weaken the crown was good news for current account deficit prospects. 

 "I think that the exchange rate prior (to Tuesday) was optimal from the point of view of maintaining competitiveness and thus also for the current account and trade deficit. I thus agree with the intervention," he told journalists. 

 Miklos said that a rate of around 43 to the euro was "balanced from the perspective of positives and negatives". 

 The central bank bid down the crown to 42.15 to the euro and in mid-afternoon to 42.3 after the currency in early trade hit its strongest level since the creation of the euro, at 42.087 according to Reuters data.

title: FOCUS -  Slovak  cbank  intervention  weakens crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 14 (Reuters) - The central bank said it intervened to weaken the Slovak crown for the first time on Tuesday, dampening enthusiasm for the currency following Friday's invitation from the European Union for Bratislava to begin accession talks. 

 The bank bid down the crown to 42.15 to the euro and in mid afternoon to 42.3 after the currency in early trade hit its strongest level since the creation of the euro, at 42.087 according to Reuters data. 

 "The National Bank really intervened because in its monetary programme it has as one of its aims a stable currency, not large fluctuations," Ivan Paska, a spokesman for the central bank, told Reuters. 

 "One of the reasons for the strengthening was entry into the EU integration process...The most pragmatic reason however is that the end of the year is drawing near and banks are closing their positions," he added. 

 The central bank's move was endorsed by Deputy Prime Minister for the Economy Ivan Miklos. 

 "I think that the exchange rate prior (to Tuesday) was optimal from the point of view of maintaining competitiveness and thus also for the current account and trade deficit. I thus agree with the intervention," he told journalists. 

CENTRAL BANK DECLINES DETAILS 

 The central bank declined to comment on the volume of its intervention, but one dealer who asked not to be named said he thought that around 30 million euros had been used. "I think that they've done around 30 million euros today...But it seems that they've accomplished what they wanted to accomplish," he said. 

 Branislav Matusek, a trader at ING Barings, said: "It seems like they are not trying to change the trend, but only to maintain liquidity in the market." 

 Dealers said the strengthening pressure on the crown came mainly from non-resident banks amid low liquidity, due to rising expectations of investment inflows after the EU issued its invitation. 

 The European Union on Friday invited Slovakia at its Helsinki Summit to begin talks on accession to the bloc. 

 "Non-residents have been selling forex in the past few days driving the crown up...Their main reasons probably are the expectations of improved ratings next year, EU accession talks and recent improvements in the balance of payments," said Dusan Svitek of Slovenska Sporitelna. 

 Finance Minister Brigita Schmognerova said on Monday she would prefer the central bank not to intervene to cap crown strength before the end of the year, as it could complicate the task of calculating currency risk for local companies. 

 However, the finance ministry said on Tuesday that intervention in the currency markets was a matter for the central bank and it was confident the bank would take steps to ensure exchange rate stability for the crown. 

 Late in November, when the crown was trading close to 43 to the euro, the central bank had said it was satisfied with the currency's level. Miklos said then that a further strengthening would be negative for the economy. 

 ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS-Dealers mixed on Slovak crown prospects.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 14 (Reuters) - Dealers and analysts said that central bank intervention to weaken the Slovak crown had been successful on Tuesday but were unsure whether or for how long the bank could continue to hold the currency down. 

 The bank bid down the crown to 42.15 to the euro and in mid afternoon to 42.3 after the currency in early trade hit its strongest level since the creation of the euro, at 42.087 according to Reuters data. 

 "If we compare the morning levels with those now, we can only say that the central bank was successful today," said Boris Somorovsky, a foreign exchange trader at Tatra Banka. 

 But, he added, it was difficult to predict what would happen next. At the end of the day's trading the crown was quoted at 42.322/402. 

 "If client orders to buy crowns and sell forex dominate on the market, pressing the crown back down to the 42.000 level, I think the central bank would have to intervene again...But there are too many 'ifs' in this." 

 The central bank said it had intervened to dampen down the crown whose gains it attributed to Slovakia's invitation to begin membership talks with the European Union and end of year position closing. 

 But analysts said there were also other factors at play which may be more difficult to counter. 

 "I'm not sure how great a success they're going to have given the euro's broad-based weakness," said Jake Moore, emerging market currency analyst at Barclay's Capital. "It (the intervention) will only be of limited impact." 

 Stefan Kolek of Hypovereinsbank said the crown would face upward pressure into next year as well, particularly because of inflows generated by the government's ambitious privatisation programme. 

 "In the next year there is a huge programme of privatisation which would push the crown stronger...We expect a soft landing next year in the economy supported basically by exports and a stronger crown would undermine seriously the business cycle." 

 "So they will have to do something and some kind of sterilisation of the FX inflows next year will come in my view," he added. 

 Slovak Deputy Prime Minister for the Economy Ivan Miklos said that Tuesday's central bank intervention to weaken the crown was good news for the country's current account deficit prospects. 

 He added that a rate of around 43 to the euro was "balanced from the perspective of positives and negatives". 

 Slovakia's reformist government came to power late last year, pledging to slash current account and budget deficits. Analsyst say it has made considerable progress although austerity measures have led to a slump in economic growth. 

 Dealers said they thought that around 30 million euros may have been used in the intervention. The central bank itself has declined to comment.

title: Emerging  FX -Zloty dips, Czech, Slovak stay strong.
text:
LONDON, Dec 13 (Reuters) - Poland's zloty	  weakened in thin emerging market currency trade on Monday after the central bank chief cooled hopes for a quick move to fully float the currency.


Central bank President Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said on Friday she was taken by surprise by Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz's statement that a decision on floating the zloty would be made soon.



The zloty	    , which surged almost three percentage points against the central bank's parity rate last week after Balcerowicz's statement, dipped to 1.53 percent above parity from 2.07 percent on Friday.



Gronkiewicz-Waltz said she thought the zloty would start to be freely traded at some point in 2000 though the central bank and government, which must both approve the decision, were not discussing the issue.



Analysts say a full float would not move the currency much because it is well within the boundaries of its trading band of 15 percentage points either side of parity. But it could provide a small psychological boost.



"It's positive because it sends a good signal of confidence to the market," said Banque Paribas analyst Sonia Hellemann, who expects a float around February or March.

The Czech crown		     , buoyed by demand from foreign business investors, was little changed near its strongest levels against the euro since October 4.



The currency, bid at 35.87 to the euro versus 35.84 on Friday, showed no reaction to producer prices data that met expectations.



Prices in November rose 0.2 percent from the previous month and 2.4 percent on the year, compared with analysts' forecasts for 0.3 percent and 2.5 percent.



Hellemann said the crown could firm to 35.6 and then 35.2 if the central bank continued to hold back from intervening to weaken it.



The Slovak crown			traded around record highs against the euro amid expectations the European Union's decision on Friday to start membership talks with Slovakia will boost foreign investment.



The crown was bid around 42.21 to the euro from Friday's close of 42.25.

title: Emerging  FX -No sign of CNB but crown nervous.
text:
LONDON, Nov 26 (Reuters) - The Czech crown came back from its highs on Friday in thin nervous trading with traders wary of the threat of intervention from the central bank, which had not so far materialised. 

 By 1139 GMT the crown was at 36.095 bid to the euro, down from a day high of 35.95 and 36.02 on Thursday. 

 "The Czech National Bank has not been in as far as I know," said one trader. 

 "Trading is shallow and a bit nervous," he added. 

 The crown had gone as high as 35.950 to the euro in the wake of Thursday's 25 basis point cut in interest rates to 5.25 percent. 

 Analysts say, however, that the rate cut will do little to hinder the crown's advance. 

 "After deciding on November 25 to cut rates by 25 basis points (without succeeding to move the exchange rate in response to the cut), and after it unsuccessfully attempted to talk the koruna weaker, the central bank is now left to consider another round of direct FX intervention to stem the relentless appreciation pressure on the koruna," CSFB said in a note to clients. 

 CSFB believes that the central bank will intervene if the crown breaks through 36 to the euro. 

 Czech central bank (CNB) Governor Josef Tosovsky said on Thursday the rate cut to 5.25 percent was aimed at meeting the bank's end-2000 inflation target. 

 Tosovsky said the rate cut was not expected to have a direct impact on the crown, which the CNB was still closely watching in case it needed to intervene to weaken the currency. 

 Elsewhere, the Slovak crown held on to some of the gains it made on the coattails of the Czech unit. 

 It was trading at 43.071 bid to the euro, still close to its day high of 43.039. The Polish zloty was in thrall to political developments, awaiting President Alexander Kwasniewski's decision on whether to sign a key tax bill. 

 The decision, on which the future of market darling Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz hangs, will be made Sunday at the latest. 

 The zloty was at 4.2857 bid to the euro, stronger than 4.30 at Thursday's close.

title: Slovak  cbank says still prepared to  intervene .
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 20 (Reuters) - Slovak central bank governor Vladimir Masar said on Thursday that the bank remained ready to intervene to support the crown on foreign exchange markets against fluctuations which were not based on fundamentals. The central bank has intervened several times during the week in the face of sustained downward pressure on the currency. Masar said the weakening that this had led to was not based on economic fundamentals. "In the development of basic economic indicators, no significant deviations took place recently...the NBS (central bank) is ready to intervene against fluctuations as it did today," Masar told journalists. 

 He added that the central bank's forex reserves as of May 18 were $2.7368 billion. 

 The Slovak government and the central bank launched a united front in defence of the crown on Thursday morning, helping the beleaguered currency mount a moderate recovery after weeks of steady decline. 

 It was quoted at 46.599/799 to the euro at 1410 GMT from records lows of about 42 on Wednesday. 

 Masar said the government's plans to bring order to the public finances and impose an import surcharge were a good sign. But they must be implemented. 

 "I see as very positive the clear signal sent by the government of the Slovak Republic...Government as well as politicians in the coalition clearly declared their will to solve problems." The central bank intervened directly to support the crown on Thursday and said exchange rate developments had priority over interest rates. The government pledged to increase VAT to raise money for the state budget and also to impose an import surcharge. 

 The government aims cut the fiscal deficit to around two percent of GDP this year and to halve the current account deficit from over 10 percent of gross domestic product last year. Deputy Premier for the Economy Ivan Miklos conceded that the fiscal target would be difficult to meet but that Wednesday's measures were a big step in the right direction. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax, 421-7-5341-8403 bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).
