title: Slovak  Natl Bker -3: Mkts Stable After  Intervention
text:
"The koruna exchange rate is now stable, it seems that the latest intervention has been effective," Masar commented. 

 "If the government loses its determination for economic reform, the exchange rate would again reflect it," central bank Vice Governor Marian Jusko said, although he added that the bank isn't planning to review its monetary plan for 1999. 

 Jusko said the interventions were aimed at stopping the continued depreciation of the koruna. He and other bank officials declined to say exactly how much the bank spent defending the currency but said the $60 million figure published by the media was fairly accurate. 

 Bank officials added that the central bank's reserves hadn't been jeopardized by the series of interventions this week, and quoted reserves at $2.74 billion on May 18, down only slightly from $2.75 billion May 12. 

 Masar admitted that the interventions have had a negative effect on interest rates, deposits and development of finances in the country but said it wasn't possible to avoid the problems. 

 He added that he realizes the economic reforms announced by the government will be tough on citizens. 

 "I do realize that the government has to adapt a handful of unpopular measures that are politically sensitive," he said. 

 As reported, the government responded to the growing crisis Thursday morning by pledging to rebalance some value added taxes, liberalize regulated prices, and cut some state administration and welfare spending. 

 There are also proposals for a short-term import tariff on some goods. 

 Slovak Premier Mikulas Dzurinda said specific dates and figures in the plan won't be announced until after further debate. 

 The koruna rebounded Thursday after the government's plans were announced and the central bank intervened again.

title: Slovak  Natl Bk  Intervenes  Again; No Threat To Reserves
text:
PRAGUE (Dow Jones)--The Slovak National Bank is confident that its interventions to support the koruna won't jeopardize its foreign currency reserves, even though it was again forced to intervene on Wednesday, an official told Dow Jones Newswires. 

 The central bank intervened after domestic corporate clients sent the koruna to a record low at SKK47.400 against the euro from SKK46.900 late Tuesday, as they continued to hedge against the further koruna weakening, said Frantisek Szulenyi, head of the central bank's foreign currency operations. 

 "The volumes we have used so far aren't too large," Szulenyi said. "We purchased some foreign currency on the domestic market in February and we still have by far not returned that amount." 

 Wednesday, the central bank intervened shortly after 0830 GMT, but at 1000 GMT, the koruna was still quoted at SKK47.300-SKK47.500, a dealer at ING Barings said. 

 "I think (the central bank) will have to intervene again. The amount they used was insufficient. And the outflow (of foreign currencies) continues," the dealer said. 

 According to Szulenyi, the bank didn't use more than $40 million in total in its recent interventions. Dealers said Wednesday, the bank didn't use more than $10 million. 

 The Slovak market is small and often illiquid, and koruna levels can change sharply on single trades. According to dealers in Bratislava, the koruna has been falling dramatically over the past weeks as the foreign investors are sidelined and domestic corporate customers have sold in a panic. 

 Analysts said the recent falls in the koruna reflect the delay in the implementation of economic reforms promised by the government after it took office in November. This has been exacerbated, however, by political uncertainty as Slovakia is facing the first-ever runoff in direct presidential elections end of May, analysts said.

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX - Currencies  in thrall to FOMC.
text:
LONDON, May 18 (Reuters) - The dramatic Labour Party victory in Israel was overshadowed on Tuesday by the meeting later in the day of the Federal Open Markets Committee and the shekel firmed only slightly. 

 By 0950 GMT, the Isreali currency was trading at 4.071 to the dollar, up from Monday's close in London of 4.105. 

 Analysts and strategists were still divided on whether the Fed would signal it is willing to tighten monetary policy in the wake of a surprising 0.7 percent jump in the U.S. Consumer Price Index for April. 

 Any tightening by the Fed would have a follow-through impact on the monetary policy of countries most closely tied to the U.S., such as Singapore, where the dollar firmed against the U.S. currency to 1.710 from a previous close of 1.715. 

 "Meanwhile, Singapore interest rates remain focused on the outcome of the FOMC meeting tonight. This will have an impact in a domestic market already worried that the stronger-than-expected U.S. inflation data for April will see a similar result in Singapore inflation for April which may turn positive when it is released next Monday," said Mitul Kotecha, currency strategist as Standard Bank in London. 

 Kotecha is expecting a tightening bias at the Fed. 

 Other Asian currencies were also firmer, with the Indonesian rupiah rising to 7,850 to the dollar from 7,950 on Monday. 

 In emerging Europe, currencies traded sideways to slightly weaker, awaiting the Fed. 

 Mark Rall, currency strategist at HypoVereinsbank, believes there is only a 40 percent chance of a tightening bias at the Fed. He said sentiment towards currencies in the region should focus on domestic factors. 

 The Slovak crown continued weaker on Tuesday in the wake of a surprisingly strong showing of former premier Vladimir Meciar in presidential elections. 

 Despite repeated intervention by the Slovak central bank, the currency continued to weaken and was trading 46.674/874 against the euro in London trade.

title: FOCUS- Slovak  cbank  intervenes  to support crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 17 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened in two waves to support the crown on Monday, buying 30 million euros worth of crowns after a corporate order of a similar amount had pushed the currency sharply lower. 

 Slovakia held the first round of presidential elections over the weekend but market players questioned by Reuters said this was not an important issue in the day's events although the conclusion of the final round in two weeks time could be a stabilising factor for the crown in the longer term. 

 "Today's weakening was purely customer driven and nothing to do with the presidential elections. Looking at it longer and broader maybe it could have some effect but this not what we saw today," said Dalibor Cernicka of MMB Brokers in Bratislava. 

 Dealers said the bank had intervened at between 46.7 and 46.3 to the euro. The central bank said that its last entry on the market had been at around 46.5. By late afternoon, the crown was being quoted at the same level. 

 Both the central bank and traders said they believed the initial weakening had been made on a single client order rather than speculation. The underlying reasons for the order were not clear. 

 "It wasn't a speculative deal, it was a corporate order of a relatively big amount and since the market is very thin the exchange rate just weakened...If market participants had big positions it wouldn't have affected the market very much," said Jan Toth, ING Bank's chief economist in Bratislava. 

 Toth said that given the size of the market, the central bank could have an effect when it intervened but that it would be ill advised to do so on a continuous basis because of the low level of offical reserves. 

 The central bank told Reuters earlier that the intervention had been in line with its established policy of moving against sharp fluctuations but not in favour of any specific rate. 

 Foreign exhange reserves stood at $2.76 billion as of May 12. 

 Slovak Finance Minister Brigita Schmognerova said on Monday that the strong showing of the government candidate in the first round of presidential elections over the weekend was a good signal for the crown. 

 "The results of the elections are a fairly good signal for the crown not to have to decline as sharply as it has up until now," she told journalists. 

 Some of the weakening of the Slovak crown last week, although not on Monday, had been attributed by dealers to nervousness from abroad about the participation of former premier Vladimir Meciar in the presidential elections. 

 Although Meciar took 37 percent of the vote he will contest the second round against clear favourite Rudolf Schuster who took 47 percent and has the backing of the four party coalition government. ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax, 421-7-5341-8403 bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak c.bank says money market moves more likely.
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 13 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank told Reuters on Thursday that any moves to influence the rate of the crown were more likely on the money markets than through direct foreign exchange intervention. 

 "What room there is for monetary policy, we see in the area of crown activities rather than in direct foreign currency interventions," Governor Vladimir Masar said in an interview. 

 The Slovak crown, which was floated in October last year, has been touching all time low levels against the euro in recent days. In early afternoon trading it was quoted at 45.45/55 to the euro. 

 The central bank said earlier that its decision not to add liquidity to the money market on Thursday was partly because of recent developments in the exchange rate. 

 However, shortly after announcing there would be no repo, what the central bank called an "extreme" reaction on the markets sent overnight rates soaring to around 17 percent from 10 percent. The bank then set an overnight repo to calm the market. 

 The central bank's foreign exchange reserves have been slowly falling in recent weeks. As of May 5, they stood at $2.7 billion. ((Robin Shepherd, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax, 421-7-5341-8403 bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovank c.bank says no need for  forex intervention .
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 12 (Reuters) - The director of the Slovak central bank's foreign currency asset department, Frantisek Szulenyi, told Reuters on Wednesday the central bank saw no need to intervene in the crown market at the moment. 

 "At the moment, the volatility does not seem such that it would be necessary to intervene," Szulenyi said. "I think it is not comparable to what we had here in March. It was a lot stronger then." 

 The central bank intervened by buying crowns early in March when low interest rates led to a sharp weakening. 

 "The monetary programme says we will not intervene against trends," said Szulenyi.. "We are monitoring the exchange rate and we will see what happens...If it is necessary, we are ready to correct developments." 

 Szulenyi said the market was illiquid and was being moved by very small trades. Dealers said earlier that the decline may have been partly due to the situation in Russia, where President Boris Yeltisn sacked Premier Yevgeny Primakov earlier in the day. 

 The Slovak crown weakened to record lows on Wednesday. It was quoted at 45.40/48 to the euro at 1205 GMT, from 45.17/27 at the open. ((Andrej Salner, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak c.bank says crown reflects fundamentals.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 22 (Reuters) - Slovak central bank governor Vladimir Masar said on Thursday that recent depreciation of the Slovak crown was a reflection of developments in the deficits of Slovak public finances and foreign trade. 

 "It is true that some depreciation has been taking place in the Slovak crown lately," Masar told a news conference. 

 "Exchange rate changes reflect the status of solving or not solving macro economic problems: development of public finances and of foreign trade...I have to still say that we unfortunately haven't recorded a reversal in the development of these two indicators," he said. 

 Masar said the Slovak crown had weakened four percent against the euro, the reference currency, since the beginning of the year. 

 The Slovak central bank has said it would not intervene to set a specific crown rate, but may intervene against high volatility not based on economic fundamentals. 

 The crown was quoted at 44.89/97 to the euro at 1025 GMT, unchanged from earlier. ((Andrej Salner, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax 421-7-5341-8403, bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak prime minister says crown fall not dramatic.
text:
FRANKFURT, March 11 (Reuters) - Slovak Prime Minister Mikulas Dzurinda said on Thursday that he did not view the recent fall in the Slovak crown as dramatic and added that he saw a level of less than 40 crowns per dollar as optimal. 

 "It is true that the crown has weakened over the last few days but I don't see this as anything dramatic," Dzurinda told a news conference hosted by Deutsche Bank AG . 

 Dzurinda added that the government's plan to slash budget and current account deficits in 1999 should offer the currency support over the longer term. 

 "It seems that it would be optimal if (the crown exchange rate) would be below 40 crowns to the dollar," Dzurinda said. 

 The crown was quoted at 40.72/82 to the dollar at 0820 GMT and 44.40/50 to the euro. It has fallen from a level of about 43 to the dollar over the last two weeks, forcing the central bank to intervene for the first time since October's crown flotation. 

Slovak Finance Minister Brigita Schmognerova said the crown's bid was triggered by a decline in short-term market interest rates. 

 Asked at what level the government would like to see interest rates, Schmognerova said that the 1999 budget plan assumed a further decline in interest rates but she offered no concrete forecasts. 

 The new Slovak government which came to power last October plans to cut the budget deficit to below two percent of gross domestic product and reduce the current account deficit to about five percent of GDP from about 11 percent of GDP last year. title: Slovak  cbank says no need to  intervene  at present.
text:
BRATISLAVA, March 10 (Reuters) - The director of the Slovak central bank's foreign currency asset department told Reuters on Wednesday that the bank saw no need to intervene to stabilise the crown at current levels. 

 "At the current level, we don't see any need to enter this market. The situation is calmer than it was yesterday," Frantisek Szulenyi said. 

 At the time of Szulenyi's comments the crown was quoted at 44.45/54 to the euro from 44.50/60 at the open. 

 Volatility began to shake the market on Tuesday morning, caused, the central bank said, by a marked decline in short term interbank interest rates itself brought on by a liquidity surplus. 

 The central bank responded directly by buying crowns. It also intervened indirectly by selling short term T-bills from its portfolio to slected banks and then on Wednesday through a repo tender to drain liquidity. All three measures were the first of their kind on the Slovak market since the crown was floated on October 1, last year. 

 Interest rates on the Slovak money market ranged from 9/10 bid/offer on overnights to 15.5/16.5 quoted for six month funds. On Tuesday, before the central bank action, they were quoted at between 4.0 and 16.0 percent, for maturities from overnights to six months. 

 Szulenyi said the stabilisation of the crown had been helped by the rise in interest rates, especially short term maturities. 

 ((Robin Shepherd, Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax, 421-7-5341-8403 bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  cenbank  intervenes  to stabilise crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, March 9 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank on Tuesday said it had intervened by selling foreign currency for crowns after the crown dipped sharply in mid-morning trading. 

 "For the first time since the (October 1998) flotation of the crown, the central bank directly intervened in the market," the director of the central bank's foreign currency asset department, Frantisek Szulenyi, told Reuters on Tuesday. 

 The central bank said earlier it had sold two-three day T-bills from its own portfolio for the first time to set a lower limit for short term interest rates, which have fallen sharply in recent days. 

 The Slovak crown came under selling pressure before midday, falling to 44.7/0 to the euro from opening levels of 43.89/98. It later rebounded to around 44.15. 

 "We had information from the market that there was no great foreign speculation behind it (the fall in the crown) just market illiquidity," Szulenyi said. 

 "The volume of the intervention was minimal. It was neither hundreds nor tens of millions of euros," he added. 

 Szulenyi said there were no fundamental reasons for the volatility. The central bank has indicated in the past it would intervene to calm the market and prevent wide fluctuations not based on fundamentals, but it is not known to have any target for the currency. 

 Szulenyi said the market now looked calmer but the central bank was ready to move again if deemed necessary. 

 ((Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-5341-8402, fax, 421-7-5341-8403 bratislava.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Slovak  cbank to  intervene  on crown if needed-paper.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Oct 15 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) said it was prepared to intervene to either support or weaken the crown but did not reveal at what level, the Narodna Obroda daily said on Thursday. 

 It quoted the National Bank of Slovakia's director of foreign exchange asset management, Frantisek Szulenyi, as saying that the bank wanted to see the crown stabilised after its flotation on October 1. 

 "The NBS again confirmed its interest in the fastest possible stabilisation of the Slovak currency and declared that if it considers its exchange rate under or overvalued, it is ready to intervene," the paper quoted Szulenyi as saying. 

 "We also stressed that an acceptable way of doing this is through a selected brokerage and five to six selected commercial banks," he said. The paper said Szulenyi spoke at a meeting of central bank representatives with selected banks on Wednesday. 

 Szulenyi did not say at what levels the central bank would like to see the currency nor at what levels it would intervene. 

 The central bank abolished the crown's plus/minus 7.0 percent band around a mark-dollar basket on October 1 after investors speculating on a devaluation sent the crown sharply lower and forced the central bank to intervene. 

 The crown dropped sharply after the flotation but has since regained some ground and has stabilised at around 12 percent below the central parity of the former basket. Pressure on the currency was caused by high foreign trade and budget deficits and mounted after a general election in late September. 

 The central bank has not intervened since the flotation. 

 The crown was quoted at 21.95/15 to the mark at 0810 GMT on Thursday, about 12 percent under the midpoint of its former basket.

title: Slovak National Bank Announces Supervised  Currency  Float
text:
BRATISLAVA -(Dow Jones)- The National Bank of Slovakia intends to pursue a policy of allowing the Slovak koruna to trade in a "supervised float," according to central bank board member Marian Jusko. 

 Speaking at a press briefing Monday following a meeting between opposition party economists and central bank officials, Jusko said the central bank will intervene on the market to assist the koruna if the central bank isn't happy with trading. 

 "If the float moves in an undesired direction, the central bank will intervene," he said, but offered few additional specifics. 

 The Slovak koruna is only in its second full day under its new currency regime. As reported, the central bank Thursday removed the fluctuation band used to guide the koruna since 1993 and let the koruna float against other currencies.

title: Slovak Natl Bank/Reserves -2: Chooses Mark As Key  Currency
text:
BRATISLAVA (Dow Jones)--The National Bank of Slovakia is satisfied with its current level of foreign currency reserves and has no plans to try and boost its holdings, Friday said central bank board member Marian Jusko. 

 Speaking at a press conference in Bratislava, Jusko said the central bank has access to foreign reserves via international banking sources, but that it sees no need at present to seek additional funding. 

 Jusko said he and others at the bank are satisfied with trading in the first day with neither band nor basket guiding the market. On Thursday the central bank removed a fluctuation band and currency basket used to guide the currency since 1993, and allowed the Slovak koruna to freely float. It wasn't necessary for the central bank to intervene on the market, Jusko said. 

 The Slovak koruna (SKK) immediately devalued by more than 6% against the dollar and the Deutsche mark. 

 The change in monetary policy followed weeks of speculation that the central bank would be forced to allow the koruna to weaken due in part to a current account deficit of 11% of gross domestic product and rising levels of external debt. 

 Jusko didn't comment on whether the central bank has any desired level at which it wants to see the koruna trading, but he did say the central bank will follow the Deutsche mark as its key currency, until 1999, when it will switch to the euro as its main currency. 

 Although the central bank reserves the right to intervene on the market to stabilize the Slovak koruna, it isn't planning to extensively manage the koruna's developments, he said. 

 Inflation, which is always a byproduct of a currency devaluation, isn't seen as a serious problem in 1999, he said, but he didn't give any specifics.

title: Slovak crown firms vs basket on Czech crown rally.

title: Emerging market  forex  - Czech recoils,  Slovak  skids.
text:
LONDON, March 31 (Reuters) - Central bank intervention prompted the Czech crown to recoil on Tuesday from its highest level against the German mark since last May's devaluation. 

 The neighbouring Slovak crown skidded too after the Republic of Slovakia's credit rating was downgraded to below investment grade by Moody's Investors Service late on Monday. 

 Elsewhere, a benign international investment environment persisted, with investors still happy to take on risky assets in return for high yields. Even the steep rise of the British pound this week is testament to this hunger for yield, analysts said. 

 The continued calm helped the Romanian leu weather Monday's resignation of Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea. 

 Ukraine's hryvnia was also little changed as Sunday's elections showed a swing to the left as the Communists took a quarter of party-list seats with half the vote counted. 

 "The recent carefree market sentiment seems to be broadly intact, but there are some signs of consolidation and profit-taking and market rallies in Asia have topped out," said one trader at a UK bank. 

 Broad-based dollar strength also pushed the South African rand weaker in the wake of Monday's drop through the psychologically-important 5-per-dollar level. 

 But central Europe remained the centre of attention, helped by the lure of long-term convergence plays as European Union accession talks started with six countries - Poland, Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovenia, Estonia and Cyprus. 

 Before the Czech National Bank's intervention on Tuesday, the crown had surged to test as high as 18.25 per mark - its strongest level since it was freely floated last May. 

 "They are squeezing domestic demand by keeping interest rates high and the currency is taking the heat in a market that seems to be happy to pick up yield anywhere," said Andrew Kenningham, east European fixed income analyst at Merrill Lynch. 

 "There might be some concern it is back to last May's level but the Czech Republic is in a better position fiscally and in terms of its balance of payments than it was last year." 

 However, analysts said further crown strength was likely to be resisted by more intervention, even if the extent and the timing of crown sales will now be very important. 

 "The way the central bank responds to further crown strength is now critical," said a senior research analyst at another U.S. investment bank. 

 "It (CNB) could have a bit of a policy dilemma if forced to intervene heavily, as this would increase domestic liquidity at a time they are trying to keep things tight to rein in inflation." 

 Earlier the Slovak crown weakened to as low as 3.0 percent below its parity against a basket of officially-targeted currencies, versus 1.70 percent on Monday. 

 Moody's downgraded the country's foreign currency debt to Ba1, one notch below investment grade. The crown recovered slightly later to trade about 2.60 percent below. 

 Analysts said that while the central bank had a tight grip on the market, ratings downgrades would further deter foreign direct and portfolio investments needed to bridge the country's current account deficit. 

 Concern about the country's ability to finance itself is also a worry because some existing foreign currency borrowings are directly linked to credit ratings. A $200 million sovereign loan made earlier this year, for example, triggers optional redemptions if the ratings fall to the equivalent of Ba3. 

 Elsewhere, the Polish zloty held firm at just under 7.0 percent stronger than its basket parity, but the central bank was not required to intervene for a second consecutive day. 


In Asia, the Thai baht underperformed after Moody's said it lowered the financial strength ratings of five Thai banks. title: SLOVAK CROWN EDGES UP AS CZECH CROWN STEADIES.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 2 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown edged up slightly against its mark/dollar basket on Tuesday morning as currency turmoil in the neighbouring Czech Republic abated a little. 

 The Slovak crown was trading at 34.604/34.654 to the dollar and at 19.489/19.528 to the mark. The crown is tied to a mark/dollar basket and may deviate from the mid-point of the basket by plus or minus seven percent. 

 At the open it was trading at as low as -2.35 percent but had recovered an hour later to around -2.20 percent from the basket mid-point. 

 "It (the crown) is strengthening a little bit this morning...It is a little bit calmer," said Tibor Fratrik of ING Bank. 

 The Slovak currency was hit hard on Monday by a wave of nervousness caused by heavy selling of the Czech crown after Czech Prime Minister Vacalv Klaus and his centre-right coalition government resigned at the weekend. 

 The Slovak central bank did not directly intervene to support the Sovak currency which dropped to a low of around -2.5 percent on the depreciation side of the basket from around -1.7 percent on Friday.

title: East Europe  Currencies /Wobble -3: Slovakia Seen Vulnerable
text:
Market participants in Bucharest also saw little threat of fallout from the koruna's troubles. 

 'The koruna won't have even the most minor effect on the leu,' said one trader at a foreign bank in Bucharest. 'The economies are in different shapes, and they attract different types of investors.' 

 He added that Romania will hold foreign investors' interest in coming weeks as the government prepares to eliminate restrictions on repatriation of foreign portfolio investment. 

 Ion Dragolin, monetary-policy director at the National Bank of Romania, also denied that the koruna's troubles would affect the leu. He said the central bank has bought more than $800 million in hard currencies on local markets since January in order to prevent the leu from rising sharply as a result of increased foreign investment and tight monetary policy. 

 But onlookers were less sanguine about the Slovak koruna's prospects. 

 Late Tuesday, the currency was trading on the weak side of the Slovak National Bank's intervention band. The band permits the koruna to fluctuate within 7% on either side of its midpoint against a basket of 60% mark and 40% dollar. 

 'The range of bid prices is 1% to 7% on the weak side of the band,' said Tibor Fratrik, chief dealer at ING Bank in Bratislava. 'There's no liquidity. You can't really predict what will happen on this market more than three hours in the future.'

title: Slovak Koruna Falls Vs Basket In Echo Of Czech Koruna
text:
BUDAPEST (AP-Dow Jones)--Tremors from the Czech Republic continued to rock the Slovak koruna Tuesday, with the Slovakian currency seen weakening against its fixing basket in highly illiquid, erratic trading. 

 Late Tuesday the koruna was seen trading on the weak side of the Slovak National Bank's intervention band, which allows the koruna to trade within a range of plus or minus 7% from the midpoint, against a basket of 60% Deutsche mark and 40% dollar. 

 'The range of bid prices is 1% to 7% on the weak side of the band,' said Tibor Fratrik, chief dealer at ING Bank in Bratislava. 'There's no liquidity. You can't really predict what will happen on this market more than three hours in the future.' 

 At 1327 GMT traders quoted the dollar at around 34.635 koruna. They quoted the mark at 20.800 koruna, in trading seen tightly focused on the Czech market, which has been rocked by speculation against the Czech koruna. 

 A spokesman for the Slovak central bank told Dow Jones Newswires Tuesday afternoon that the bank's monetary policy 'remains stable' and hasn't changed. 

 That's in stark contrast to the Czech central bank, which announced abruptly late Monday that it would discontinue its own intervention band to let the Czech currency float freely with a peg against the mark.

title: Slovak  crown settles after Czech cbank  intervenes .
text:

 "It seems there will be no dramatic movement as nothing special is happening on the market at the moment," Dusan Svitek of Slovenska Sporitelna said. 

 In early trading, the crown moved to -0.68 percent against its mark/dollar basket parity after opening at around 55 basis points below the midpoint. It then settled at about -0.63 percent. 

 Svitek said he expected it might move back to around -0.55 percent, which would pre-empt and Slovak central bank intervention. "But the central bank fixing will be important to this (development)," he added. 

 On Thursday the NBS fixed the crown/dollar at 32.990, and the crown/mark at 19.542, implying a deviation against the basket of -0.25 percent.

title: Slovak c.bank says ready to support SKK if needed.
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 15 (Reuter) - The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) said on Thursday that it was ready to move quickly to support the Slovak crown if the situation gets "out of control". 

 "We are following the Czech development very closely, and the Slovak crown is under control at the moment, but we are ready to quickly react and support it if it gets out of control," NBS Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi said. 

 The Slovak crown weakened by some 40 basis points in nervous afternoon trading on Thursday to around -0.70 percent versus its mark/dollar basket parity. 

 The Czech crown plunged about one percent in early Thursday trading before the Czech central bank intervened on the market to boost the ailing currency. 

 Szulenyi would not say at what levels the NBS saw it neccessary to support the Slovak crown, nor would he disclose what tools would the bank use if the intervention was needed. 

 "There are some signals that we can expect stronger pressure on the Slovak crown in the near future, involving larger volumes than we have seen so far," he said. 

 Traders estimated that up to $100 million has left the country so far today as market volatility increased. 

 Traders say foreign players are trading the Czech and Slovak crowns together, effectively implying a depreciation trend on both currencies. 

 Some dealers said they expected the Slovak crown to weaken further during the day and that it could even test the 1.0 percent level on the depreciation side of the currency basket midpoint. 

 Szulenyi said the NBS so far did not need to directly intervene on the market to support the Slovak crown, but that an indirect intervention through its fixing helped the crown stay steady two weeks ago. 

 On Thursday the NBS fixed the crown some 45 basis points above the market levels, and some dealers said this could be seen as a signal that the central bank does not want the crown to fall too much.

title: FOCUS-SLOVAK C.BANK SIGNALS SUPPORT FOR CROWN.
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 15 (Reuter) - The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) sent a strong signal on Thursday that it would support the Slovak crown to prevent turmoil on the Czech market from pulling the Slovak currency down. 

 NBS Treasury Director Frantisek Szulenyi told Reuters the Slovak crown was under control at the moment, but added the bank was ready to "react quickly and support the currency if neccessary". 

 The Slovak currency was hit by what dealers said were massive sales of Slovak crowns resulting from the fall of the Czech crown earlier in the day. The Slovak crown lost some 45 basis points as about $100 million left the country. 

 "This (statement) really showed a new direction and helped to calm down the market," said Dusan Svitek, an FX trader at the largest Slovak market player, Slovenska Sporitelna. 

 Svitek said the crown strengthened by around 25 basis points after the central bank comment and moved to around -0.50 percent versus its mark/dollar basket parity. 

 "Though further development will still much depend on the Czech crown moves, I see the Slovak crown ranging between parity and one percent in the depreciation sphere, a point at which the central bank could intervene," he said. 

 The Slovak crown is closely related to the Czech crown since foreign banks often play the two currencies together so the currencies usually move in tandem. 

 The Czech and Slovak republics used to be united in the Czechoslovak federation which split peacefully in 1993 and the two economies are still very closely linked. 

 Svitek noted that the NBS sent also a second, indirect, signal to the market through its fixing on Thursday, indicating it would not let the Slovak crown fall too far. 

 The NBS on Thursday fixed the crown at 32.990 to the dollar and at 19.542 to the mark, implying a deviation of -0.25 percent versus the basket midpoint. 

 The crown was trading at -0.61 percent at the time of the fixing calculation. 

 Tibor Fratrik, a dealer at ING Bank, said he saw the run on the Slovak crown earlier on Thursday as pure speculation and not based on fundamentals. 

 "I would say it was just bargain hunting, in which also some domestic banks were involved," he said. "This decline (of the Slovak crown) seems to me a short-term phenomena which will not set a longer-term trend." 

 Fratrik said he expected the crown to move between parity and -0.1 percent versus the midpoint and that the central bank appeared content for it to stay within this range.

title: Slovak  c.bank says  interventions  effective-agency.
text:
BRATISLAVA, May 3 (Reuters) - The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) considers its interventions last week to halt a weakening of the crown currency to have been effective, central bank governor Ivan Sramko was quoted on Tuesday as saying.  

The NBS intervened on the foreign exchange market to prop up its currency on Friday for the first time in more than two years, although it intervened repeatedly to slow a sharply rising crown earlier this year.  

"In our view, the crown had approached a level where it might have threatened our main inflation goal," the official TASR news agency quoted Sramko as saying. "That is why we reacted how we reacted, and the move proved to be effective."  

The bank started to buy crowns on the market when the unit touched a six-month low of 40.000 per euro. The crown traded at 39.265/295 to the euro as of 0930 GMT on Tuesday.  

Sramko's comments echoed similar statements made by central bankers after the bank's monthly monetary policy meeting on Friday.  

The NBS fought hard to slow what it considered too fast a crown firming for over a year. It bought three billion euros in interventions aimed at halting the crown rise in the first quarter of this year.  

But the crown weakened sharply in the past month due to outflow of capital from central European markets, falling from all-time highs of 37.510 per euro seen early in March.  

Dealers said Friday's intervention volume was small compared with amounts of euros the bank bought in its attempts to slow crown firming, estimating that the NBS might have sold up to 200 million euros on the market.  

The NBS has not elaborated on Friday's interventions, but Sramko reaffirmed on Tuesday that the bank would stay ready to use its tools to protect its inflation goals.

title: UPDATE 2- Slovak  c.bank  intervenes  to halt crown fall.
text:
BRATISLAVA, April 29 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market on Friday to halt a weakening of the crown currency after outflow of hot money pushed it to a six-month low against the euro, dealers said.  

The bank's action was the first move to support its currency in more than two years after it had intervened repeatedly over the past year to curb what it saw as an excessively rapid crown appreciation.  

Dealers said the central bank started buying crowns when it weakened to 40.0 per euro on Friday, levels last seen at the end of October.  

"The NBS has shown that it does not like the crown above 40.0... It can be expected that they will come again above that level," said Slovenska Sporitelna dealer Vladimir Gajdos.  

The central bank, which holds its monthly monetary policy meeting on Friday, was not immediately available for comment.  

The action pushed the crown as far as 39.400 per euro, but some traders said another move towards the 40.0 level was possible as foreign players might want to use the intervention to close positions accumulated during the crown's fast rise.  

The Slovak unit had strengthened quickly in the first weeks of the year, rising to a record high of 37.510 per euro in early March, which forced the central bank to use all its tools to halt the firming, including interventions and an interest rate cut.  

But the crown has fallen more than 5 percent against the euro in the past month, as foreign investors have fled European emerging markets due to political uncertainty in the region and the prospect of rising interest rates in the United States.  

Market watchers said the intervention could be seen as the central bank returning some euro liquidity into the thin market after it had bought more than 3 billion euros during its fight against crown firming between December and March.  

However, the estimated intervention volume on Friday was small at up to 100 million euros.  

"This step should put a cap on SKK volatility, which has dramatically increased since mid-March," ING Bank Chief Economist Jan Toth wrote in a market note.  

ING does not expect the crown to firm quickly in the near future, partly because hundreds of millions of euros are expected to leave the market in dividend payments to foreign owners of Slovak companies in the next few weeks.  

However, analysts see the crown returning to the firming path later this year, helped by Slovakia's strong economic growth and expected foreign direct investment projects.  

"We might no longer see weak levels beyond 40 (per euro) in May, and a gradual strengthening towards 37 by year-end would be a logical move, taking into account the strong fundamental story," Toth said.  

At 0800 GMT the crown was quoted at 39.475/495 to the euro, compared with Thursday's close of 39.850/880.

title: Emerging  FX -Slovak crown holds near record peaks, zloty steady.
text:
LONDON, March 1 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown remained firm on Tuesday in spite of signs the central bank is taking a tougher stance against its strength, with the Polish zloty also holding close to 2 1/2 year highs versus the euro.  

Strong foreign investment inflows continue to buoy the Slovak currency in the face of strong intervention against it from the authorities.  

The central bank intervened to sell crowns again on Monday, after earlier cutting key interest rates by 100 basis points, but still weakened the currency only a few pips from record highs against the euro.  

"They're stepping up intervention, there's no question about that. We estimate that interventions in February could have been as much as 1.8 billion euros, which is a massive amount in a market as small as this," said Koon Chow, emerging markets strategist at CSFB.  

It would also be a big leap after the bank said it bought 290 million euros in interventions in January.  

"But I get the sense the central bank is in a mindset to curb appreciation rather than trigger a reversal of the trend. I don't get a sense they're out to trigger stops or force a messy exit by trading desks," Chow added.  

By 1115 GMT, the crown traded at a bid price of 37.825 per euro , little changed on the session.  

The reformist credentials of the Slovak government have laid a platform for strong foreign investment inflows into the country.  

A growing number of foreign manufacturers are setting up plants in Slovakia and the government is hoping to seal a S.Korean investment project worth 500 million euros in coming weeks.  

Chow said the one near-term risk factor was the size of long positions that have been built up in the crown, making the market vulnerable to a sharp decline in the event of an external shock.  

ZLOTY HOLDS FIRM  

The Polish zloty remained within touching distance of 2 1/2-year highs against the euro, still finding support from a backdrop of a broadly soft dollar and low global interest rates.  

The market shrugged off comments from the leader of Poland's main opposition Civic Platform party, Jan Rokita, that zloty strength is starting to become excessive.  

Rokita, whose party is well ahead in the polls in the run up to elections later this year, also said he would consider unilaterally adopting the euro as a means of preventing too much currency strength.  

"(Rokita's) are not too much to worry about. Certainly, the government is keeping an eye on zloty strength, but the rhetoric is mixed at moment," said Osman Wahid, emerging markets strategist at J.P.Morgan.  

"The central bank won't want it to continue the sharp appreciation of the past 8 months, but you also have to consider that when euro/polish was at its highs most people thought the zloty was undervalued, so in that sense its been coming back into line."  

Wahid said the factors to watch out for a potential end to the zloty rally were analysts starting to cut back their growth forecasts and when the central bank starts cutting interest rates.  

The central bank Monetary Policy Council shifted its monetary policy bias to "easing" from "tightening" following its monthly meeting last Friday, but the move had little impact on the zloty.

the dollar        from 2.9413.

The crown weakened only slightly after the intervention, moving to 37.870 to the euro.   

The crown has gained 2.3 percent against the euro this year, boosted by Slovakia's encouraging economic performance and expectations of strong foreign investment inflows.

The central bank's fight against crown firming has sparked market talk about an interest rate cut at the February monetary policy meeting.

title: Emerging  FX -Upside pressure on forint eases, Czechs eye rates.
text:
LONDON, Feb 24 (Reuters) - The strong upside pressure on Hungary's forint subsided on Thursday, though analysts said it could be a temporary lull, while Czech crown dealers awaited a key interest rate decision.  

The forint tracked back from near two-year highs hit against the euro earlier in the week, giving the central bank some breathing space after it rose close to the upper limit of its trading bands, which comes in around 240 to the euro .  

Central bank Governor Zsigmond Jarai said on Wednesday the bank would, if necessary, defend the bands, though he said it had no plans to intervene on the market as long as the bands hold.  

"The key point is when you get closer to bottom of the bands you will see higher volatility. Today's move higher (in euro/forint) is part of that," said Martin Blum, head of emerging markets research at HVB in Vienna.  

"I don't think it signifies a change in the trading environment and the rate could move lower again."  

By 1015 GMT, the forint was a touch down on the session around 242.50 to the dollar.  

"Nobody is under the illusion that the band would be moved, but by the same token central bank comments that it has no problem with the forint trading in its current range means perceptions of the risk of it moving higher are limited," Blum added.  

Blum said as long as players did not perceive a risk of a sharp move back to 245, the trend would remain for the forint to strengthen towards the band limit.  

The forint trades in ERM2-style bands allowing 15 percent fluctuations on either side of a central parity rate against the euro.  

The Czech crown was little moved around 29.90 per euro ahead of the central bank's monthly interest rate decision. Most analysts expect rates to be left on hold, but the market was wary following January's surprise cut to 2.25 percent.  

"Our bias is against a cut. New board members will want to become more familiar with the data, and the bank may also see some scope for euro/czech to move higher on political uncertainty," said Blum at HVB.  

Three new board members will sit on the seven-member panel.  

Prime Minister Stanislav Gross on Thursday called on President Vaclav Klaus to step into talks to resolve an excalating row within the ruling centre-left coalition, which threatens to cost the government its majority in parliament.  

The junior coalition partner, the Christian Democrats, have called on the Social Democrats to replace Gross due to questions about his personal finances.  

Meanwhile, the Slovak crown traded at 37.84 to the euro , a fresh record high against the euro.  

The Slovak central bank intervened for the third time this week on Thursday, but did little more than hold up the crown's progress.  

LIRA UP ON IMF HOPES  

The new Turkish lira strengthened to under 1.3 per dollar , its best levels in 2-1/2 years, helped in part by comments from Finance Minister Kemal Unakitan on Wednesday that three key reform bills would be submitted to parliament over the next few days.  

Passage of the bills on social security, tax and banking are a pre-condition for the International Monetary Fund board approving a new $10 billion loan package to replace the $19 billion deal that expired this month.  

"Saying the social security bill would be forwarded next week is a step in the right direction," said Debbie Orgill, emerging markets analyst at ABN AMRO.  

"That's the biggest of the three because it would mean a big improvement for the fiscal outlook." The lira traded at 1.2960 to the dollar on the interbank market from 1.303 at Wednesday's close.  

Orgill said the market would be wary of the risk of central bank intervention to cap lira gains under the 1.3 per dollar handle, especially with the Turkish currency also rising against the euro - the currency of its main trading partner.

title: UPDATE 1- Slovak  cbank  intervenes  again to rein in crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 23 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank resumed its long battle against a sharp rise of the crown on Wednesday, intervening on the foreign exchange market after the currency hit a record high of 37.870 per euro. The crown started surging after the local market close on Tuesday, breaking beyond the psychological level of 38.0 per euro, which has been long defended by the central bank.   

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) has used a mix of direct market interventions and repo tenders to halt the unit's rise in recent weeks. Its action on Wednesday was the second direct intervention this week and eighth such move this year. "I can confirm we are intervening. The reasons remain the same as with the previous interventions," central bank spokesman Igor Barat told Reuters.   

Dealers estimated the NBS bought roughly 200 million euros in Wednesday's intervention, less then estimated 300 million euros on Monday. The NBS has been trying to fight off inflows of speculative capital for more than a year to counter what it sees as unwarranted exchange rate moves, using its entire arsenal.   

The NBS has been criticised by analysts and international institutions such as the International Monetary Fund for managing the exchange rate too tightly, but the bank said too strong a currency could harm the economy and endanger adoption of the euro.   

The crown eased to 37.966 to the euro following the NBS action. But it recovered quickly to trade at 37.890/930 per euro at 0815 GMT.   

Analysts said the NBS strategy would curb firming pressure on the crown only temporarily, saying the currency had potential to rise further in the longer-term due to an improving performance of the new EU member's economy.   

"We believe that the Slovak central bank will lose the battle against the fundamentals in the long run," said Danske Bank analyst Christian Vincens. "The fundamentals and the structural nature of the Slovak economy is too solid to have the crown trading at these levels."   

The central bank has said it did not oppose a gradual firming of the crown, but said the exchange rate movements were often inappropriate compared with real improvements to the country's economic trends.   

The market expected the central bank to cut interest rates formally by 75-150 basis points this month to bring the key two week repo rate in line with interbank deposit rates, which fell sharply in the past weeks due to the NBS's repo tender tactics.   

The central bank rejected all bids in its last four repo auctions to reduce the crown's attractiveness to short-term capital.   

The NBS slashed borrowing costs by 200 basis points last year, bringing the two-week repo rate to 4.0 percent, but later turned to interventions after the rate cuts failed to weaken the crown.

title: UPDATE 1-Emerging  FX -Forint dips further after rate cut.
text:
LONDON, Feb 21 (Reuters) - The Hungarian forint added to earlier losses on Monday after the central bank cut interest rates by a larger than expected 75 basis points while the Slovak central bank intervened to weaken the crown.  

Hungary's Monetary Council said a favourable inflation outlook had allowed them to lower key rates to 8.25 percent, but added it would toe a cautious line going forward given the country's sizeable current account and budget deficits.  

The forint fell as low as 243.85 after the decision, but by 1454 GMT had recovered somewhat to trade around 243.40 per euro .  

Most analysts had expected the bank to cut by 50 basis points, but said surprisingly benign January inflation data and last week's forint strength had probably tipped the scales in favour of a bigger move.  

Some said the central bank may be disappointed if it hoped that in moving more aggressively it would help take some of the steam out of the forint's rally - it struck near two-year highs against the euro last week.  

"You can read it in two ways. A big easing now may persuade people to reduce long positions, on other hand you could take it as very bullish for bonds," said Zsolt Papp, emerging markets analyst at ABN AMRO.  

"The market might be inclined to go for the second reading."  

Foreign inflows into the bond market have driven the forint higher in recent weeks as investors bet on an accelerating pace of rate cuts boosting prices.  

Four new Monetary Council members, hand-picked by Prime Minister Ferenc Gyurcsany, are expected to give the rate-setting body a more dovish bias in future meetings.  

The forint is not far off the strong limit of its trading bands against the euro, which comes in around 240, though Governor Zsigmond Jarai said on Monday he was not concerned.  

The market was awash with rumours last week of sizeable positions being taken in the options market betting that the limit would be breached.  

SLOVAK CROWN DOWN AFTER INTERVENTION

The Slovak central bank confirmed it had intervened to weaken the crown on Monday, after the currency had earlier risen to a fresh record high of 37.95 per euro , in its fourth market intervention in the past two weeks.  

"We are intervening because we are still not satisfied with the pace of the crown firming," central bank spokesman Igor Barat told Reuters.  

Analysts said with foreign investment inflows continuing to pour into the country, the best the bank could hope for was to hold the crown steady.  

"Including today, they've probably now intervened to the tune of over $1 bln in recent weeks, and only succeeded in keeping the crown flat," said Koon Chow, emerging markets strategist at CSFB.  

The Slovak crown traded a shade down at 38.03 per euro.  

It was a less bullish picture for the neighbouring Czech crown, which retreated from 2 1/2 year highs against the euro as the pressure was cranked up on Prime Minister Stanislav Gross to resign. Gross vowed to fight on after a weekend meeting with President Vaclav Klaus following calls for him to quit from junior coalition partners, the Christian Democrats, over questions about the funding of his flat and his wife's business.  

The crown eased off its highs, but losses were fairly limited. It was down 0.2 percent to the euro at 29.91 .  

If the Christian Democrats leave the coalition, the government would lose its one-vote parliamentary majority, though analysts said they would probably not want to trigger early elections.  

Shares in the country's leading phone company Cesky Telecom (SPTTsp.PR) dipped on concerns the political spat was a threat to the firm's upcoming $3 billion privatisation.  

The crown's strong gains so far this year have, in part, been built on expectations of strong foreign inflows arising from the Cesky sale.

text:

The NBS has been trying to slow what it sees as unjustified crown appreciation for more than a year, saying it could damage the economy and endanger euro adoption later this decade.   

Dealers said the bank intervened to weaken the crown twice on Thursday, first using covert deals with London-based banks when the unit touched a record high of 38.000 per euro.   

It stepped into the market again when the currency rebounded to 38.030 per euro from 38.100.   

"I can confirm we have intervened. Today's intervention was motivated by the NBS's ongoing dissatisfaction with the currency developments which are harmful to the economy," central bank spokesman Igor Barat told Reuters.   

He said the bank would keep watching the crown moves and was ready to use all available tools to correct unwarranted exchange rate swings in the future, echoing the NBS's recent comments.   

The Slovak unit retreated back towards the 38.100 per euro level following the second round of the NBS action. It traded at 38.048/098 per euro at 1525 GMT.   

The bank has intervened on the market four times this year to keep the crown in check. It has also left the money market in a huge liquidity surplus in the past week to deter inflows of short-term capital.   

The crown, which is up 1.7 percent against the euro this year, has been rising rapidly over recent months boosted by Slovakia's improving economic performance, expectations of foreign direct investment and debt rating upgrades.   

The NBS has said it is not against gradual crown firming based on improving productivity, but has warned the market that it would carry on its crusade against the unit's rally if it is not in line with economic trends.   

The NBS board used hefty rate cuts last year to make the crown less attractive for speculators, but has indicated recently that it would stick to other tools as the unit's rise seemed to be no longer driven by interest differentials.   

However, analysts said that positive January inflation figures, released earlier on Thursday, created room for the bank to bring the key two-week repo rate, which stands at 4.0 percent, down further to ease firming pressure on the crown.   

The NBS trimmed credit costs by 200 basis points last year despite analysts' warnings that such a policy loosening might trigger demand-led inflationary pressures in the future.   

Traders said the bank's latest action would soften the crown only temporarily as weaker levels usually trigger more crown buying, adding players would keep testing its determination to defend the psychological 38.0 per euro level in the coming days.   

"They (the NBS) will not reverse the firming trend... they can only slow it down temporarily," said ING Bank dealer Jan Rafaj. The NBS was estimated to have bought foreign currencies worth roughly 200 million euros in Thursday's interventions, compared with around 400 million on Monday.

title: Emerging  FX -Zloty uneasy after Hausner quits, Slovaks  intervene .
text:
LONDON, Feb 7 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty tripped up from two year highs against the euro on Monday after Economy Minister Jerzy Hausner quit the ruling party.  

The Slovak crown's rally also paused following the central bank's third intervention against it this year, while the South African rand and Turkish lira awaited key interest rate decisions later in the week.  

The zloty extended its recent upward charge early on, setting new peaks around 3.9520 before Hausner's departure triggered a bout of profit taking.  

Analysts said Hausner's decision to leave the leftist Democratic Left Alliance, after the party tamed his plans to control public spending, could knock the firming zloty in the short-term if he forms another party to contest the elections.  

"If a new party did form in the coming months and that did have some participation from present government members that could disturb the zloty," HVB analyst Martin Blum said.  

By 1125 GMT, the zloty was down 0.16 percent at 3.97, but still close to 25-month highs .  

Government officials said Hausner should resign from the cabinet and he has said he may work with a new movement potentially involving Prime Minister Marek Belka.  

Polls predict the ruling party could lose elections this year.  

However, a new reform-based centrist party could ease external concerns about the influence of extreme political parties ahead of this year's elections and boost the zloty.  

"It could reduce the level of support for some of the more activist parties which would reduce election risks," Blum said.  

SLOVAKS INTERVENE AGAIN  

Market watchers said the Slovak central bank's intervention, pulling the crown back from the 38.00 per euro barrier, would not have much long-term impact because of continued strong investment flows.  

The central bank has attempted to stem the crown's rise out of fear that a strong currency will hurt exports. The bank last intervened on Thursday.  

"The response of the Slovak crown to this intervention has been very shallow," Credit Suisse First Boston strategist Koon Chow said. "We have a constructive medium term view on the crown."  

The crown was down 0.17 percent to 38.06 per euro , off of all-time highs set last week.  

However, Chow said investors looking for positive economic data similar to that in the Czech Republic last week could be caught out.  

"My one nagging concern is that investors may have a very positive expectation of trade data out this Friday and there could be scope for disappointment," he said.  

Elsewhere, the Czech crown continued to rise, equalling Friday's 2-1/2 year highs at 29.90 per euro .  

Analysts said the South African rand's slide against the dollar bucked the trend among other commodity producers.  

"People are increasingly concerned about the rand which may increase ahead of the Monetary Policy Council meeting this week," Chow said.  

Opinion is divided on the direction of Thursday's policy meeting. Some analysts expect rates to stay at 7.5 percent but others have not ruled out a cut.  

The rand was down a touch against the dollar at 6.14 .  

The Turkish central bank will also decide the direction of monetary policy this week, with some analysts expecting another 100 basis point cut from the meeting slated for Tuesday and Wednesday.  

The overnight borrowing rate is currently 17 percent and the overnight lending rate is 21 percent. The lira held firm at 1.3145 per dollar in interbank trade .

title: UPDATE 1- Slovak  cbank  intervenes  as crown nears record highs.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 7 (Reuters) - Slovakia's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market to check the crown as it approached all-time highs on Monday, the latest move in a long battle to curb the rising currency.   

Traders said the National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) stepped into the market when the crown traded at 38.020 against the euro, near record highs of 38.000.   

"We consider the pace of crown appreciation to be too fast and harmful for the economy," NBS spokesman Igor Barat said.   

Barat gave no details about the crown sales, which were the second direct action on the market in less than a week and the third intervention this year.   

He declined to comment whether the NBS did not want to see the crown firming through 38.000 per euro, but dealers said they expected the central bank to keep protecting the psychological level in the near future.   

The intervention pushed the crown as low as 38.140 per euro, but it quickly rebounded to 38.050/100.   

The crown has repeatedly hit new record highs in the past few weeks and it is up 1.8 percent versus the euro since the beginning of the year.   

The NBS has said it was slowing crown appreciation to avoid hurting the economy as well as to smooth the path to meeting inflation and currency stability criteria for adopting the euro.   

Traders said the NBS was selling crowns in several rounds on Monday. But they added there was strong interest in buying the Slovak unit at around 38.100 per euro, which prevented the intervention from having a more significant impact.   

"I don't see a longer-term impact... We will be under 38.000, it's just a matter of time," one dealer from a foreign bank said.

text:
BRATISLAVA, Feb 3 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened directly on the foreign exchange market for the second time this year on Thursday to halt a sharp rise in the crown .   

"The crown's firming pace is not in line with the development of economic fundamentals and is harmful for the economy," National Bank of Slovakia spokesman Igor Barat told Reuters.   

"We will keep using our tools if this harmful development continues."   

Traders said the central bank stepped into the market when the crown touched the psychological level of 38.000 to the euro, notching a 1.8 percent gain since the start of the year.   

They estimated that the NBS might have bought 100-150 million euros in the first round of intervention.   

The crown has repeatedly hit new record highs since the beginning of 2005 and the central bank has been trying to slow the firming pace with direct intervention and by managing liquidity.

The crown weakened after Thursday's intervention, briefly touching 38.200 per euro, but traders, mainly foreign banks, used the move to buy cheaper crowns again.   

"The market seems to be calming down at the moment. I would expect the central bank to do the same (intervene) if the crown moves to 38.0 again in the afternoon," said Slovenska Sporitelna dealer Vladimir Gajdos.

title: Emerging  FX -Zloty leads C.Europe higher, hits 25-month highs.
text:
LONDON, Feb 3 (Reuters) - Central European currencies hit new highs on Thursday, led by the Polish zloty which scaled 25-month peaks against the euro on talk of strong foreign demand.  

A fresh bout of zloty strength began on Wednesday after Economy Minister Jerzy Hausner signalled there was little he could do to stop it rising further.  

The Polish currency extended gains under the four-per-euro level on Thursday, with dealers reporting a combination of option-related and hedge fund buying.  

"There has been some interest from hedge funds. On one level people have been hedging options positions, while those who trade the zloty on a technical basis will have been brought in by a strong close last night," said one London analyst.  

One dealer said the market had knocked out key options-related levels between 4.05-4.00, triggering automatic euro sell orders.  

"With the dollar rangebound elsewhere, the big hedge funds are keen to put their money to work in high yield emerging market currencies, in particular the zloty, Brazilian real and Mexican peso," the analyst said.   


By 1007 GMT, the zloty traded at 3.9908 to the euro  from 4.0674 late
on Wednesday and at 3.0648 to the dollar        from 3.1095.
  

As widely expected, the U.S. Federal Reserve lifted key U.S. interest rates by 25 basis points to 2.5 percent, but kept to its line that monetary policy would be tightened at a measured pace.  

Analysts said the Fed move would do little to erode the attractiveness of high yield currencies, with the focus now shifting to Friday's U.S. jobs report for the latest clue on the rate outlook.  

Signs of a more dovish rate outlook in Poland were said to inspire strong demand at a domestic bond auction on Wednesday, further buoying the currency.  

"Demand at the bond auction was more locally driven, with the speculation the central bank is moving to more expansionary monetary policy stance providing support to the bond market," said Caio Natividade, emerging markets strategist at Deutsche Bank.  

Natividade added that yield erosion was unlikely to become a factor undermining the zloty anytime soon, with interest rates not seen coming down until the second half of the year.  

The Hungarian forint tracked zloty gains to hit its best levels against the euro in two months around 244 .  

CZECH, SLOVAK CROWNS BUOYANT  

The soaring run enjoyed by the Czech and Slovak crowns so far this year extended on Thursday, with the Czech currency setting its best levels since September 2002 under 30 per euro and the Slovak hitting record highs around 38 per euro.  

Strong foreign investment inflows, rather than high yields, have been the driving force behind the rallies in both currencies, though the threat of central bank action to guard against excessive strength is ever present in both.  

Slovak Finance Minister Ivan Miklos said on Wednesday the crown rise was dangerous for the economy, underlining the risk of further crown-selling intervention from the central bank.  

"Strong economic and fiscal fundamentals, coupled with highly positive market sentiment towards the region should sustain the appreciation pressure," said analysts at BNP Paribas in a research note.  

"We expect, however, the central bank to step in with direct intervention once euro/Slovak crown breaks below 38.0."  

The Slovak crown was a touch firmer at 38.03 per euro , with the Czech crown at 29.99 .

title: Emerging  FX -Markets becalmed pre-Fed, Slovak crown nudges down.
text:
LONDON, Feb 2 (Reuters) - Emerging market currencies were broadly calm on Wednesday awaiting the outcome of the U.S. Federal Reserve monetary policy meeting later on, though the Slovak crown dipped on wariness over potential intervention.  

A further 25 basis point hike from the Fed is seen as fully priced in, with focus likely to be on the accompanying statement for any sign of a shift in the measured pace of tightening stance.  

"Everyone is expecting a 25 basis point hike, it's the language that really matters and there's nothing to suggest a shift away from this measured pace," said Dwyfor Evans, emerging markets analyst at Bank of America.  

"If that's the case, it's unlikely to have any impact on the high yielders, they should be able to carry on plugging away strongly."  

Euro/dollar nudged firmer ahead of the decision, expected at 1915 GMT, lending some support to the South African rand which tends to track the rate closely.  

By 1054 GMT, the rand was bid at 6.01 per dollar , off intra-day peaks around 5.9825.  

The Turkish lira edged up, continuing its strong run following the European Union's decision late last year to allow Turkey to begin entry negotiations in October.  

Underlining Turkey's increasing attractiveness, a consultant to Calpers, the biggest U.S. pension fund, said on Wednesday Turkey was now eligible to join the fund's list of emerging markets for investment.  

The lira traded at 1.3265 to the dollar on the interbank market , from 1.3275 at Tuesday's close.  

SLOVAK CROWN DIPS  

The Slovak crown eased off record highs against the euro with the market wary of the risk of central bank intervention to weaken it.  

The bank intervened indirectly on Tuesday by flooding the repo market with crown liquidity. It rejected all bids totalling 116.107 billion crowns at a weekly repo tender.  

"It's another signal they're opposed to rapid appreciation of the crown and people are perhaps also taking a breather with the market approaching a round number (38 per euro)," said Lucy Bethell, emerging markets analyst at Royal Bank of Scotland.  

The crown was marginally down at 38.09 per euro .  

Bethell added investors would still be happy to sell into euro rallies on the view the central bank can only really slow the pace of gains. Foreign investment inflows into the country also show no sign of slowing.  

Slovakia earlier this week announced plans to offer incentives to a Ford Motor Co. (F.N) venture to invest 345 million euros on a new gearbox plant in the country and also hopes to attract 500 million euros worth of fresh investment from South Korea.  

The Polish zloty showed little negative reaction to the likely scolding Poland will receive from the European Commission later today for insufficient progress on fiscal reform.  

In an assessment of Poland's "convergence plan", obtained by Reuters on Tuesday, the EU executive will say the country is unlikely to reach its target of lowering the budget gap below the EU's three percent of GDP limit in 2007.  

"Despite the criticisms of (Economy Minister Jerzy) Hausner's fiscal reform plans, he has still got a lot through," said Evans at BoA.  

"I'd say Poland is still a low level risk. There should be a sufficient level of reform done by the new government, and fiscal revenues should be pretty robust."   


The zloty traded at 4.0518 to the euro  from 4.0508 and at 3.1030 to
the dollar        from 3.1115.

title: Emerging  FX -Turkey acts to curb lira, new high for Slovak crown.
text:
LONDON, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Further strengthening in emerging European currencies triggered direct intervention in Turkey and raised the prospect of similar action in Slovakia on Thursday, while the Czech crown calmed ahead of an interest rate decision.  

The Turkish central bank said it bought dollars for lira to curb exchange rate volatility, in its first market intervention since February 2004.  

The new lira has risen to near 10 month highs following the European Union's decision in late December to allow Turkey to start entry talks in October, raising expectations of a surge in foreign investment inflows.  

By 1041 GMT, the new lira was at 1.3440 per dollar in interbank trade , down from pre-intervention highs around 1.3215. Turkish banking sources said the central bank had bought around 150-200 million dollars on the market.  

"It's probably a combination of the size of flows coming into the bond market and the extent of the lira move that has triggered the intervention," said Lucy Bethell, emerging markets analyst at RBS Financial Markets.  

"People had been getting increasingly short (of dollars), but the question now is whether they'll take it as cue to book profits, or an opportunity for better entry levels.  

"Sentiment is so strong on Turkey at the moment that at some point I'd expect people to get back in."  

Foreign trade minister Kursad Tuzmen said he hoped the lira would fall to 1.5-1.6 per dollar. Its strength has contributed to large trade and current account deficits.  

NEW HIGHS FOR SLOVAK CROWN  

Dealers are also on intervention red alert in Slovakia after investors' ongoing enthusiasm for the country pushed the crown to an all-time high against the euro on Thursday.  

The crown was flat percent at 38.44 per euro, having briefly touched a fresh high earlier at 38.376 .  

The Slovak central bank has tried to stem the crown's rise since mid-2003, intervening twice in the last month to keep the unit above 38.50 per euro, but said it had no comment on the latest move.  

The bank could cut rates at its monthly interest rate meeting on Friday, though further intervention is seen as more likely given the crown has grown increasingly immune to rate cuts following a 200 basis point loosening to 4.0 percent last year.  

Even that is unlikely to reverse the crown's uptrend.  

"If you believe the central bank will intervene most people would believe that any setback in the currency would be rather small and temporary," Barclays Capital emerging markets analyst Jeff Gable said. The Czech crown dipped from Wednesday's 28-month highs to trade around 30.12 per euro ahead of an interest rate decision.  

The central bank is widely expected to hold rates steady at 2.5 percent and market watchers will focus on any comments about currency strength arising from an afternoon monetary policy news conference.  

The crown has risen almost 10 percent in the past 12 months, most recently boosted by speculation about the sale of state-owned phone group Cesky Telekom (SPTTsp.PR) for an estimated $3 billion.  

Further evidence of a benign inflation environment in South Africa came from December producer price numbers, with the annual rate well below expectations at 1.9 percent, down from 2.5 percent in November.  

The news had little impact on the rand, which found good support from the buoyant tone across emerging markets. It traded virtually flat around 5.93 per dollar .  

The Romanian leu eased about three quarters of a percent against the euro, weighed by Prime Minister Calin Tariceanu's comment there might be a delay to plans to allow foreigners access to leu deposits from April, following talks with the IMF.  

Analysts said the Fund might call for a delay due to the risk the move triggers a wave of speculative capital, complicating the central bank's task of curbing inflation.  

The leu was down 0.73 percent at 28,938 per euro .

title: UPDATE 2- Slovak  cbank signals may favour crown  intervention .
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 18 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) signalled on Tuesday it is likely to use direct intervention rather than interest rate cuts to stem the pace of crown firming and keep the country's euro adoption goal on track.  

The NBS has intervened repeatedly in the foreign exchange market to slow the crown's rise to record highs against the euro. It has also slashed interest rates in its fight to deter speculative capital.  

But NBS Vice-Governor Elena Kohutikova told a meeting of corporate leaders that the country's higher interest rates compared with major markets were no longer the driving factor for the crown, with inflows now attracted by expectations of future crown firming.  

"We are reacting to exchange rate developments and we will continue reacting in the future," Kohutikova said.  

"We are not against a gradual appreciation, but we are against a scenario that the exchange rate is defined by short term capital rather than the economy."  

The crown closed at 38.630/680 versus the euro , its main reference unit, on Tuesday, a touch weaker than the 38.500 level where the NBS intervened last week, buying euros to flood the market with crowns.  

"The central bank is beginning to feel that (crown firming) is not about interest rate differential and this suggests that it would prefer interventions rather than rate cuts to influence the crown," said ING Bank Chief Economist Jan Toth.  

Toth added he expected the crown to firm at a slower pace than in 2004, predicting a four percent rise this year after a six percent jump last year.  

Several economists have criticised the NBS for managing the exchange rate too tightly at the time when its monetary policy switched to inflation targeting as of 2005.  

But Kohutikova said the central bank's policy was designed to ensure the smooth fulfilment of euro adoption criteria.  

"We want the exchange rate to develop in a way that can be backed up by the economy so that it does not bring danger to inflation criterion as well as the ERM-2 (currency fluctuation) criterion," she said.  

The Slovak convergence programme expects the country to meet all euro adoption criteria by end-2007 so the new EU member can adopt the single currency at start of 2009.
