title: UPDATE 2- Slovak  cbank to  intervene  against crown if CPI good.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 17 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said on Monday it may use interventions to slow the crown's rise if such action did not endanger its inflation goal, and analysts said the warning signalled a continued fight against currency firming.  

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) has intervened repeatedly in the foreign exchange market over the past year to slow the crown's rise to record highs against the euro, sparked by an outlook for strong investment inflows.  

Several economists have criticised the NBS for managing the exchange rate too tightly at the time when its monetary policy switched to inflation targeting as of 2005.  

But NBS board member Martin Barto dismissed such criticism of policy inconsistency in remarks to reporters in parliament.  

"You can use interventions but you have to be sure that the subsequent monetary policy easing will not endanger your inflation target," Barto said.  

"And if the (inflation) development is even better than expectations, then there is no problem."  

The NBS has described the currency rise as too fast compared with improvement in economic fundamentals, such as productivity growth, and said that such a sharp firming may have hurt the economy in the longer term.  

Barto's remarks followed comments by central bank governor Ivan Sramko, who said last week the NBS would use all tools to counter unjustifiably quick crown firming. The latest comments signalled more interventions were in the pipeline.  

"Foreign exchange interventions will continue, until a point where the NBS calculates that it could jeopardise its inflation goals," said CSOB Bank analyst Marek Gabris.  

PAUSE FOR RATE CUTS?  

In addition to forex interventions, the central bank also cut interest rates by a total of 200 basis points last year to make the crown less attractive for speculators taking advantage of higher rates compared with major markets.  

Slovakia posted better than expected inflation data in December 2004, which some analysts said could provide an argument for more monetary policy easing if the central bank needed to use the cost of money as a tool to curb crown rise.  

However, when asked if December inflation opened room for more interest rate cuts, Barto said: "We need to see what happens in the first months of this year. I would not draw major conclusions (from December data)."  

Data released on Friday showed a headline inflation rate of 5.9 percent in December, near the lower end of the central bank's target range of 5.7-7.0 percent.  

The Slovak crown gained more than six percent to the euro last year despite central bank attempts to halt the rise and hit a record high of 38.500 last week.  

The currency closed at 38.610/630 to the euro on Monday, only slightly weaker from Friday's 38.568/618.  

Dealers said the market will become more sensitive when the crown moves close to its all time highs again because of fears of new central bank intervention, but a majority of players expects the unit to appreciate throughout the year.  

"The market can now easier absorb interventions than one or two years ago. The NBS will have to act repeatedly to slow the (firming) trend," said Tatra Banka dealer Boris Somorovsky.

title: Emerging  FX -Zloty tracks bonds lower, Slovak crown edges up.
text:
LONDON, Jan 13 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty eased in line with a weaker tone on the domestic bond market on Thursday, while the Slovak crown got only a minor boost from a credit rating upgrade the previous session.  

Dealers said jitters crept into the Polish fixed income market after reported comments from central banker Halina Wasilewska-Trenkner that interest rate cuts in 2005 looked unlikely.  

"Local players had got over long at the short-end of the interest rate curve, expecting a cut. These comments triggered a sell off in local debt, which is feeding into zloty," said one London trader.  

The zloty spiked down to lows around 4.0915 per euro , before recovering to trade at 4.0818 by 1103 GMT.  

"Euro/dollar is up and down, there's no clear trend there, so people are not putting much money to work in the zloty. When they do they're getting in and out quickly, which creates volatility," the trader said.  

He added the sharp moves seen on Thursday were not yet indicative of a reversal in the zloty's bullish trend: "Unless we cross 4.20, the move shouldn't be that much worry."  

The Turkish lira capitalised on a broadly weaker dollar tone following Wednesday's news of a record United States trade deficit in November, firming over one percent against the dollar in interbank trade.  

Investors remain bullish on Turkish markets following last month's decision by European Union leaders to grant Turkey a date to begin accession talks.  

The lira traded at 1.3550 to the dollar in interbank trade , from 1.3760 at Wednesday's close.  

SLOVAK CROWN EDGES UP  

The Slovak crown nudged higher against the euro on Thursday to trade around 38.6 , with more good news on the country's investment outlook coming from a Moody's ratings upgrade the previous session.  

Moody's lifted Slovakia's long-term foreign currency debt ceilings to "A2" from "A3", citing the government's solid progress on structural reforms and an improving medium-to-long-term fiscal outlook.  

Analysts said the upgrade was a mild positive, with the crown's upward path seen entrenched by strong foreign investment inflows, even with the threat of central bank intervention against the currency still hanging over the market.  

"It's adding to the positive sentiment but I don't think this is the determining factor," said Jeff Gable, senior strategist at Barclays Capital.  

The Slovak central bank intervened on Monday after the crown surged to record highs against the euro at 38.50.  

"In trying to take a view on Slovakia, what's most important presently is just how serious the Central Bank is at leaning against appreciation pressure and to gauge what pace of appreciation they consider acceptable," said Gable.  

"We think the direction of the Slovak crown on a weekly basis is pretty clean - it's going to go stronger," Gable said. The Czech crown eased slightly after Czech current account data showed a deficit of 6.05 billion crowns ($262.6 million) in November, nearly the double the consensus market forecast of 3.2 billion crowns, though down from 12.94 billion in October.  

Adding to the softer tone was central bank board member Jan Frait's comment on Wednesday that there was little room for further crown appreciation against the euro and dollar based on economic fundamentals.  

Frait also said in a Reuters interview that interest rates may stay low for some time to come to shield the EU newcomer's very open economy from any possible fallout from weaker growth abroad. Key rates are at 2.5 percent.  

"With interest rates being so slow, I think the case for significant crown appreciation from where we are now is a difficult one to make," Gable said.  

The Czech crown traded at 30.36 against the euro .

title: ANALYSIS- Slovak intervention  dips make good crown buy points.
text:
PRAGUE, Jan 11 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank may pull out all the stops to stem a firming crown, but strong investment flows and economic growth in the new EU member make any dips on a good time to jump into the currency, analysts said.  

The central bank bought 100-250 million euros from the market on Monday, according to traders' estimates, in the latest intervention against what it calls the excessive pace of firming, mostly made on foreign direct investment inflows.  

The action was the first under new chief Ivan Sramko, who took over this month from outgoing Marian Jusko, and suggested the bank was mostly sticking to the intervention course seen throughout last year although analysts said the stance against the crown may become a little softer.  

A strong economy, growing at 5.3 percent in the third quarter, and the FDI makes the crown a safe bet over the longer term, and any dip versus the euro creates a good entry level for positions in the currency, analysts said.  

Morgan Stanley emerging markets analyst Oliver Weeks said the country's inflation targets for 2006-2007 of 2.5 and 2.0 percent were the toughest in the region and implied a tight monetary stance, which could mean a more relaxed approach to the crown by the central bank.  

"While the new Bank Board and Governor will not want to encourage FX speculation by a clear shift in policy we see room for a gradually increasing tolerance of steady crown appreciation," he said.  

The latest intervention came when the crown hit an all-time high of 38.500 to the euro , prompting the central bank into action, knocking it back to 38.640 on Tuesday, still more than six percent up since the start of 2004.  

A little softer stance on further firming would give further support to long-crown trades.  

This view was also shared by Ceska Sporitelna analyst Miroslav Plojhar.  

"The interventions they have been doing are a way how to jump into the crown," he said.  

"There already is some tolerance to crown firming... Maybe it is higher now that Jusko has gone, but this is not to mean they would just let the crown be."  

The Slovak drive to slash inflation is guided by their aim of joining the euro zone in 2009. The target this year is 3.0-4.0 percent, from 6.3 percent reported in November.  

Therefore, the central bank is unlikely to slash interest rates much further from the current four percent, a 200 basis points worth of cuts over the past year.  

SOME RESISTANCE NEEDED  

Slovakia became a darling of foreign investors due to labour market and tax reforms as well as government investment aid.  

Total net FDI in the first nine months last year reached 34.3 billion crowns and the financial account surplus was 56.6 billion, versus current account gap of 27.7 billion.  

Martin Blum, head of European emerging markets research at HVB in Vienna said the central bank was essentially doing a good job given the narrow scope of options amid the balance of payments pressure and with interest rates already low.  

"You could envisage a scenario whereby if the national bank failed to intervene on the FX market at all, you would really have euro/Slovak accelerating its movement south," he said, adding the banks still favoured long crown positions.  

"It would potentially push inflation down too fast and more importantly, it would risk future reversal which is not something the national bank would want to deal with either."  

Blum added the central bank would likely allow something like the same pace of appreciation as seen in 2004. The central bank itself has said real firming of 2-3 percent per year looked acceptable.  

"It is reasonable to use these FX interventions as a device to slow the appreciation of the crown which is what they were trying to do in 2004 as well, and I think they are doing basically the most sensible thing in quite a constrained situation," said Blum. - Additional reporting by Jan Korselt.

title: UPDATE 1-Emerging  FX -Lira edges up after rate cut.
text:
LONDON, Jan 11 (Reuters) - The Turkish lira nudged higher after a surprise interest rate cut on Tuesday, while the Slovak crown was flat after Monday's intervention from the central bank to weaken it.  

Turkey's central bank cut both its overnight borrowing rate and overnight lending rate by one percent to 17 percent and 21 percent respectively.  

The timing of the move took analysts by surprise, coming hard on the heels of a two percent cut on Dec. 20 following the European Union's decision to grant Turkey a date to begin entry talks, though some said there had been scope for further easing.  

"Inflation expectations are very close to end-year expectations and there was also a tightening impact coming from the strengthening of the lira. There were all the key ingredients to have a rate cut," said Sonal Desai, senior emerging markets economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Wasserstein in Milan  

"It'll have a positive impact on Turkish markets, but the impact on the lira is close to zero," she added.  

The move triggered a half percentage point fall in benchmark Turkish bond yields and also boosted Istanbul's main share index, though the lira ticked only modestly higher.  

By 1345 GMT, the lira traded at 1.3785 to the dollar on the interbank market from 1.3850 at Monday's close.  

The prospect of further inflows into Turkish bonds, on expectations of more easing to come, are seen offsetting the potential negative effect of lower returns on long lira positions.  

SLOVAK CROWN STEADIES AFTER INTERVENTION

The Slovak crown crept higher on Tuesday, resuming its upward path after central bank intervened to weaken it on Monday.  

The bank stepped in after the crown surged to record highs against the euro around 38.5 early on Monday , triggering a move back to 38.74 initially, before the crown recovered some ground.  

Finance Minister Ivan Miklos backed the central bank's stance on Tuesday, saying the crown's firming was too strong and could hurt the new EU members' economy, in comments reported by a domestic news agency.  

Even so, most analysts continue to see the central bank fighting an unstoppable strengthening trend in the Slovak currency, driven by strong foreign investment inflows.  

Carlos Teixeira, analyst at Goldman Sachs, said the Slovaks' latest intervention was no surprise.  

"Their action may stem appreciation temporarily, as last happened in December, but we expect the currency to resume its strengthening," Teixeira said in a research note.  

"This will help the central bank meet its inflation target and leaves the door open to further rate cuts."  

A bigger than expected November trade gap held up the crown's rise only briefly, with the deficit widening to 3.953 billion crowns ($134.5 million), above a market consensus forecast of 2.7 billion.  

The crown was up 0.16 percent on the session at 38.63 per euro.

title: UPDATE 2- Slovak  cbank  intervenes  again to slow crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 10 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) on Monday continued its crusade against the record rise of the crown, intervening on the market to weaken the currency after it hit record highs against the euro.  

The central bank has been fighting against what it sees as excessive crown appreciation for more than a year, saying it could hurt the new EU member's economy.  

On Monday the NBS showed its policy had not changed despite the Jan. 1 appointment of Ivan Sramko as the new governor.  

According to dealers the NBS started to intervene against the crown late in the session when it hit 38.510 per euro , and sold the currency up to 38.750 per euro after it traded near record highs of 38.500 earlier in the session.  

"I can confirm we are intervening. The reason remains the same - too rapid a firming of the crown, which is not in line with economic fundamentals," central bank spokesman Igor Barat told Reuters.  

The Slovak unit lost more than 0.5 percent to the euro following the NBS move to close at 38.696/746 per euro.  

The monetary body last intervened to dent firming pressure on the crown in December when the currency jumped to 38.530 per euro following a two-month rally fuelled by encouraging economic data, expectations of large FDI inflows and a rating upgrade.  

Sramko took over stewardship of the central bank after Marian Jusko's six-year term ended on Dec. 31 pledging to continue to fight against a rapidly rising currency.  

The crown has been firming rapidly over the past year, gaining more than six percent to the euro despite central bank attempts to halt its rise with direct and off-market interventions, hefty rate cuts and liquidity-draining tenders.  

The NBS has said it does not oppose gradual crown firming based on improving productivity, and it expects a stronger crown in the longer term, but it wanted to battle hot-money inflows.  

Analysts had expected the central bank to soften somewhat its stiff opposition to the strong crown this year after it said last month it would turn its focus to inflation-targeting from managing the exchange rate moves.  

Traders said the central bank's action would have only a temporary impact on the market's bullish mood as softer levels usually attract more crown buying.  

"There is still high demand for crowns, so we do not expect it to weaken significantly after this intervention," said VUB Bank dealer Laco Benedek.  

Market watchers expected the crown would probably settle above 38.600 per euro in the coming days, saying it was unlikely to retreat above a strongly defended level of 38.800 per euro.  

They said, however, the crown would probably resume firming in the coming weeks, adding the central bank might try to curb its advance again if it nears its record highs too quickly.  

The central bank was estimated to have bought foreign currencies worth 100-150 million euros in Monday's interventions, down from estimated 400-500 million in December.

title: INTERVIEW-UPDATE 1- Slovak  cbank - crown  interventions  successful.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Jan 1 (Reuters) - Slovak central bank Governor Ivan Sramko said on Saturday that recent interventions to halt the sharp rise of the crown currency against the euro were successful.  

He also told Reuters after being officially approved as the new central bank governor by the president that further actions to stem the crown's rise are on the cards if the currency firms out of line with economic developments.  

"The basic goal we had with the interventions was to prevent the crown from excessive firming ... and this was met," he said in a brief interview after the swearing in ceremony, noting that a two to three percent real annual rise in the crown was realistic.  

"We will continue to monitor the crown and as we have said (after December's monetary policy meeting), if the firming is not in line with economic developments, we will use all tools to correct it," he added.  

The Slovak crown closed 38.723/773 to the euro on Friday, ending the year more than six percent stronger helped by a series of positive economic data and FDI news, which fuelled its late-year charge.  

The central bank intervened to counter the crown's strength last week, after the currency jumped to an all-time high of 38.530 per euro following its two-month rally.  

But the central bank did not move to ease interest rates at its final policy meeting of the year in December, and Sramko said current settings are correct.  

"We think that according to our latest decision, the monetary policy settings are good and are in line with conditions in the Slovak economy," he said.  

Analysts expect the bank to shift its focus in 2005 to inflation targeting from correcting the exchange rate moves after the recent changes to its policy-making board including replacement of the central bank governor Marian Jusko, whose term ended on Dec. 31.  

Dealers said the crown would probably pick up steam again later in January to wage a fresh attack on record highs to the euro, adding it might firm to levels of around 38.0 per euro by the end of the first quarter.

BRATISLAVA, Dec 23 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank said it had intervened directly on the foreign exchange market for a second day in a row on Thursday, and warned it would continue fighting to prevent the crown appreciating too quickly.   

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) has been battling against what it calls unjustified crown firming for more than a year, saying it could hurt the new EU member's economy.   

"We will continue to assess development of the crown's exchange rate, and if the dynamics of appreciation do not correspond to development of the economy, we will be ready to use monetary tools to correct such undesired movements," central bank spokesman Igor Barat told Reuters.   

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) started to intervene against the crown on Wednesday when the unit traded near its all-time highs at 38.550 per euro.   

Traders said the NBS stepped into the market on Thursday when the crown was at around 38.700 per euro.   

This week's intervention is the first since July, when the central bank bought foreign currencies worth a combined 766 million euros.   

The crown has risen rapidly against the euro this year, hitting a record high of 38.530 on Monday to notch up a 6.2 percent gain since January.   

The central bank has said it does not oppose gradual crown firming based on improving productivity, and it expects a stronger crown in the longer term, but the monetary body wants to continue fighting inflows of speculative capital.   

Apart from direct interventions, the central bank has also cut its main interest rates by a total of 200 basis points this year to make the crown less attractive for speculators who seek higher rates compared with major markets.   

The crown weakened to around 38.850-880 per euro after Thursday's intervention, from 38.700, easing slightly less compared with the reaction in the previous session.   

Traders said a major crown fall was unlikely in the near future as weaker levels attracted more crown buying from both domestic and foreign banks, which expect the unit to continue appreciating next year.

title: Emerging  FX -Rand and lira test highs -  Slovak  cbank  intervenes .
text:
LONDON, Dec 23 (Reuters) - High-yield emerging market currencies firmed against a broadly weak dollar on Thursday, with the rand and lira both testing fresh highs while the Slovak central bank intervened to weaken the crown for a second day.  

The euro rose to within a quarter-cent of record highs against the U.S. currency in technically-driven trade as dealers wound down for the year-end holiday period.  

South Africa's rand coined a new six-year high of 5.6110 per dollar late on Wednesday and hovered close to that mark in light trade on Thursday. By 1100 GMT, it had eased a shade to trade at 5.6238 .  

"The rand will probably go marginally weaker from here, but I don't see a major sell off," said Gregory Kronsten, emerging markets analyst at WestLB.  

Kronsten added that South Africa's combination of high interest rates and a rising currency had proved a strong enticement to long-term investors, helping fuel rand gains of over 18 percent against the dollar in 2004.  

November producer price data did little to change a growing view among analysts that key interest rates may now have bottomed out at 7.5 percent.  

South African November producer prices rose at an annual rate of 2.5 percent, up from 1.9 percent the previous month, and followed a faster-than-expected 4.6 percent year-on-year rise in the November CPIX indicator, released on Wednesday.  

"Some people think that because the central bank didn't cut in December, they'll cut in February, but I don't expect any cooling in domestic demand by then," said Kronsten.  

"My own view is that easing has come to an end and that rates could go up a bit towards the end of next year."  

A broadly weaker dollar helped the Turkish lira firm to its highest level since May, continuing its strong run following last Friday's decision by European Union leaders to let the country start talks on Oct. 3 2005 to join to the bloc.  

The lira traded at 1,381,100 to the dollar on the interbank market from 1,390,000.  

SLOVAK C.BANK DENTS CROWN  

The Slovak central bank followed up Wednesday's intervention to weaken the crown by selling it again at weaker levels around 38.70 per euro .  

Its action moved the euro/crown rate up to 38.85 initially, though analysts are sceptical the central bank can do any more than slow the pace of crown gains such is the volume of foreign investment inflows into the country.  

The Polish zloty drifted down from late Wednesday's near-two-year high against the euro, hit after Finance Minister Miroslaw Gronicki appeared relaxed about the currency's charge higher this week.  

Gronicki said the move reflected year-end effects from low-volume trade, while analysts continue to see little on the near-term horizon to halt the Polish currency's bull run. "The bottom line is there's not a consensus in policy making circles that they want a weaker zloty," said Martin Blum, emerging markets analyst at HVB in Vienna.  

"The zloty has actually appreciated very little in real terms over the past five years and with the productivity gains seen in Poland it's still not overvalued. It's also helped bring down public debt-to-GDP levels and that helps explain Gronicki's comments."   


The zloty traded at 4.0851 to the euro  from 4.0793 late on Wednesday
and at 3.0365 to the dollar        from 3.0453.
  

Blum said the zloty could target further gains to 3.90 per euro in the first quarter of 2005.  

"As (the euro/zloty rate) moves further south we will have policymakers becoming more aggressive in talking about foreign exchange intervention.  

"But the headwind won't prevent further downside. There's a lot of inflows into emerging Europe funds, the political backdrop in Poland is OK, yields are still OK and there's also a generally favourable environment for emerging market currencies."

title: Emerging  FX - Slovak  crown falls on  intervention , rand firm.
text:
LONDON, Dec 22 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown dropped off record highs against the euro on Wednesday after intervention from the central bank, while the dollar's weak tone helped the South African rand hit fresh six-year highs.  

The Slovak central bank was seen stepping in around 38.55 crowns per euro prompting a retreat to 38.90, but the currency soon recovered some of the lost ground as foreign banks resumed buying.  

The bank had warned at its policy meeting the previous day it would take action if crown movements did not reflect economic fundamentals, though analysts said it was fighting against an unstoppable tide of inflows.  

"Markets are completely dead at this time of year so it's easy to move the rate around, but I don't think intervention will end up being successful," said Lars Christensen, emerging markets analyst at Danske Bank.  

"The central bank has been emphasising hot money flows, but the flows are real money. The reason the crown has gone so strong is that Slovakia has been pursuing the right economic policies.  

"They should be happy about that because it's putting a dampener on inflationary pressures."  

By 1038 GMT, the crown traded at 38.76 to the euro.  

Christensen said it seemed strange for the bank to intervene, just a day after revealing a switch to fixed inflation targeting.  

"It suggests they're pursuing two monetary policies, which is not really do-able."  

The bank's monetary programme for 2005-2008 set an end-2005 inflation target of 3.0-4.0 percent, down from the expected range of 5.7-7.0 percent for December 2004. Formerly, it had an implicit targeting system, when it only estimated price growth.  

"They should perhaps follow the Czech example of not intervening, but using interest rates to hit its inflation target."  

The rest of the central Europe region traded calmly with the Polish zloty hovering just under Tuesday's 22-month highs against the euro at around 4.10.  

RAND STEADY AFTER CPI  

The South African rand nudged to a fresh six-year high of 5.6505 per dollar in thin trade, showing little reaction to a faster-than-expected rise in inflation in November.  

South African November CPIX inflation rose at an annual pace of 4.6 percent, above a consensus forecast of 4.4 percent and up from 4.2 percent in October, going some way to justifying the central bank's decision to leave rates on hold earlier this month.  

"It was definitely higher than the market anticipated, but inflation could still start to dip as fuel price cuts start to feed through," said Razia Khan, chief Africa economist at Standard Chartered.  

"The number is not going to do much to change expectations on interest rates. If the rand remains strong, there could well be a rate cut in February."  

The rand was flat at 5.64 to the dollar .

title: UPDATE 2- Slovak  cbank  intervenes  to slow crown firming.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Dec 22 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened directly on the foreign exchange market on Wednesday, selling its currency as part of its long-lasting effort to prevent the rising crown from hurting the economy.   

The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) has been trying to rein in the crown for more than a year, saying the unit's advance is too quick and does not correspond to fundamentals in the new EU member's economy.   

"We maintain what we have stated for several times," central bank spokesman Igor Barat told Reuters. "The appreciation of the Slovak crown is too fast; the aim of the action was to slow down this movement."   

The crown has risen rapidly against the euro this year, hitting an all-time high of 38.530 to notch up a 6.2 percent gain since January.   

The unit was trading near record highs when the NBS entered the market on Wednesday, and the action briefly pulled the unit to 38.900 per euro. But the crown quickly rebounded and the bank intervened for a second time.   

Wednesday's intervention was the first such direct action since July when the central bank bought foreign currencies worth a combined 766 million euros.   

The central bank has said it does not oppose gradual crown firming based on improving productivity, but that it will continue to fight inflows of speculative capital.   

The NBS has cut rates by a total of 200 basis points this year to make the crown less attractive for speculators seeking higher yields than those on offer in major markets.   

Wednesday's intervention came a day after a meeting at which it left its key two-week repo ceiling at 4.00 percent.   

MORE FIRMING SEEN   

Analysts have long questioned the central bank's reasons for capping the crown's rise, saying the Slovak currency is gaining due to solid economic growth and rising flows of foreign direct investment.   

"We believe that the direct FX intervention will have only short-term impact as fundamentals and FDI inflow will support the currency in the course of 2005," Komercni Banka analysts said in market note. Bullish market sentiment was boosted further on Tuesday, when the central bank's monetary programme for 2005-2008 showed predictions of accelerating economic growth in the next three years.   

The central bank also said it would switch to inflation targetting from 2005, setting the end-year target at 3.0-4.0 percent, compared with this year's estimate of 5.7-7.0 percent headline price growth.   

The monetary body will target inflation of under 2.5 percent in 2006 and below 2.0 percent in 2007 and 2008, which analysts said were ambitious goals.   

Some economists have warned that the central bank will only achieve its long-term inflation goal, needed for euro adoption, with the help of a firming crown, and urged the bank to let the currency appreciate more freely.   

Slovakia plans to meet all criteria for joining the euro in 2007, so that it could adopt the single currency two years later.   

"The NBS will need strong currency to meet its inflation target. We therefore suggest clients to take advantage of FX intervention and buy SKK (crowns)," Komercni Banka said.

title: Slovakia - Factors To Watch on Dec 16.
text:

Outgoing Slovak central bank Governor Marian Jusko said he was in favour of intervening to stop the crown's rapid appreciation and would approve the use of any the bank's tools if proposed by the board.

The Slovak government nominated Martin Barto as a new central bank vice-governor, a former commercial banker who is expected to have a strong influence on monetary policy. Parliament is expected to vote in January on the nomination.

Slovak Economy Minister Pavol Rusko said he expected foreign investors to continue flocking to the new EU member country next year with FDI seen at least at the same pace as in 2004. The Slovak unit of Canada's Kouei Industries said on Wednesday, it planned to invest 22.5 million euros to build tyre and plastics recycling plants in central Slovakia.  

JOBLESS RATE DROPS TO 12.6 PCT IN NOV  

Slovakia's unemployment rate fell for the tenth consecutive month in November, easing to 12.58 percent from 12.72 percent in the previous month.

title: Slovakia - Factors To Watch on August 2.
text:
BRATISLAVA, Aug 2 (Reuters) - Here are news stories, press reports and events to watch which may affect Slovak financial markets on Monday:  

FINMIN TO RELEASE JAN-JULY STATE BUDGET DATA  

The finance ministry will release the state budget data for the January-July period. Slovakia's state budget showed a deficit of 12.455 billion crowns in the first six months of this year. The 2004 state budget was approved with a ceiling for the deficit of 78.495 billion crowns.  

C.BANK TO AUCTION 15-YR TREASURY BONDS  

The central bank will hold an auction of the third tranche of the 15-year, 5.30 percent treasury bonds on behalf of the finance ministry's debt and liquidity agency. The state sold 5.232 billion crowns worth of the paper at an average yield of 5.232 percent in the last tender on June 21. Total demand was 8.192 billion crowns.  

C.BANK TO RELEASE JAN-MAY C/A DATA  

The central bank is expected to release the current account data for the January-May period. The country's current account showed a surplus of 4.0 billion crowns in the first four months of the year.  

C.BANK LEAVES RATES ON HOLD  

The central bank held interest rates steady on Friday, but kept the market on its toes by signalling willingness to ease the costs of credit further in light of muted price pressures. The decision, which left the main two-week repo rate at 4.50 percent, was widely expected by the markets due to the crown currency's recent retreat to weaker levels.  

C.BANK REVEALS COVERT FX INTERVENTION IN JUNE  

The Slovak central bank bought 87 million euro through a direct foreign exchange deal in June, the bank said on Friday. The bank refrained from covert interventions against the strong crown in May and April, but bought foreign currencies worth a combined 277 million euro in the first three months of this year.  

STATE BATTLES TO MEET KIA LAND HANDOVER DEADLINE  

Slovakia may not be able to hand over on time a construction site for a one billion euro ($1.2 billion) car plant of South Korea's auto maker Kia Motors , the economy ministry said on Friday. The state has run into difficulty purchasing land for the Kia plant, which will be the new EU member's largest ever greenfield foreign project, as several landowners refused to accept the price offered by the state.  

C.BANK FOREX RESERVES DROP  

The Slovak central bank's foreign currency reserves fell to $13.321 billion in the week to July 28, from $13.530 billion one week earlier, the bank said on Friday.

title: Slovak crown eases, seen locked in narrow range.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 22 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown closed a
touch softer to the euro in quiet summer holiday trading on
Thursday, and dealers said a fresh impulse would be needed to
drive the unit out of its current narrow range.
    The crown has been hovering in a tight corridor of
39.800-39.900 to the euro for the past few days as the market
sought new reference levels following the central bank's heavy
intervention early last week.
    The Slovak unit firmed to 39.830 per euro early on Thursday
after a London-based bank started selling euros, but later
slipped to 39.870 on euro purchases by a local bank.
    Dealers said the crown, which hit a record high of 39.675
per euro earlier this month, should drift in its recent range in
the coming days in the absence of market-moving news.
    "The trading should be calm until next Friday, when the
central bank holds its monetary meeting. But there is nothing
special expected," said ING Bank dealer Jan Rafaj.
  


    All analysts surveyed by Reuters earlier in July expected
the central bank to stay on hold this month after it cut rates
by 50 basis points in June to dent the crown's firming
potential.
 
    The bank has eased credit costs by 150 basis points this
year to stop hot-money inflows from boosting the crown.
    However, policy makers recently resorted to direct crown
selling after the wave of rate cuts, off-market crown sales and
repo tenders failed to weaken the currency as hoped.
    But dealers said the bank would have no reason to consider
  

further market intervention if the crown, which is up 3.2  

percent to the euro this year, remains close to its current  

levels.  

The bank has been battling the rapid rise of the crown for  

months, saying its pace was too quick despite improving economic  

fundamentals.

title: UPDATE 1-Slovak cbank accepts all bids in 2-wk repo tender.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 20 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank (NBS) accepted all bids in a two-week repo tender on Tuesday, surprising analysts who expected it to leave the market drowning in liquidity to weaken the crown currency.  

The NBS said it drained 90.999 billion crowns ($2.8 billion) of surplus liquidity from the money market, at an average rate of 4.41 percent in the operation.  

The market had eyed the outcome of the repo tender to gauge the central bank's reaction to the crown's quick recovery from six-weeks lows of 40.050 per euro it touched last week following massive interventions.  

Recently the central bank has repeatedly rejected at least some bids to deter inflows of short-term capital, which is taking advantage of the interest rate differential with the euro zone. The NBS did not comment on the result of Tuesday's tender.  

The crown firmed to 39.801/851 per euro after the tender from the opening level of 39.845/895. Dealers said it was likely to test the key 39.800 per euro level in the coming days if the central bankers remain out of the market.  

"The crown firmed after the repo tender results. It seems that they (the central bank) accept that the crown could be a little stronger," said ING Bank dealer Jan Rafaj.  

Over the past week the central bank intervened heavily to knock the crown off its record high of 39.675 per euro.  

But the currency has since erased most of its losses as the the central bank quit the market saying it was satisfied with the intervention result.  

The Slovak unit, which is up 3.3 percent against the euro this year, has been firming sharply in the past months due to the country's solid economic performance and expectations of investment inflows from abroad.  

On Tuesday, the minimum rate was 4.20 percent, while the maximum accepted yield stood at 4.50 percent, matching the central bank's limit rate for two-week tenders.

title: Emerging  FX -Zloty holds firm pre vote, forint awaits data.
text:
LONDON, July 15 (Reuters) - The Polish zloty held firm close to 10-month highs against the euro on Thursday ahead of a key vote on pension reforms in parliament, while the Hungarian forint traded quietly ahead of key budget data.  

The zloty extended this week's strong gains on Wednesday after news of a jump in June consumer price inflation stoked rate hike expectations. The annual inflation rate hit 4.4 percent, above market forecasts and up from 3.4 percent in May. A calmer tone set in on Thursday with dealers looking ahead to a vote in parliament on Friday on pension reforms - a key pillar of the government's efforts to curb spending.  

"The pension reform vote will only be a factor if it fails, we think it's largely been priced in," said Tania Kotsos, currency analyst at Royal Bank of Canada.  

"The zloty is behaving as a carry trade, especially in the summer months with people happy just to hold their positions to pick up the yield."  

Analysts said the June CPI number increased the chances of a further rate hike in July to follow June's 50 basis point increase, though Monetary Policy Council member Halina Wasilewska-Trenkner said she expected price pressures to begin to ease in August.  

Kotsos said that on a technical basis, the zloty needed a decisive break under 4.4250 to open up levels of 4.40 and beyond.   


By 0915 GMT, the zloty traded at 4.43 to the euro  from 4.4395 and at
3.5870 to the dollar        from 3.5880.
  

FORINT EYES BUDGET DATA  

The Hungarian forint hovered around the 250 per euro level, with the market seen subdued ahead of final June and preliminary July budget data due at 1100 GMT.  

Analysts said the sacking of two finance ministry officials on Wednesday was perhaps an indicator of bad news to come, with the market already sceptical about the government's chances of hitting a 4.6 percent-of-GDP deficit target for 2004.  

"It is suspicious and could make things worse for the budget, but it's uncertain at this stage," said Caio Natividade, emerging markets currency analyst at Deutsche Bank.  

There has also been talk that the departure of Elemer Tertak, administrative state secretary with responsibility for the budget, and his deputy Akos Cseres, was simply a case of a personality clash with Finance Minister Tibor Draskovics and would have no bearing on Thursday's numbers.  

Natividade said that while there was downside risk in the forint, he still favoured this week's uptrend to remain intact: "As far as momentum is concerned, the market is going to 247.50."  

Speculation is also mounting that the central bank may take advantage of the forint's move to two-month highs against the euro this week to trim interest rates at its next policy meeting on Monday.  

Key rates are at a lofty 11.5 percent having been jacked up to deter outflows from the bond market and the forint.  

The forint traded was little changed at 249.55 to the euro .  

The Slovak crown held to narrow ranges around the 39.90 area against the euro with the market still nervous about the potential for further central bank intervention to weaken the currency.  

The Slovak May trade gap came in at a bigger-than-expected 2.1 billion crowns, but with some analysts expecting foreign direct investment inflows to outpace the current account deficit by a ratio of 3:1 this year, the crown uptrend is expected to remain intact.

title: UPDATE 1- Slovak  cbank says  FX intervention  changed trend.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 14 (Reuters) - Slovak central bank Governor Marian Jusko said on Wednesday he was satisfied with the outcome of intervention on the foreign exchange market over the past week designed to halt a rapid firming of the crown.   

The central bank started intervening on the forex market last Thursday in the first such direct action since May 2003, and it continued to sell crowns on Monday and Tuesday.   

The bank knocked the crown off its the all-time high of 39.675 per euro, pushing the unit to around 39.910 in late Wednesday trading.   

"I am satisfied with the outcome of interventions," Jusko told journalists after the regular government meeting.   

"There was a clear trend of excessive crown firming in the past few days and weeks and this tendency has been reversed," he added.   

The Slovak monetary body has been trying to slow crown appreciation for over a year, saying the firming has been too fast and could hurt the economy which entered the EU in May.   

Jusko said on Wednesday the central bank considered a wide range of issues when it decides on its policy moves.   

He said the possible negative impact of strong currency on exporters was one of the factors, but not necessarily the main reason behind the latest action against the crown. "In recent past, we have met with 15 representatives of industrial chambers. There was not a single voice that would want a strong crown. The voices ware rather contrary," Jusko said.   

The central bank did not disclose the amounts of foreign currencies it had bought from the market, but the market estimated the volume at 400-500 million euros.   

Despite the initial fall of the crown, the central bank met stiff opposition from foreign banks at around 40.000 per euro as investors appeared to believe that the Slovak currency had the potential to firm again.   

Analysts said the central bank might keep the crown off record highs for some time.   

But they predicted inflows of foreign capital to prevail in the long term due to Slovakia's good economic fundamentals, such as an improving trade balance, strong GDP growth and prospects of foreign direct investment projects.

title: Slovak  crown slides as cbank keeps  intervening .
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 13 (Reuters) - The Slovak crown ended
weaker on Tuesday, hit by the third wave of the central bank's
direct interventions aimed at undermining the currency's firming
potential, dealers said.
    The central bank stepped into the forex market on Tuesday
for the third time in less than a week, trying to weaken the
crown through a psychological level of 40.000 per euro.
 "The central bank started buying euros as soon as the crown
touched 39.900 (per euro) and it succeeded in sending it up to
40.035," said ING Bank dealer Jan Rafaj.
    Market watchers said the central bank might have bought
around 100 million euros on Tuesday, less than the 200 million
it was estimated to have bought in each of the previous
intervention rounds on Monday and Thursday.
    Dealers said the central bank was probably aiming to push
the crown beyond the next strong level of 40.100 per euro,
hoping that it would trigger a wave of stop-loss orders.
  


    "I think that 40.100 (per euro) level will be defended very
strongly and that the central bank will not push the crown
through it alone," Rafaj said.
    The central bank started to intervene on the forex market
after interest rate cuts and money market tools failed to
discourage foreign capital inflows and reverse crown firming.
    Traders said the crown could float in a range of
39.900-40.050 per euro in the coming days, but added that
investors would keep testing the central bank's determination to
fight market flows with direct interventions.
    Analysts have said the central bank's attempts to stop the
surging crown would have only a temporary impact as the
country's sound economic performance was likely to keep
attracting foreign investors.

title: UPDATE 1- Slovak  c.bank  intervenes  again to weaken crown.
text:
BRATISLAVA, July 13 (Reuters) - The Slovak central bank intervened on the foreign exchange market for the second consecutive day on Tuesday, continuing its fight against crown firming.   

Central bank spokesman Igor Barat confirmed Tuesday's intervention, but he declined to give any details about the action.   

The central bank started selling crowns directly on the market on Thursday last week, saying it viewed the currency's firming since the beginning of the year as too quick.   

Traders said the central bank entered the market on Tuesday when the crown traded near 39.900 per euro, which is a weaker level compared with the previous intervention rounds.   

"This time, it started when it looked that the crown could go under 39.900 (per euro)... It seems they are trying to move the crown above 40.000," one Bratislava-based dealer said.   

This month's intervention is the first direct action on the market since May 2003, but the Slovak central bank has been fighting against crown firming for more than a year.   

It has used interest rate cuts and money market instruments to discourage inflows of foreign capital, saying that that gains which are too sharp could hurt the small and open economy that joined the European Union in May.   

Tuesday's intervention pushed the Slovak unit to 40.030 per euro. The crown hit an all-time high of 39.675 per euro last week, which was around 3.7 percent up from the beginning of the year.   

The central bank considers the crown's rally to be fuelled by inflows of speculative capital, but many analysts say foreign investors are attracted mainly by Slovakia's good economic fundamentals. The central bank has said there will be some room for crown firming in the long term, but it added that it would continue using its monetary arsenal to prevent sharp market moves.
